articles.title: The Marker Drift Problem: Measuring LLM-Assisted Writing with Unstable Lexical Indicators
articles.authors: Serhii Nazarovets
articles.abstract: Lexical markers are increasingly used to estimate the prevalence of large language model (LLM)-assisted writing across large publication corpora. However, longitudinal applications of this approach rely on an important assumption: that the relationship between these markers and LLM use remains sufficiently stable over time. Recent research suggests that once publicly identified, individual markers may lose their diagnostic value due to adaptation by users and the evolution of language models. Furthermore, lexical markers may reflect not only LLM use, but also linguistic competence, AI-assisted editing, and broader forms of stylistic convergence. This paper introduces the Marker Drift Problem to describe a methodological challenge in which indicators change alongside the phenomenon they are intended to measure. Marker drift raises questions about temporal comparability, as observed changes in marker prevalence may reflect changes in LLM use, changes in the indicators themselves, or both. Without attention to the temporal stability and construct validity of lexical indicators, increasingly precise estimates of LLM-assisted writing may be based on unstable measurement instruments.

articles_hidden.title: Automatic Prompt Optimization for Policy Documents Classification
articles_hidden.authors: Hanif Sajid
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, I leverage three automatic prompt optimization (APO) algorithms to search for optimal prompts that enable large language models to classify policy documents accurately, without requiring task-specific training data. I evaluate the performance of these optimized prompts using OpenAI’s GPT-4o-mini model, comparing them against prompts created by domain experts as a baseline. Experimental results show that all three algorithms significantly outperform the baseline. Among the algorithms, APE, which induces simple prompts from input-output example pairs, significantly outperforms GRIPS and performs comparably to ProTeGi. Additionally, ProTeGi demonstrates similar performance to GRIPS. However, neither the optimized prompts nor the human-designed ones achieve a research-grade performance (defined as an F1-score of 70%) with the GPT-4o-mini model. To reach research-grade performance in policy document classification using APO methods, future work could explore the use of more powerful models, hybrid APO systems, cross-model evaluations, and inference-time enhancements.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: The Behavioral Cost of Memory-Driven Attentional Capture: Eye-Movement Evidence for Post-Capture Attentional Dwell
articles.authors: Keyang Liu; Chen Wang; Qiang Liu
articles.abstract: During visual search, task-irrelevant distractors matching current visual working memory representations can capture attention, but less is known about how their influence continues after capture. Using a memory–search dual-task paradigm with eye tracking, we distinguished initial oculomotor selection from processing after distractor fixation and examined their associations with working memory capacity (WMC). Memory-matching distractors produced longer overall search RTs and were more likely than neutral distractors to receive the first fixation. When the critical distractor was not fixated, memory matching produced no reliable additional search-time cost. When it was fixated, however, memory matching prolonged conditional dwell time. WMC showed no clear association with the memory-matching effect on first fixation, whereas higher WMC was associated with less additional post-capture dwell. These findings indicate that the influence of memory matching can persist after attentional selection. The behavioral cost of memory-driven distraction may therefore reflect not only whether a distractor is selected, but also how processing unfolds after selection, with WMC-related differences more clearly expressed in post-capture processing than in initial oculomotor selection.

articles.title: Perceptibility of Error Outcomes Shapes the Direction of Post-Error Adjustment: Evidence From 6.7 Million Moves in Online Chess
articles.authors: Yunjeong Jeong; Younggyu Kim
articles.abstract: Whether post-error slowing requires noticing the error is unresolved, because in laboratory tasks errors and the noticing of them covary. Chess separates them: engine evaluation identifies errors that leave no trace on the board, whereas material loss is visible. Analysing 1.06 million event observations from 222,099 games played by 2,014 players, we found that the sign of the adjustment reversed with the visibility of the outcome. Blunders that left material intact were followed by slower moves (+0.154 within-person SD), whereas the two conditions in which material disappeared were followed by faster ones (-0.493, -0.631). The conditions differed by 0.65 SD in all five rating tiers, and neither error magnitude nor the change in legal move count accounted for this. Reliability approached .70 for material loss but was near zero for blunders. Post-error adjustment followed two patterns, divided by whether the outcome was visible.

articles.title: Knowledge: The Real Durable Skill What the Skills Conversation Lost, and How Employers, Educators, and the Workforce Field Can Put It Back
articles.authors: Caleb Braxton Bragg
articles.abstract: Employers say they want durable skills: communication, critical thinking, teamwork, leadership. The label comes from an analysis of 82 million job postings that sorts what workers bring into two bins, technical skills that perish and durable skills that travel. This whitepaper argues the bins are backwards. The durable skills employers name are knowledge in use, organized bodies of domain information deployed on a task, and they look free-floating only because the measurement tradition that could see knowledge was abandoned. Job analysis kept knowledge, skills, and abilities as distinct constructs and showed that job knowledge is the path from ability to performance. Competency modeling replaced task-anchored constructs with behavioral labels, and the posting taxonomies that generate today’s durable-skills evidence fold knowledge into skill by definition. What remains of a job after that instrument is applied is “critical thinking.” The paper engages the transfer literature directly, offers re-planting as what actually carries across jobs, and argues that durability is appetite for knowledge rather than independence from it. It closes with three practical moves for employers and educators, a testable prediction about employer calibration, and three distinctions to replace perishable and durable.

articles.title: Public attention to artificial intelligence predicts helping between humans across 86 countries
articles.authors: Chenxi Li; Xiaoxue Hu; Xue Wang; Mengchen Dong
articles.abstract: The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has provoked debate about its consequences for human social life. Yet, whether and how public attention to AI shapes human relationships globally are largely unknown. In a global online game, we linked daily country-level AI attention from Google Trends to more than 1.5 million player-day records of voluntary helping among 9,167 players across 86 countries. Higher national attention to AI predicted increased helping behavior between players, an association robust across samples, measures, and specifications. This link was corroborated by quasi-experimental analyses around OpenAI DevDay, a major AI event, showing that helping rose in proportion to countries’ attention responses and shifted upward at the event date. The response was stronger where a shared human identity was likely salient and AI-related change likely felt pressing. Amid narratives casting AI as a threat to humanity, strengthened interpersonal bonds may mark a collective human adaptation to its rise.

articles.title: Perceptibility of Error Outcomes Shapes the Direction of Post-Error Adjustment: Evidence From 6.7 Million Moves in Online Chess
articles.authors: Yunjeong Jeong; Younggyu Kim
articles.abstract: Whether post-error slowing requires noticing the error is unresolved, because in laboratory tasks errors and the noticing of them covary. Chess separates them: engine evaluation identifies errors that leave no trace on the board, whereas material loss is visible. articles.title: The prose penalty in AI-assisted authorship
articles.authors: Faisal Feroz; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Jim Albert Charlton Everett; Sebastian Porsdam Mann; Brian D. Earp
articles.abstract: Generative AI based on large language models (LLMs) is increasingly used in academic, journalistic, and other professional and online writing, yet its implications for human authorship remain contested. We asked whether assignment of authorship credit depends on which task within the larger writing process a writer delegates to an AI assistant; whether any observed credit penalty is unique to AI; and whether credit can be restored through personalization: using an AI trained on one’s own previous writing. Across two preregistered studies (N = 878 US participants), observers evaluated a writer who either wrote unaided or delegated brainstorming, outlining, drafting, editing/revising, fact-checking, or all five tasks to an LLM or human assistant. In Study 1, although delegating a single task reduced authorship credit on average, the largest penalty by far applied to delegated drafting of prose, regardless of whether the helper was human or AI. Only the perceived originality needed for each task was independently associated with differences in credit assignment; perceived effort and skill were not. Perceived writing quality was also lower with LLM than human assistance, despite evaluated passages being randomly drawn from the same pool. In Study 2, using an LLM personalized on the writer’s own prior work increased both authorship credit and perceived writing quality relative to using a standard LLM. These findings show that authorship judgments depended principally on whether the writer produced the prose, regardless of helper type; that credit tracks judgments of originality, rather than effort or skill; and that the “prose penalty” on authorship attributions in AI-assisted writing can be partially reduced through personalization.

articles.title: Facing Trust: How Anthropomorphism and Individual Differences Shape Perceptions of Robot Faces
articles.authors: Lian Fingal; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Trust is essential to the development and maintenance of human relationships, and perceptions of trust based on the face alone can occur in as little as 100ms. Humans also tend to make trust estimations of robots based on their physical design, and these assessments can lead to successful acceptance of the robot or result in rejection. As robots are being designed to integrate into our daily lives, examining the factors that contribute to robot trustworthiness is a crucial component to understanding Human-Robot Interactions (HRI). Anthropomorphism is the attribution of human-likeness to objects, and it is suggested that imbuing robots with human characteristics can facilitate perceptions of trustworthiness. This study investigated the association of anthropomorphism with perceptions of trustworthiness of robot faces and whether there is a potentially predictive role of the tendency to anthropomorphise that would mediate trustworthiness perceptions. 43 participants rated their impressions of 30 robot images on trustworthiness and human-likeness. Participants also completed the individual differences in anthropomorphism questionnaire (IDAQ; Waytz et al., 2010). We hypothesised that anthropomorphic ratings on the Godspeed Anthropomorphism questionnaire (Bartneck, Kulić, et al., 2009) would be associated with perceptions of trustworthiness on a single item measure of trustworthiness. We did not find support for this hypothesis (r(41) = .041, p = .795, N = 43). We hypothesised that individual differences in the tendency to anthropomorphise would be associated with human-likeness of robot faces. We found that IDAQ scores were not associated with anthropomorphism (Estimate = .219, S.E. = .286, C.R. = .766, p = .444). Finally, we hypothesised that individual differences would mediate the relationship between anthropomorphism and  perceptions of trustworthiness of robot faces. We found that there was no significant relationship between IDAQ scores and trustworthiness perceptions (Estimate = -.005, S.E. = .135, C.R. = -.039, p = .969). These findings suggest that participants accessed prior negative knowledge about robots and applied them to the robot images in this study. Additionally, the results suggest that trust affordances cannot be detected simply in the physical features of a robot. Limitations include the experimental design, especially the one-item measure of trustworthiness and the lack of contextual cues.

articles.title: Pop-Culture Psychopathy: How Media Exposure Affects Laypersons’ Recognition of Clinical Psychopathic Traits
articles.authors: Robyn Marshall; Samuel Bennett
articles.abstract: Entertainment media has proven to be an essential source of information about mental disorders and crucial in educating the public about these conditions. Consequently, how the media portrays the mentally ill is very important, yet they continue to be depicted alongside images of violence and crime. Psychopathy has been portrayed as a disorder of deceit, manipulation and charm despite research continually confirming otherwise. The inaccurate portrayals of psychopathy have far-reaching consequences, most alarmingly in the criminal justice system. These ‘psychopaths’ work alongside stigmatisation, categorisation theories and social learning and cultivation theories to encourage false beliefs about the disorder. This study uses a quantitative approach, collecting responses to a questionnaire through social media, to investigate the influence of inaccurate media depictions on the layperson’s ability to diagnose psychopathy accurately. The study compares psychopathy to participants’ ability to diagnose antisocial personality disorder (ASPD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia. The author then looks for a relationship between participants’ ability to diagnose psychopathy, their confidence in their knowledge about psychopathy and their interaction with media depictions of psychopaths before finally investigating the influence of several demographic characteristics. A non-parametric repeated measures ANOVA revealed that participants’ ability to diagnose psychopathy is significantly worse than their ability to recognise the other conditions in vignettes. A multiple linear regression analysis revealed that a participant’s ability to identify psychopathy increased as their confidence increased and decreased as their media diversity score increased, however only the relationship between ability to identify and confidence was significant. Finally, multiple ANOVAs revealed that age and previous psychological knowledge had a significant impact on a participant’s ability to identify psychopathy accurately.

articles.title: When Are Less Precise Predictions More Credible?
articles.authors: Eitan David Rude; Amin Shiri; Felipe M. Affonso; Hal Hershfield; Craig R. Fox
articles.abstract: People expressing uncertain values frequently offer point predictions or intervals of varying widths (e.g., “I’d say your investment will be worth $6,000” versus “I’d say your investment will be worth $5,000–$7,000”). Interestingly, prior research has drawn conflicting conclusions concerning the credibility of more versus less precise predictions. We resolve this inconsistency by identifying a key moderator: the perceived nature of uncertainty. Specifically, we find that under epistemic (“knowable”) uncertainty, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ degree of confidence, and more precise predictions are seen as more credible. Under aleatory (“random”) uncertainty, however, predictions are seen as conveying experts’ assessments of the degree of outcome variability, and less precise predictions are seen as more credible (provided they are within reasonable bounds). These results inform literatures on both the communication of uncertainty and the interpretation of confidence intervals.

articles.title: Bringing our tribes together:  The promise and peril of interdisciplinary research on epistemically suspect beliefs
articles.authors: Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Raunak M Pillai; Steve Rathje
articles.abstract: Epistemically suspect beliefs are studied across multiple disciplines, yet these literatures have developed largely in parallel. We argue that integrating research from clinical, social, cognitive, and political psychology offers an important opportunity to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the origins and consequences of these beliefs. In particular, research on social identity can help explain how people select information and social environments, evaluate evidence, and process information in ways that affirm their identities. Extending these insights to clinical contexts raises new questions about how social and personal identities shape susceptibility to certain beliefs, including in emerging information environments shaped by artificial intelligence. However, interdisciplinary research faces substantial institutional and psychological barriers. Academic incentives often reward disciplinary competition, simple theories, and surprising findings over integration, encouraging researchers to defend disciplinary identities and caricature competing perspectives. Building a robust science of beliefs therefore requires a culture of cooperation that prioritizes explanatory utility and theoretical synthesis over disciplinary dominance, and needs to be supported by interdisciplinary funding, hiring, training, conferences, and journals.

articles.title: Is there a “shape bias” for places?
articles.authors: Yi Lin; Kirsten Mark; Moira Rose Dillon
articles.abstract: Early emerging biases support our learning of new words, like a tendency to extend novel nouns referring to objects to other objects of the same shape. The present work tests the generalizability of this “shape bias” in another foundational domain of everyday life — the domain of places. Adults and 6-year-old children, but not 3-year-old children, extended novel nouns to places of the same shape over places composed of the same-colored walls, regardless of whether places were described by novel nouns in labeling phrases or in more place-relevant prepositional phrases. All age groups, by contrast, showed a shape bias for objects that matched many features of the place stimuli. This relatively delayed shape bias for places suggests that at least some word-learning biases may emerge separately for different domains.

articles.title: Fear, Conformity, and Phantom Majorities
articles.authors: Cory J Clark
articles.abstract:
In many ways, modern human brains are not adapted to modern environments, and our social worlds are one of the most significant evolutionary mismatches. Humans evolved in small-scale interdependent tribes, where information about local peer networks was observable or obtainable through mutual acquaintances. In such environments, people would have relatively good information about the prevalence of certain beliefs (a numerator) and a clear sense of their network size (a denominator), and thus could assess the relative popularity of different views and values. This assessment of majority views would help humans navigate their social worlds, allowing them to conform to popular beliefs and values or at least avoid visible violations of those beliefs and values. Given the small size of these environments, if dozens or hundreds of people appeared to support a particular perspective–and especially if one did not share that perspective–that perspective would be socially important and warrant consideration.
In modern environments, and particularly on social media, we routinely encounter views endorsed (via likes and reshares) by dozens, hundreds, thousands, or tens of thousands of people, where those seemingly popular views might represent <1% of the people who saw and thus could have endorsed the content. Human psychology is not adapted to intuit that thousands of people might be a socially insignificant percentage of people. I refer to these illusory crowds as “phantom majorities”: psychologically imposing masses of people that are experienced as far more representative of a population (and thus far more socially powerful) than they are in reality. In this short essay, I contend that (1) outgroup phantom majorities have contributed to exaggerated negative perceptions of outgroups and reactive extremism, and (2) ingroup phantom majorities have contributed to self-censorship, preference falsification, and mistargeted viewpoint conformity. Because both ingroup and outgroup phantom majorities can polarize, they may also contribute to self-fulfilling prophecies whereby seemingly popular fringe views become more popular, increasing their prevalence on social media and feeding back through the cycle.

articles.title: Revisiting Gino, Ayal, et al.’s (2009) Contagion and Differentiation in Unethical Behavior: A Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Esra Aslan
articles.abstract: Individual behavior is often shaped by observing others’ actions. The seminal Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) study found that individuals behave more dishonestly after witnessing blatant dishonesty by an ingroup member than by an outgroup member. However, because there was no group-irrelevant baseline condition, it remains unclear whether ingroup contagion, outgroup differentiation, or both drive the effect. Furthermore, using natural groups of university students leaves it unclear whether distinct properties of natural groups are necessary, or if mere categorization into arbitrary groups suffices. In this registered report, we tested Gino, Ayal, et al.'s (2009) general hypothesis that exposure to ingroup dishonesty norms increases individual dishonest behavior more than exposure to outgroup dishonesty norms. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of their Experiment 1 with 3,323 U.S. Americans using both minimal and natural groups. Participants were exposed to standardized information about others' dishonest behavior, where we systematically varied the group identities of dishonest others. Then, they completed an incentivized coin-flip task where participants could double their earnings by lying. Despite manipulation checks suggesting that participants processed norm information and strongly identified with natural groups, the pre-registered ingroup-outgroup hypotheses were not supported. Bayesian analyses provided moderate to strong evidence for null effects across comparisons (BF₀₁ = 3.15-14.71). The core ingroup-versus-outgroup prediction received particularly strong null evidence (BF₀₁ > 14). We conclude that exposure to ingroup versus outgroup dishonesty norms, delivered through descriptive statistics in online settings, might not differentially affect individual dishonest behavior, revealing a boundary condition of the original finding.

articles.title: A Bayesian Structure Inference Account of Biases in the Formation and Updating of Group Moral Impressions
articles.authors: Jieyun Li; Fuying Chen; Yi Hu
articles.abstract: Evaluating a group's morality requires integrating its members' behaviors to form an impression, and updating these evaluations as new information emerges. We captured both impression formation and updating within a single Bayesian nonparametric framework: observers infer latent structures from group's behavioral distributions, thereby generating systematic biases in both static and changing contexts. During moral impression formation, when a group exhibits both common (dense) and rare (sparse) moral behaviors, the structure inference account (formalized by the Chinese Restaurant Process, CRP) predicts a sparsity bias, where rare behaviors trigger the inference of more latent structures. This opposes the "Common Is Moral" (CIM) heuristic, which predicts a density bias anchored to the high-frequency majority. Behavioral and computational modeling results (Experiments 1a-1b) showed a sparsity bias better explained by structural inference rather than frequency heuristics. Representational Similarity Analysis (Experiment 2) further revealed that observers' mental representations of groups organize around these inferred structures. Critically, moving to moral impression updating (Experiment 3), we found that impression biases track the shifting valence of newly sparse information. We captured the underlying structural evolution by extending the framework to changing environments via the Recurrent CRP (RCRP). Together, these findings suggest that the formation and updating of moral group impressions can be understood under a single cognitive perspective, implying that social biases could be mitigated by strategically altering information distributions.

articles.title: Reframing the Unconscious: A Conceptual Mapping of Jungian Analytical Psychology onto Indian Knowledge Systems
articles.authors: Manoj Kumar Mallick
articles.abstract: Carl Jung engaged Eastern thought throughout his career, writing psychological commentaries on The Secret of the Golden Flower, the Tibetan Book of the Dead, and Kuṇḍalinī yoga, yet this engagement remained impressionistic rather than systematic. No existing review pairs his core constructs with named terms from classical Indian philosophy. This paper proposes a term-by-term conceptual correspondence between six constructs of Jungian analytical psychology and six terms drawn from Sāṃkhya, Patañjali's Yoga, and Advaita Vedānta. It does not introduce a new theoretical model, acronym, or unifying framework. The paper follows Jaakkola's Theory Synthesis template for conceptual articles, distinguished from Theory Adaptation, Typology, and Model approaches. Four criteria guided term selection: definitional precision, scope-matching, textual traceability, and precision over popularity. Each correspondence was checked against primary Jungian texts and established secondary scholarship in Indology. Six correspondences are proposed: Collective Unconscious–Mahat, Archetypes–Tattva, Persona–Vyavahārika, Anima/Animus–Puruṣa/ Prakṛti, Shadow–Kleśa, and Individuation–Svarūpa-bodha. A central divergence emerged alongside these resemblances. Jung's individuation preserves a differentiated, related self, while Advaita's deeper vocabulary points toward non-dual dissolution of that self. This paper treats the divergence as a substantive finding, not a flaw in the method. The mapping offers culturally grounded vocabulary for teaching analytical psychology in Indian settings and for developing culturally resonant counseling language, illustrated through a brief clinical vignette. Risks of essentialism, translation distance, and untested clinical application are named explicitly, with concrete directions proposed for future empirical and textual work.

articles.title: Expressions of Self-Censorship
articles.authors: Jabin Binnendyk; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract:
Self-censorship poses a considerable threat to public discourse as it can undermine key
democratic processes, such as the wisdom of crowds. While existing conceptualizations of self-
censorship use the lens of avoidance (i.e., withholding of one's opinion), we argue people express
self-censorship in several manners: avoidance, aversion to provocation, epistemic uncertainty,
and conformity. Across seven studies (N = 4,447), we developed and validated the Expressions
of Self-Censorship scale (ESC), a 16-item measure. Confirmatory factor analyses supported a
four-factor structure, suggesting that individuals differ not only in the extent to which they self-
censor but also in how they do so. We then examined the predictive validity of the ESC scale in
two novel contexts: i) willingness to share (publicly and anonymously) and edit a controversial
opinion (N = 555) and ii) discussing an active unionization campaign among other graduate and
professional students at a major U.S. university (N = 146). Across both contexts, the ESC
predicted self-censorship-related behaviors, including willingness to share opinions, whether and
how they edited their controversial opinion, and comfort discussing each of these topics across
different audiences. Further, we found that each of the expressions of self-censorship were
associated with distinct patterns of behaviors, supporting our claim that self-censorship is not
only the absence of voicing an opinion, but can also be the presence of an ingenuine opinion. At
the societal level, this work highlights the importance of understanding both the information
within public discourse along with those opinions that are modified or withheld.

articles.title: Semantic Information Shapes Gaze Patterns During Naturalistic Movie Viewing: Evidence from computational models of vision and language
articles.authors: Xing Su; Aditya Upadhyayula; Jeffrey M. Zacks
articles.abstract: When people watch everyday activity or movies, the eyes are drawn by visually salient features, and also by features that are semantically meaningful. However, saliency and meaning often co-occur, making it difficult to isolate their individual influence on gaze. Here we leveraged a large language-image model (CLIP: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) to isolate these influences. Eighty-one participants watched four movies of everyday activities and eye movements were recorded. CLIP embeddings were used as a metric to measure semantic content and were compared with the gaze maps. The embeddings were generated for both upright and inverted frame versions, because frame inversion selectively disrupts semantic information while preserving saliency. Upright CLIP embeddings predicted viewers’ gaze patterns better than inverted embeddings, and this advantage persisted even after accounting for low-level saliency and other random-noise controls. Finally, temporally aligned action descriptions predicted gaze better than shuffled descriptions across multiple text-based representations, suggesting that action meaning itself carries information about where viewers look. Together, these findings suggest that gaze during naturalistic movie viewing is sensitive to semantic information at fine temporal scales, and that computational vision-language models provide a useful approach for studying cognitive processes in naturalistic environments.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Trust Talk Is Scoped and Unlexicalized: How People Express Trust in AI, and What Standard Instruments Cannot See
articles.authors: Muhammad Ali Shahidy; USHA LAKSHMANAN
articles.abstract:
Trust-in-automation research has recognized since the mid-1990s that trust can attach to a system's particular functions rather than to the system as an undifferentiated whole, and Lee and See (2004) explicitly recommend maximizing this functional specificity to prevent misuse and
disuse. Widely used self-report trust instruments nonetheless ask respondents to rate "the system" as a single referent; no item in any instrument examined here lets a respondent name the task or capability their rating concerns. This paper reports Phase 1 of a project measuring how far naturalistic discourse about trust in AI diverges from that instrument design. A prevalence sample of 20,000 items was drawn without trust-relevance filtering from a corpus of 12,497,945 items across 17 AI-focused subreddits, December 2022 through January 2026. Among 2,924
trust-relevant items, 96.97% (95% Wilson CI [96.27%, 97.52%]) expressed a trust or distrust evaluation without using trust-specific vocabulary. The same items were coded for whether their evaluation attached to AI as an undifferentiated category or to a specific object; as directly measured, 84% were object-scoped, a figure corrected to approximately 92% after hand verification identified a one-directional coding error in the global label. A keyword-based approximation of the explicitness codebook achieved only κ = 0.464 against the same gold standard, with roughly two-thirds of its positive calls false. The two findings are reported as separable: implicitness in trust vocabulary is documented directly, and scoping is offered as an explanation for it, not as something the data alone demonstrate. If trust evaluations are formed at the level of a specific object in roughly nine cases in ten, and conveyed using trust-specific vocabulary in barely three cases in a hundred, general single-item trust instruments are summarizing a considerably more differentiated attitude structure than the number they return.

articles.title: Losing nuance in camouflaging research: the unintended harms for research, clinical practice, and public discourse
articles.authors: Ailbhe McKinney; Connor Tom Keating; Holly Elizabeth Anne Sutherland; Rae Field; Jiedi Lei
articles.abstract: Camouflaging refers to the conscious or subconscious suppression of autistic (or neurodivergent) behaviours, and/or the use of compensatory strategies, to navigate social interactions with the aim of being perceived as neurotypical and to keep safe. The field is currently at an important turning point: camouflaging is now firmly established within autism research, but its rapid movement into public discourse and clinical practice has outpaced conceptual and measurement precision. In this Personal View, we identify two related challenges. First, existing conceptualisations often capture only one slice of the relationship between camouflaging and other outcomes (e.g. mental health), treating camouflaging as unidimensional and its associations with outcomes as linear, potentially obscuring more complex and heterogeneous relationships. Current frameworks similarly tend to quantify camouflaging behaviours without in-depth functional analysis to capture differences in agency, context, and cognitive mechanisms that may give rise to different behaviours and outcomes. We propose a multidimensional framework to capture these distinct but interacting processes and support more precise mechanistic research. Second, simplified clinical and public narratives increasingly frame camouflaging as uniformly harmful and “unmasking” as inherently desirable. We argue instead for a nuanced, neurodiversity-affirming approach centred on safety and personal autonomy. Applying the multidimensional framework clinically may help practitioners understand when, why, and how camouflaging is helpful or harmful for a particular person in a particular context.

articles.title: LLMs are transforming persuasion: A scoping review of LLM-powered social bots
articles.authors: Desislava Bocheva; Patricia Hajszan; Joanne Hinds
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified concerns about their capacity to shape human attitudes, beliefs, and behaviours across politics, health, education, and marketing. This scoping review synthesises evidence from 200 academic, policy, and industry sources to examine whether LLM-powered social bots can persuade, how effective they are, and the mechanisms driving persuasive effects. Findings suggest that LLM-generated content can match or exceed human persuasive performance while being difficult to distinguish from human-authored communication. Persuasive effects appear shaped by personalisation and adaptive interaction, vary across individual differences, and may be amplified through coordinated activity across social networks at scale. However, evidence remains mixed and context-dependent, with limited understanding of longer-term behavioural outcomes. These findings suggest that as AI systems become increasingly embedded across society, anticipating and responding to adaptive and scalable forms of LLM-powered persuasion may become one of the defining challenges of the AI era.

articles.title: Sadism is Linked to Greater Habituation to Schadenfreude
articles.authors: Drew M. Parton; Emily Pappalardo; David Skylan Chester
articles.abstract: People sometimes enjoy being passive spectators to others’ pain (i.e., schadenfreude). Yet, sadistic individuals actively inflict such pain themselves for the pleasure it brings. What differentiates those who passively versus actively enjoy others’ suffering? In individuals predisposed to enjoying others’ suffering, diminishing hedonic returns from schadenfreude may motivate sadistic pursuits to better satisfy hedonic goals. To test this, 297 undergraduates from a Minority Serving Institution reported their sadistic tendencies and then repeatedly watched and reported their enjoyment of two blocks of videos that either depicted people being moderately harmed or non-harmful pleasant scenes. Sadism was positively correlated with schadenfreude (i.e., participants with more sadistic tendencies reported greater enjoyment of the harm videos than those lower in sadism). Yet, sadism was also linked to a greater habituation to schadenfreude, in which more sadistic individuals showed steeper drops in their enjoyment of harm videos over subsequent videos than others, even when we adjusted for corresponding declines in their enjoyment of non-harm videos in the control condition. Indeed, the extent to which sadism was linked to greater enjoyment of harm videos more than halved over the course of the task.

articles.title: Rare on screens but on everyone's mind: a systematic review of misinformation prevalence, exposure, and concentration
articles.authors: Sacha Altay
articles.abstract:
How much misinformation do people encounter? Published estimates range from a fraction of
one percent to strong majorities. We systematically reviewed 443 studies reporting 1048
estimates of misinformation prevalence, exposure, sharing, and concentration. In behavioural
studies, misinformation is a median 1.3% of what people consume online; it reaches 12.0% of
people at least once and makes up 13.0% of what they share. In surveys, 57.7% say they have
seen misinformation and 19.8% say they have shared it. In content analyses, 23.0% of items are
classified as misinformation. How misinformation was identified (by fact-checkers, domain lists,
researchers, or classifiers) and at which level (sources or items) explained more of the variance
between estimates than what the study was about; platform and topic explained less. The top 1%
of users account for a median 70% of misinformation sharing or exposure. These results help
contextualize the diversity of misinformation estimates.

articles.title: Subtractive Epistemology at the Metadata Layer: How the Scholarly Record Registers Retraction and Not Refutation
articles.authors: Tomasz Witkowski
articles.abstract: In the 25 highest impact factor journals of general and internal medicine, 61 systematic reviews included at least one study since retracted, and among those examined the retraction arrived after publication in 74% of cases. Retraction notices are dated, name the paper and are machine readable, yet nothing obliged anyone to carry them into the syntheses that relied on them. That is the favourable case. The controlled vocabularies through which the scholarly record registers subtractive events supply a standardised entry for every event triggered by misconduct or procedural defect and none for an honestly derived claim turning out to be wrong. The absence follows from the shape of responsibility rather than from schema design: a publication has a keeper who answers for it, a claim has none. Systems that answer questions about what is known must now resolve the current state of the corpus continuously and cannot decline, making them the first agents to bear, for reasons unconnected with methodology, the obligation that produced derogation in law and the withdrawal of recommendations in medicine. A minimal form for an act of withdrawal would cost the addition of terms to vocabularies that already exist. Who would issue it remains open.

articles.title: The virtual crime scene:  Virtual reality context reinstatement as a means to increase the quality of eyewitness statements.
articles.authors: Jeroen Timmer; Peter W. de Vries; Jordy F. Gosselt
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Eyewitness statements often determine the direction and the success of police investigations. However, eyewitnesses’ recollection of events may become inaccurate or even incorrect over time. Moreover, eyewitnesses’ expressed confidence in the quality of their statements tends to be a rather weak indicator of actual quality. The current study explores how different types of context reinstatement compare in terms of quality of eyewitness statements and how they influence the confidence-quality relationship. Of particular interest is a new type of context reinstatement: virtual context reinstatement.
Methods: Participants (N = 98) were asked to take part in a group experiment in which an incident was staged. A week later, participants were subjected to virtual context reinstatement (VCR), physical context reinstatement (PCR), mental context reinstatement (MCR), or a no context reinstatement (control) procedure, and were subsequently asked to give an eyewitness statement. 
Results: During free recall, eyewitness statements in both the VCR and PCR conditions contained significantly less confabulated details compared to statements of participants in the control group. During cued recall, participants in the VCR condition reported more correct details in their statements than participants in the MCR and PCR conditions. Moreover, VCR appears to result in a stronger confidence-quality relationship compared to the other types context reinstatement. 
Conclusions: PCR and VCR showed fewest confabulated details in eyewitness statements and are therefore most beneficial to police investigations. The stronger confidence-quality relationship as a result of VCR can help to support the decision-making process of police investigators and other professionals who rely on eyewitness statements.

articles.title: Gender Gap in Eco-friendliness: Is It Mostly in Our Head?
articles.authors: Olena Vitkovska; Veronika Job; Christina Bauer
articles.abstract:
Do women want to engage in more eco-friendly behaviors compared to men? Popular 
media sometimes suggest as much, but it is unclear whether such portrayals reflect actual gender 
gaps or stereotypes (i.e., shared beliefs about gender differences that may not align with reality). 
To address this, we examined both in two studies: Study 1 (N = 274, convenience sample) and 
Study 2 (N = 615, US census-representative sample), using frequentist and Bayesian analyses, 
thus testing for both the presence and the absence of a gender gap in eco-friendly behavioral 
intentions and attitudes. Overall, we found strong and consistent evidence for stereotypes. The 
means indicate that gender stereotypes were driven by perceptions of women as highly 
compatible with eco-friendliness, whilst men were perceived as moderately compatible. At the 
same time, evidence for gender gaps in eco-friendly intentions and attitudes was weaker. Study 1 
found no evidence for a gap, whereas Study 2 found small effects on two out of four measures. 
Overall, this research shows that perceptions of women as more eco-friendly than men are 
largely driven by gender stereotypes rather than by the extent to which men and women actually 
differ in their eco-friendly behavioral intentions and attitudes. Thus, the present research 
counters essentializing views of men and women.

articles.title: The Bridge-or-Trap Model of Companion AI: When Emotional Support Connects or Substitutes.
articles.authors: Ho Nam Cheung
articles.abstract: AI companions are increasingly used for emotional support, yet their relational consequences appear sharply divergent. The same qualities that make these systems comforting, availability, nonjudgment, and low interpersonal risk, may help some users move toward human connection while drawing others away from it. This paper proposes the Bridge-or-Trap model to explain this divergence. The model argues that AI-mediated relief becomes bridge-oriented when it reduces the expected cost of approaching a real person and supports human-directed action, such as disclosure, repair, help-seeking, or re-entry into social settings. The same relief becomes trap-oriented when it remains contained within the AI relationship, preserving avoidance and reducing opportunities for corrective human experience. The model specifies five interacting constructs: anticipated interpersonal cost of human closeness, AI relational reinforcement, relational-orientation state, ecological protection and affordance, and adaptive relational resilience. It further proposes that repeated AI-contained relief may produce path-dependent substitution, with entry and exit thresholds that can be tested empirically. Drawing on attachment theory, social anxiety research, resilience theory, social ecology, social exchange theory, and emerging evidence on AI companionship, the model reframes the central question from whether AI companions help or harm to when emotional support becomes a bridge back to people and when it becomes a substitute for them. The paper identifies three decisive tests: target-specific transfer, viable-alternative boundaries, and asymmetric recovery from AI-contained substitution.

articles.title: Evidence of Preserved Function in Semantic Dementia
articles.authors: Chelsea-Leigh Marie McKenzie; Melissa E Meade; Marieke Mur; John Paul Minda; Stefan Kohler
articles.abstract: This narrative review examined clinical assessments and empirical research on semantic dementia to understand the nature of preserved semantic function alongside impairment across different disease stages. The first section describes the clinical characteristics, staging, and diagnosis of semantic dementia, and concludes by summarizing the implications of these characterization differences. The next section presents a collection of studies with tasks specifically designed to explore spared semantic processing in semantic dementia. The final section synthesizes and discusses these findings and their utility in leveraging remaining cognitive processing. We conclude that a complete and accurate clinical picture of semantic dementia, and an understanding of semantic memory more generally, requires considering both impaired and spared aspects of conceptual processing and relevant cognitive functions that support semantic memory. The findings summarized in this review will be useful to researchers and clinicians interested in episodic and semantic memory.

articles.title: Investigating effects of day-to-day variations in environmental exposure on the human brain: study protocol for the Day2Day Environment project
articles.authors: Kim Falkenstein; Claire Pauley; Simone Kühn
articles.abstract:
Background: Understanding how daily environmental exposures influence the human brain and mental health is increasingly important in the context of global urbanization and climate change. Previous studies have focused primarily on long-term environmental factors or isolated features like green space and air quality, neglecting the interaction between multiple exposures encountered in everyday life. This protocol paper describes the study design and dataset of the Day2Day Environment project, an ongoing study investigating how real-world, day-to-day environmental variability affects brain structure, function, and well-being.
Methods: This dense longitudinal study collects multimodal data from 30 participants over 25 testing sessions, including neuroimaging and tracking of physiological, behavioral, and environmental variables. Using wearable devices, geographic ecological momentary assessments, and GPS-based geospatial tracking, we collect data on air quality, noise, light exposure, physical activity, stress, cognition, and affect. Neuroimaging measures include T1- and T2*-weighted images during rest and tasks, quantitative multi-parameter mapping, high-resolution proton density imaging of the hippocampus, and diffusion tensor imaging sequences.
Conclusion: The Day2Day Environment dataset offers a unique opportunity to study short-term neuroplasticity in response to the dynamic interplay between multiple environmental exposures. Furthermore, the diversity of measurements in this dataset may be valuable for addressing research questions beyond environmental neuroscience.

articles.title: Proposition-Based Theory Specification (PBTS): A Structured Workflow for Analyzing and Refining Verbal Theories in Psychology
articles.authors: Andreas Glöckner; Tilmann Betsch; Daria Lisovoj; Jennifer Biehl; Jasper Zeno Siol; Fiona tho Pesch; Susann Fiedler
articles.abstract: Many theories in psychology are formulated as verbal narratives. Although verbal theories can be scientifically useful, there are no commonly accepted standards for making their inferential structure, definitions, boundary conditions, and links to observation explicit. This can leave unclear what a theory predicts in a given situation, whether it applies, which statements constitute the theory, or which version is current. We introduce Proposition-Based Theory Specification (PBTS), a structured, low-threshold workflow for improving verbal theory specification and analysis. PBTS requires researchers (a) to represent a theory as source-traceable verbal propositions, (b) to connect propositions through explicit implications, (c) to define all concepts and uncommon operators, and (d) to provide and document operationalizations and auxiliary assumptions. The workflow supports independent reconstruction, structured comparison, consensus building, versioning, and the assessment of theory-specification reproducibility. We provide step-by-step guidelines for specifying existing and new theories and for analyzing ambiguities, inconsistencies, tautologies, and missing elements. Evidence from an initial feasibility demonstration, a published case study, and two waves of the ManyTheorists collaboration indicates that substantively focused researchers can apply PBTS across a broad range of social psychological theories. PBTS complements rather than replaces mathematical, computational, and other formal approaches and can serve as an accessible intermediate or documentation layer.

articles.title: Socio-functional model of attitudes towards migrants: the role of institutional distrust, sense of threat and conspiratorial thinking
articles.authors: Nina Holičková; Peter Teličák; Jakub Šrol; Magdalena Adamus
articles.abstract: Across three studies the current paper unpacks negative attitudes towards migrants in the context of the socio-functional model that binds together the sense of threat, institutional distrust, and conspiratorial thinking. Using a comprehensive multi-country dataset (Study 1) and two longitudinal studies from Slovakia and Czechia (Studies 2 and 3), the paper delves into the roots of anti-migration stances among European citizens. In Study 1 (N = 41,455), we analysed the ESS wave 10 data about conspiracy beliefs, institutional distrust, migration policy preferences, and the sense of threat allegedly posed by migrants. Study 2 (N = 938) shows that, at the between-participants level, conspiracy beliefs about the Russian invasion of Ukraine, institutional distrust and attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees are associated. No clear effects hold at the within-participants level, though. Finally, Study 3 (N = 856) shows that conspiracy mentality – rather than specific conspiracy beliefs about migration – is bidirectionally associated with the sense of threat allegedly posed by the migrants, pointing to conspiratorial thinking as a generalised metacognitive tendency to construe outgroup intentions and actions as malignant. Jointly, the studies explain the logic of anti-migration attitudes as immersed in the socio-functional model in which threat appraisals, conspiratorial thinking and attitudes towards outgroups are intertwined.

articles.title: Degree Distributions in Psychological Networks: When Centrality Conveys Consequential Information
articles.authors: Jonathan JaeHong Park; Mijke Rhemtulla; Omid V. Ebrahimi; Denny Borsboom
articles.abstract:
Network analysis is an increasingly popular methodological tool in the
social, clinical and behavioral sciences because of its ability to represent
phenomena as systems of interconnected variables. A key result is a set
of centrality indices intended to quantify the “importance” of individual
vertices. However, debate over centrality in psychological networks has
rarely considered that the relevance of these indices may depend on the
broader configuration of edges described by a graph’s degree distribution.
Many real-world systems self-organize into distinct degree distributions,
yet their implications for psychological networks remain understudied. We
used Monte Carlo simulations of weighted threshold cascades to examine
when different graph structures give rise to consequential central vertices.
Differences between cascades initiated at the most and least central vertices
were greatest under moderate activation thresholds and most pronounced
in scale-free graphs. By contrast, selection of the most central vertex mattered
relatively less in the case of small world graphs. Taken together,
these results indicate that centrality should be interpreted as one feature of
a network’s broader structural organization rather than as an isolated measure
of substantive importance or intervention relevance, with the utility
of these metrics contingent on the topology in which they are embedded.

articles.title: The Adaptation Dilemma: Cultural Fit Does Not Guarantee Safety during Mental-Health Interactions with LLMs
articles.authors: Maya Low; Ian Gold; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: People increasingly take mental-health concerns to general-purpose AI chatbots. A first wave of safety research has begun to map LLM failure points in this context. When that work considers culture, it usually reads the problem as a lack of fit: if the model does not match the user, the fix is to make it match more closely. We argue that this perspective is incomplete, because cultural fit and safety are not the same thing. By safety we mean the absence of harm caused by the interaction itself. We sort these harms into two classes: imposition, where the model forces its default on a user it does not fit, and collusion, where it adapts to a framing that keeps the user unwell. Because a response that fits a user’s own framing is more credible to them, moving a model toward that framing lowers the risk of imposition while raising both the likelihood of collusion and the damage collusion does when it occurs, so improved cultural sensitivity trades one exposure for another rather than reducing exposure overall. We argue that the reinforcement learning layer increasingly pushes these models toward collusion, while the safeguards in current use are poorly suited to detecting that failure or to limiting the harm it does. We propose a taxonomy of six culture-related failure modes, three of imposition and three of collusion. We argue that evaluating safety requires an anchor outside the user’s in-the-moment approval: responses must be assessed against the harms and benefits the interaction produces for the user, judged both by an external standard and against the goals the user has stated for their care.

articles.title: Quality Control Exclusion Gaps: How routine processing of sensor data threatens the validity, generalizability, and racial diversity of research using psychophysiological methods
articles.authors: Boluwatife Dogari; Alicia Carmichael; Brandon P. Labbree; Donna Walter; Richard Gonzalez; Nicholas Paul Camp
articles.abstract: Scientists have long used physiological recording to study bodily processes underlying emotions. However, sensors are often affected by hair or skin characteristics that impair the accuracy of their measurements in Black individuals. We draw attention to an underrecognized consequence of such recording biases: differential exclusion of Black participants during Quality Control (QC) stages of the data pipeline, what we call the QC exclusion gap. These routine procedures receive less attention than other stages of the research process; yet, disparate participant exclusions during QC can undermine the internal and external validity of research utilizing physiological recording. Using Electrodermal Activity (EDA) as an illustrative example, we walk through QC analyses of Black (N= 72) and White (N=68) participants’ Skin Conductance Levels (SCL) during a baseline passive listening task. Black participants exhibited significantly lower SCL (M = 4.13μS, SD = 2.49) than White participants (M = 7.95μS, SD = 3.19), p < .001. As a result, Black participants’ EDA data received lower quality grades during QC, leading to differential attrition during triage. We offer immediate recommendations to compensate for the QC exclusion gap, such as integrating quality monitoring feedback into recruitment procedures and reporting exclusion rates by demographic group, and identify broader directions for sensor development and analytical methods. Quality control is often considered a prelude to data analysis; by attending to who is excluded or included, however, we can design a more inclusive science.

articles.title: Psychosocial Characteristics and Objective Performance in Immersive Virtual Reality: Associations of Social Support, Psychological Distress, and Education with Psychomotor Speed and Cognitive Flexibility
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Lydia Asimakopoulou; Katerina Denaxa; Maria Roussou; Petros Roussos
articles.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) can quantify cognitive and psychomotor performance, but interpreting its scores requires establishing whether they also vary with psychosocial characteristics. This study examined associations of perceived support, psychological distress, and education with immersive performance across adulthood, including whether support associations differed by interaction mode, age, or education. Two hundred and two adults aged 19–90 years completed a five-mode VR Fitts' law task, the Trail Making Test in VR (TMT-VR), the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales. Hierarchical mixed-effects models retained the repeated task structure; multiplicity-controlled exploratory analyses examined the complete 26-variable TMT-VR battery and focused moderation tests. In the Fitts task, distress showed no clear association with task time or the application-defined Accuracy Index, and education added no independent task-time association beyond age. Higher support accompanied slightly slower adjusted task times, opposite to expectation, without supported differences by mode, age, or education. In TMT-VR, age and Part were the principal correlates of completion time. Support, distress, and education did not show broad associations with completion time, wrong-target errors, or error-adjusted time after multiplicity correction. One exploratory association survived correction: participants reporting more support showed a smaller increase in wrong-target errors from Part A to Part B, with no difference in overall error level. Distress was unrelated to every TMT-VR outcome after correction, including the application-defined mean selection distance. Within this generally high-support, low-symptom sample, psychosocial differences between participants were therefore not consistent correlates of conventional immersive cognitive outcomes. This finding informs the interpretation of non-clinical assessments without implying that support or distress is unimportant within an individual. Longitudinal studies should test whether changes in a person's psychosocial circumstances accompany cognitive change during healthy ageing or cognitive vulnerability. The support association with the Part B minus Part A error increment shows how a contrast between task demands can carry information that neither the overall error level nor completion time captures; it is exploratory and requires replication.

articles.title: Preferred Terminology for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) Among ADHD-Related Interest Groups
articles.authors: Naomi Dodgson; Carolynn Hare; Renee Leow-Guerville; Rachel Mack; Katarina Jovanovic; Ryan A Stevenson
articles.abstract:
The conversation surrounding disability and mental health has changed dramatically in recent decades, with many groups advocating for the use of new language and forms of social analysis. We examined preferences for different Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) related terminology, including person/identity first language, and describing ADHD as either a form of neurodiversity or a disability. Three ADHD interest groups participated: people with ADHD (n=232), parents of ADHD people (n=79), people who work in an ADHD-related field (n=172), and members of the public (n=134; total N=536). All groups preferred person-first language, and framing ADHD as something that you have. Opinions of identity-first language, and framing ADHD as something you are were correlated with one another, but not our measure of ADHD identity; we therefore believe these to reflect a preference for grammatical correctness, rather than a statement on one’s views of ADHD as an identity.

Keywords: ADHD, Neurodiversity, Disability, Terminology

articles.title: Communicating the Economic Impact of Science Funding Cuts Changes Attitudes and Motivates Action
articles.authors: Alyssa Hannah Sinclair; Mallory Harris; Danielle Cosme; Angela Fagerlin; Ellen Peters; Clio Andris; Colin Cooke; Emily B. Falk; Joshua S. Weitz
articles.abstract: Federal science funding cuts in the United States negatively impact research, healthcare, and the economy. Despite prior research investigating strategies to communicate scientific findings to the public, there is substantially less evidence on strategies to communicate how policy shapes the process and societal impact of science. Here, we demonstrate that across political divides, behavioral interventions that interactively communicate the impact of science funding cuts influence policy support, awareness, and intentions to take action in support of science funding. In two preregistered experiments with politically-balanced samples (N=5,177), we tested novel text, quiz, and map-based interventions illustrating economic losses resulting from science funding cuts. Across the political spectrum, the interventions robustly decreased approval of funding cuts and increased perceived knowledge and perceived negative local impact. We scaled these interventions via a public website (https://scienceimpacts.org/); a third study analyzing data from >24,000 website users revealed converging evidence of effectiveness. Crucially, we demonstrate that even simple text interventions that highlighted local economic impact effectively changed attitudes. However, adding active engagement via interactive quizzes and maps selectively increased action intentions (e.g., contacting representatives, sharing information). Surprise in response to the information, and time spent actively engaging with impact maps, predicted intervention effects on policy approval, knowledge, action intentions, and sharing behavior. Overall, interactive interventions revealing community-level economic impact changed attitudes and increased action intentions related to science funding cuts.

articles.title: Online Discourse is Falsely Polarized by Self-Selection
articles.authors: Will Schulz; Claire Elizabeth Robertson; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Ashwini Ashokkumar; Lisa Oswald; JungHwan Yang; Simon Munzert; Jay Joseph Van Bavel; Andrew Markus Guess
articles.abstract: We present comprehensive evidence quantifying the magnitude and scope of false polarization (i.e. the impression that opinions on political issues are more polarized than they actually are) on social media, driven by users' selective posting behavior. Using more than a decade of social media behavior connected to individual ideological attitudes in 1.7 million posts, a series of controlled experiments, and a large global survey covering 40 countries (total N = 49,222), we find that (1) strong ideologues post their opinions significantly more often than moderate individuals, and (2) extreme attitudes are posted more often than moderate attitudes. This general pattern replicates robustly across 40 countries, spanning diverse political cultures. Indeed, across studies we find extreme opinions are overrepresented on social media by at least 6% and up to 22% compared to their true prevalence in our samples. Furthermore, the opinions that users post are more hostile and toxic than the beliefs they keep to themselves.  These results were not explained by political interest or consistent left-right differences, suggesting that political extremity has an independent effect on social media behavior. Thus, most of the observed polarization of online discourse in recent years may be attributable to the systematic over-representation of pre-existing extreme political views, rather than the causal effects of platforms.

articles.title: Perceptions and Outcomes of Artificial Intelligence Among Back-office Employees: A Systematic Literature Review
articles.authors: Maria Igorevna Efremova; Oliver Runswick; Myanna Duncan
articles.abstract:
Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace is rapidly evolving. Employees’ perceptions of AI are of increasing interest, particularly in relation to their psychological wellbeing and performance outcomes. This systematic review extends existing research by synthesising recent empirical evidence on the impact of AI among back-office employees across a range of industries and functions, an occupational group that is particularly exposed to AI-driven technologies. Following PRISMA guidelines, eight databases were searched for peer-reviewed empirical studies published in English between January 2022 and January 2026. A total of 40 eligible studies were included in the review. Findings indicated that employee perceptions of AI were largely positive, although experiences across industries and occupations varied. AI adoption and performance outcomes were commonly related to perceived usefulness, ease of use, and the extent to which the organisation was ready to adopt AI. These outcomes were also associated with fears of job displacement and de-skilling, but these relationships were unexamined quantitatively. AI’s workplace value appears contingent on employee perceptions and organisational context, rather than just on the technology. 

Key words: AI at work, AI adoption, back-office employees, technology acceptance

articles.title: Perspective taking is context-dependent: The relation among perspective taking, sleep, and affect in an acute psychiatric sample
articles.authors: Emily Michelle Bowers; Courtney Beard; Chloe Hudson
articles.abstract: Perspective taking is a central component of social cognition linked to interpersonal functioning and psychiatric symptomatology. Although it is traditionally viewed as a stable trait, emerging evidence suggests it may fluctuate with momentary contextual factors. In the current study, we investigated the longitudinal association between perspective taking, sleep, and affect in a clinically heterogenous psychiatric sample. Participants were 900 patients (M age = 36.33, SD = 14.50, 58.89% female, 78.89% non-Hispanic White) who completed the Interpersonal Reactivity Index Perspective Taking subscale, Positive and Negative Affect Schedule, and the Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index throughout a two-week partial hospital program. Our multilevel modeling results indicate that greater positive and lower negative affect were significantly associated with more frequent perspective taking. Sleep duration was not significantly associated with perspective taking. The results support a shift toward conceptualizing perspective taking as a contextually sensitive process in psychiatric populations.

articles.title: What the Tally Hid: Screening Live-Observation Codes for Saturation, Floor Effects, and Degeneracy Before Piloting
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract: We set out a pre-piloting screening protocol for live-observation coding instruments (Table 1), usable in any brief structured behavioural-coding task, with a worked case study and a Monte Carlo calibration. In 15 stranger dyads a ten-code sheet produced a healthy-looking composite (M = 26.63, SD = 9.64), yet four engagement codes ran at 74-94% of their protocol maximum, three withdrawal codes were floored at 0-8%, and only three carried usable variance. Resampling the deposited counts (40,000 pilots per size), detection under the all-code conjunctive rule is 100% at every pilot size; one code (monologue) was never observed, and the all-code result is reported as a primary finding, with false positives against no-pathology nulls reaching 32.3% at N = 2 and falling to 9.3% at N = 4. In a sensitivity analysis excluding monologue and silence, detection remained high but non-monotonic (91.0% at N = 4; 87.1% at N = 6), with a closely comparable false-positive profile (6.1% at N = 4). Threshold distance and degeneracy, rather than pilot size, govern screening. The practical rule that follows is to report, for each code, its mean as a percentage of its protocol maximum, its between-unit variance, and its signed distance to the nearest threshold, rather than a recommended pilot N. The protocol and its two generalizable principles are offered as provisional and unregistered, pending independent replication on a second bin-level dataset. All counts derive from a single non-blinded coder, a limitation discussed throughout.

articles.title: Reframing Acculturation:  When (and Why) Acculturation Science Warrants a Systems Explanation
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Karen Phalet
articles.abstract: Acculturation has always been understood as a process of change, and contemporary research examines that change from several complementary perspectives, including developmental trajectories, reciprocal intergroup relations, ecological contexts, situated cultural processes, and multilevel social change. The field therefore contains many elements of a systems account without a shared architecture for relating them. This article offers a selective integrative review and metatheoretical synthesis using complex dynamic systems theory (CDST). CDST provides a coordinating framework that complements existing acculturation theories and encounter-level models of adaptation. It distinguishes five explanatory questions distributed across different traditions: what form change takes, who or what influences whom, how change moves across levels of organisation, where broader conditions become relevant, and how processes unfolding at different rates become linked. We organise these questions through five dimensions: nonlinear dynamism, relational reciprocity, multilevel emergence, situated adaptation, and multiscale temporality. Together, they provide a way to examine how patterns of acculturative change depend on prior experience, relationships, local conditions, levels of organisation, and processes unfolding at different rates. For each type of systems claim, we specify a linear-additive alternative and the evidence needed to distinguish between them. Power differences and prior history are treated as conditions that can shape how the system operates and changes. The framework therefore shifts attention from average associations between acculturation variables and outcomes toward explaining how acculturative change is organised, when different processes become connected, and when a systems explanation adds value beyond conventional models.

articles.title: Acculturation as a Situated Transactional Process
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu
articles.abstract: Acculturation research commonly links broad preferences for heritage-culture maintenance and participation in the receiving society to psychological and sociocultural adjustment. Yet meta-analytic and longitudinal evidence shows that these associations are often weak, heterogeneous, and limited over time, suggesting that broad preferences alone cannot explain why cultural engagement leads to different outcomes across situations. This conceptual article develops a situated transactional framework within a broader complex dynamic systems account. Building on established work showing that acculturation is contextual, domain-specific, and interactional, the framework specifies how these influences come together within concrete encounters. It proposes a process in which locally relevant conditions shape appraisal, the mobilization of culturally patterned resources, response, relational and institutional reception, multidimensional outcomes, and feedback into later encounters. The article also distinguishes the adaptation process, understood as the continuing person-environment transaction, from adaptation outcomes, including psychological, sociocultural, relational, and externally observed consequences. By organizing these elements into an explicit recursive architecture, the framework generates testable predictions about context-specific responses, reception, multidimensional outcomes, learned response patterns, and structural change. It thereby provides a concrete empirical agenda for testing whether these mechanisms improve explanation and prediction beyond broad-orientation and contextual-moderation accounts.

articles.title: Fetching a Problem's Solution from a Computer Does Not Lead to an Impoverished Affective Footprint
articles.authors: Patrick P. Weis; Johannes Bernau; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Problem solving relies on purely internal processing (IP) or extended processing (EP) which additionally draws on external resources like computerized equipment. IP can initially cause negative affect due to effort or cognitive conflict, followed by positive affect after success. Such affective dynamics matter as they influence learning, well-being, and cognitive control. Yet, little is known about affect in EP, which this study examined. Participants solved alpha-numeric problems (is “D+4=I” correct?). IP required mentally counting up letters from “D”, while EP involved revealing the correct answer (“H”) by hovering a cursor over a box. Affect was measured using affective priming (Experiment 1), facial muscle activity (Experiment 2), and explicit ratings. We hypothesized that IP produces more negative affect during problem solving but more positive affect afterwards compared to EP. Results provided little support for such a general claim. Affective priming suggests that IP-related operations like matching men-tal representations to sensory input can indeed cause positive affect, which can however also be part of EP. Facial muscle data indicated broadly comparable affective dynamics between IP and EP. These results add an affective spin to the cognitive impartiality hypotheses (Clark 2011), which suggests that neither IP nor EP is privileged by problem solvers.

articles.title: What beliefs are most debunkable?
articles.authors: Esther Boissin; Thomas H Costello; David Gertler Rand; Gordon Pennycook
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can persuade people to revise their beliefs, but it is unclear which beliefs are most "debunkable," and why. Across three pooled studies, participants (N = 3,341 online U.S. adults) discussed a self-reported conspiracy or other epistemically suspect belief with GPT-4, instructed to debunk it using facts and evidence. An LLM classified each belief by content domain (i.e., conspiratorial, paranormal/supernatural, pseudoscience, political, religious, other) and evidential status, from strong counterevidence to supported by evidence. Confidence decreased in every domain, but belief updating tracked evidential status rather than domain: reductions were substantial wherever the belief was open to counterevidence — strong, weak, or uninvestigated — and small for non-falsifiable and supported beliefs.
