Domain no longer predicted change once evidential status was accounted for, and the counterevidence the LLM deployed partially mediated the gradient. AI debunking appears most effective for falsifiable beliefs resting on weak evidence.

articles.title: Gaze on IPCC climate maps carries behaviour-specific signals for intended low-carbon action
articles.authors: Étienne Serbe-Kamp; Ayshan Aliyeva; Candelaria Belen Krick; Candela I. Jantus; Yaning Han; Joaquin Navajas; Bahador Bahrami; Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Climate maps are among the most widely shared products of climate science, yet their effect on the people who look at them is measured almost entirely with questionnaires. We recorded gaze with mobile eye-trackers while people freely viewed climate-projection maps from the IPCC Interactive Atlas, and asked whether how someone looks carries information questionnaires miss. It does, for only one of the three outcomes we tested. Gaze improved prediction of intended low-carbon behaviour in viewers the models had never seen, beyond a broad battery of climate measures and in every model tried. The same features said nothing about how anxious those viewers were, or which audience segment they placed themselves in. Attention to climate information is therefore not a general marker of engagement. It tracks readiness to act. Because a visualisation can be designed around where people look, this opens a route to evaluating climate communication while people are looking.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Reliance on Generative AI in Schoolwork: The Role of Executive Functioning Difficulties, Perceived Usefulness, and Habitual Use
articles.authors: Johan Klarin; Eva Hoff; Daiva Daukantaite
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are becoming an increasingly common part of adolescents’ everyday and academic lives. This raises the question of which individuals are more likely to rely on GenAI in their schoolwork, with reliance defined as a dispositional tendency to turn to GenAI in preference to one’s own effort or teacher support, as well as difficulty initiating schoolwork without it. Drawing on theories of technology adoption, habit formation, and self-regulation, the present study examined a sequential mediation model of the associations between executive functioning (EF) difficulties and reliance on GenAI through perceived usefulness and habitual use. The model was tested using structural equation modeling in community samples of lower secondary school students (N = 849, Mage = 14.8 years, 49.4% girls) and upper secondary school students (N = 898, Mage= 17.4 years, 55.2% girls), with analytic samples of 735 and 839 GenAI users, respectively. Across both groups, EF difficulties were positively associated with perceived usefulness, habitual use, and reliance on GenAI (rs = .14–.33, ps < .001). Consistent with the hypothesized model, a sequential indirect association through perceived usefulness and habitual use was significant in both groups (βs = .08–.10, ps < .001). Specific indirect associations through perceived usefulness were consistently observed in both groups, whereas those through habitual use alone received more limited support despite the strong association between habitual use and reliance (βs = .60–.69, ps < .001). The findings identify EF difficulties as an important individual-difference correlate of reliance on GenAI and suggest that perceived usefulness may be particularly relevant to understanding the indirect association between EF difficulties and reliance. More broadly, the results highlight the relevance of self-regulatory capacities for understanding individual differences in adolescents’ reliance on GenAI.

articles.title: A Bayesian method for representing the process of accumulating evidence over time: The case of forgetting curve models
articles.authors: Yui Furukawa; Kensuke Okada
articles.abstract:
In the practice of cognitive modeling, comparing and organizing proposed models plays a crucial role in refining psychological theory. Secondary data analysis provides a useful framework for such evaluations, enabling researchers to assess models across multiple datasets. Bayes factors (BFs) are valuable tools for evaluating the generalizability of cognitive models in this context. However, a standardized framework for model evaluation using BFs across multiple secondary datasets has yet to be established.
This study proposes a Bayesian model comparison method for assessing the generalizability of cognitive models, focusing on how evidence changes as secondary datasets accumulate over time. The proposed method enables (1) quantitative evaluation of model support across all datasets, (2) evaluation of how model support changes as datasets accumulate, and (3) parameter interpretation alongside model comparison. Using the forgetting curve as an illustrative example, we confirmed the method’s basic properties under the examined simulation conditions and examined its usefulness using secondary datasets.
In the simulations, BF-based model comparison supported the data-generating model under many examined conditions, and the method produced outputs corresponding to the intended properties. In the empirical study, the most strongly supported model differed across retention-interval subsets. The exploratory expectation of a publication-year-related shift from the power model to the linear model was not supported. Overall, the results illustrate how the proposed method can be used to evaluate model support across multiple datasets and to trace how evidence accumulates over time.
The Stage 1 protocol received in-principle acceptance on 13 May 2026 and is available at https://osf.io/z74cn.

articles.title: Assessing complex belief structures with the triads task: Reliability and validity
articles.authors: René Dutschke; Gundula Thiele; Martin Schoemann; Caroline Surrey; Stefan Scherbaum
articles.abstract:
Research on attitudes and beliefs often relies on assessing people’s agreement with several explicit
statements. We promote a different approach, focusing on the interconnectedness of beliefs and
their cognitive and affective components. Here, we present the triads task as a procedure to
measure complex belief networks. Leaning on similarity and difference judgments for three
concepts at a time, the triads task allows us to derive similarity scores for each pair of concepts in
a topic domain, which provide insights into belief networks of individuals and groups.
Furthermore, we propose a procedure to translate similarity scores into belief network
visualizations, inspired by cognitive-affective maps (CAMs). For a sample of 56 participants, we
show that similarity scores are retest reliable in a two week interval (averaged individual retest
correlation: r = .78) and that participants communicatively validate our visualization procedure.
We highlight the benefits of the triads task in measuring belief networks and further discuss this
procedure with regards to its potential as a research and intervention tool.

articles.title: Lab culture and the PI
articles.authors: Rosanne L. Rademaker; Christine Pfund; Wei Ji Ma
articles.abstract: Academic scientists are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of mentorship and the cohesion of a lab community for research productivity and trainee well-being. Moreover, funding agencies have started to mandate action around mentorship and management of interpersonal relationships within labs. Here, we consider these aspects in the context of the broader culture of a lab and emphasize the crucial role that the principal investigator plays in shaping that culture. We propose a framework for thinking about lab culture in terms of norms, values, responsibilities, expectations, processes, and procedures. We describe how lab documentation can support a strong lab culture and mentoring environment by making the elements of lab culture explicit and clear, while still allowing for flexibility and continual revision. We outline practical ways to get started on lab documentation, discuss contexts beyond the lab, and suggest strategies for troubleshooting. We hope that our framework will foster intentional and thoughtful approaches to lab documentation.

articles.title: Ageing, Digital Literacy, and Interaction Modality in Immersive Virtual Reality: Psychomotor Performance, Cognitive Flexibility, and Their Processing-Speed Association
articles.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Katerina Denaxa; Lydia Asimakopoulou; Petros Roussos; Maria Roussou
articles.abstract: Extended reality (XR) increasingly supports training and cognitive assessment, yet the age sensitivity of its interaction techniques is unclear. This study examined age, digital literacy, and interaction modality as correlates of psychomotor and cognitive-flexibility performance in immersive virtual reality (VR). Two hundred and two adults (19–90 years) completed a five-mode Fitts' law task (eye-gaze, head-gaze, controller ray-casting, virtual finger, and controller direct touch), the Trail Making Test in VR (TMT-VR), and a digital-literacy questionnaire. Age was associated with slower task times across modes, but controller direct touch carried the steepest relative age gradient yet remained among the fastest in absolute terms; technique altered relative age sensitivity without determining absolute efficiency. Higher digital literacy was associated with faster TMT-VR completion but not Fitts task times. A Fitts-derived speed score predicted TMT-VR performance beyond age and partly accounted for its age association, consistent with shared processing-speed variance; an exploratory full-battery extension confined the Fitts-score association to completion-time and error-adjusted-time indices and the digital-literacy association to error-adjusted-time indices, not wrong-target errors, mean selection distance, or relative Part B indices. Age-inclusive XR assessment should standardise interaction modality, evaluate rather than exclude mid-air di-rect selection, and interpret cognitive scores alongside digital literacy and psychomotor speed.

articles.title: AI’s Frontline
articles.authors: Alex Taylor; Jina Suh; Marlyn Thomas Savio; Sinead O'Dwyer; John Caesar De Villa
articles.abstract:
1.	AI’s safety and reliability depend on a globally distributed workforce
2.	Data workers feel an ambivalence towards their work: operating in a space of tension between monotonous and potentially emotionally taxing work, and feelings of individual and collective agency in contributing to new tech. 
3.	The space of tension opens up a space for thinking productively about the importance of data work and the active role data workers can play in shaping AI development.

articles.title: Shared research materials in psychology are widely downloaded but often difficult to reuse
articles.authors: Daniel S Quintana
articles.abstract: Open science reforms have made posting data and code common, but are shared materials actually used, and easily reused? Treating download counts of Open Science Framework (OSF) supplements as a usage index, I analysed 1,660 articles from four psychology journals (Cognition, Psychological Science, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Journal of Memory and Language) across three years (2015, 2020, 2025). OSF sharing rose from 9% in 2015 to 82% in 2025. Among 652 papers with download data, materials were downloaded a median of 135 times; fewer than 1% went undownloaded. Download volume was associated with citation count and altmetric attention. Availability did not ensure easy reuse: only 30% of repositories provided documentation, 34% were flagged for a hard-coded file path, and 40% referenced a missing file —shortcomings that did not improve as sharing grew. Altogether, shared materials are being used, but often not easily reusable

articles.title: The cascade from basic visual processing to social dysfunction: An extended path model in a transdiagnostic sample of youth.
articles.authors: Kelly Mathis; Scott D. Blain; Laura Rose Locarno; Carly A Lasagna; Colombi Costanza; Katharine N. Thakkar; Cynthia Z. Burton; Ivy Fei Tso
articles.abstract:
Background
Social dysfunction is widespread across psychiatric disorders, but treatments remain limited. Identifying underlying mechanisms could inform novel treatment approaches that meaningfully improve clinical outcomes. We previously showed that basic visual processing deficits cascade through gaze perception and emotion recognition to impair theory of mind. Here, we test an extended model assessing whether this cascade ultimately predicts real-world social dysfunction via theory of mind in an expanded sample.

Methods
A combined sample of 202 psychiatric patients with varying levels of social dysfunction and healthy individuals completed basic visual processing tasks, a multi-level social cognition battery that included measures of gaze perception, emotion recognition, and theory of mind, and clinical assessments of social functioning. A five-level path model evaluated the sequential cascade from visual processing to gaze perception, emotion recognition, theory of mind, and social functioning.

Results
The extended five-level path model demonstrated good fit to the data. Poorer basic visual processing sequentially predicted deficits across intermediate social cognitive domains, culminating in theory of mind, which directly predicted worse social functioning.

Conclusion
These findings indicate that basic visual deficits cascade through social cognitive steps to impair everyday social functioning. As a candidate shared mechanism contributing to social dysfunction, basic visual processing represents a promising target for psychiatric interventions.

articles.title: Psychotic-like experiences and neurobehavioral reward processing in adolescents who use cannabis
articles.authors: Shelley Gresko; Elizabeth Thompson; Meghan A. Gonsalves; Gillian LeBlanc; Elizabeth Lorenc; Jane Metrik; Michael Frank; Sarah Ryan; Emily Olenik; Leslie Brick
articles.abstract: Importance: Cannabis use (CU) in adolescence is linked to increased risk of developing psychotic-like experiences (PLEs) that can lead to lifelong impairment. A candidate mechanism may be disruptions in reward processing supported by dopamine but this association has not yet been tested in adolescents with CU and PLEs. The objective of the study was to assess the interrelation between CU, PLEs, and neurobehavioral markers of reward processing (behavioral reward motivation, tissue iron signal [1/nT2*], an indicator of dopamine-related neurophysiology). Methods: Participants were adolescents (aged 14 - 17) with either >11 lifetime cannabis episodes or <5 lifetime cannabis episodes (controls). CU quantity was assessed with the Daily Sessions, Frequency, Age of Onset, and Quantity of Cannabis Use Inventory. PLEs were assessed with the Achenbach Youth Self-Report Thought Problems Scale. Reward motivation (proportion of hard choices) was assessed using a behavioral task. 1/nT2* was derived from functional magnetic resonance imaging. Hypotheses, formulated during data collection as recognition grew of the risk factors of developing PLEs with CU, were: PLEs will magnify negative associations between CU and reward motivation; the positive association between greater CU and PLEs will depend on subcortical 1/nT2*. Results: 81 participants included 47 control and 34 cannabis group participants: mean [SD] age, 15.53 [1.12]; 52 female (64%). There was a significant interaction between CU and PLEs on reward motivation (OR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.10, 5.27, p=0.028), depending on reward amount and effort required. At high PLEs, the cannabis group, compared to controls, were less motivated to work for a reward when effort required was low and medium.  Associations between CU quantity and PLEs depended on 1/nT2* (at high 1/nT2*, CU positively predicted PLEs). Daily concentrate hits interacted with 1/nT2* in the left putamen (β=51.58, 95% CI, 12.07, 91.09, p=0.01) and right thalamus (β=70.93, 95% CI, 12.32, 129.54, p =0.02), daily cannabis grams in the left putamen (β=73.34, 95% CI, 12.32, 129.54, p=0.02), right putamen (β=101.69, 95% CI, 41.72, 161.67, p=0.001), and right thalamus (β=102.38, 95% CI, 28.00, 176.77, p=0.01). Conclusions and Relevance: Adolescent CU was associated with alterations in dopamine-relevant neural and behavioral indices as a function of PLEs. Behaviorally, this manifested as less reward motivation and strategic action. Consistent with prior research on psychosis-spectrum vulnerability and dopamine-related neurophysiology, elevated 1/nT2* was observed to moderate the link between CU and PLEs in key subcortical brain regions. Longitudinal studies are needed to understand the timing and mechanism of neurobehavioral reward processing alterations.

articles.title: Chatbot and Problematic Integration: Two Tests among U.S. Users
articles.authors: Junwen M. Hu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are token-based, probabilistic engines that produce most likely answers based on trained models and user input. In this work, I draw upon the problematic integration (PI) theory to conceptualize human-AI interaction (HAII) as communication processes that are aimed to address users’ problematic probabilistic orientations (PP). I propose that (1) PP prompt people to seek answers from AI chatbots and (2) that the extent to which chatbot responses address PP shapes interaction outcomes. Two studies tested these propositions using national age-matching samples of AI chatbot users in the United States (age range=18-85 years; mean age=41 years). Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey and Study 2 was an interactive experiment where participants talked to chatbots about one of twenty validated and pretested life concerns and rated chatbot-generated responses addressing their concern. Findings lend partial support to my propositions and offer insights into how AI chatbots may shape communication and human cognition.

articles.title: Now You See Me: Associations between Student Outcomes and Instructor Visibility in Online Learning Contexts
articles.authors: Lindsay Ackerman; William J. Chopik
articles.abstract: Online classroom environments may be associated with compromised student engagement and learning outcomes and behaviors, partially arising from a lack of instructor visibility. We tested the effect of watching instructor-led videos on learning outcomes in online environments. Study 1 (N = 600) was a randomized experiment testing whether participants who watched videos of an instructor delivering information reported higher engagement and understanding compared to participants who read equivalent text. In a small, applied Study 2 (N = 30, in an online course), we investigated classroom associations between watching instructor-led videos and subjective (e.g., self-reported engagement) and objective (e.g., time spent on course page) student learning outcomes and behaviors. In the classroom study, watching the instructor-led videos was associated with course engagement, connection to the instructor, and objective learning behaviors. However, in the experimental study, those who read the text performed better than those who watched the videos, though applications to classroom contexts may be limited. This work provides insight into the utility of visual and audio instructor representation in facilitating positive learning outcomes for students in online classrooms and invites educators to consider how best to engage students in online courses.

articles.title: Beyond delay: Discounting rewards for sustained self-control
articles.authors: Justin Wahlers; Jonathan Westlake; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Steven Seung-Suk Kang; Delwyn Catley; Seung-Lark Lim
articles.abstract:
Conventional intertemporal choice measures (e.g., delay discounting) often focus on the
cost of waiting for a reward. Yet, achieving many long-term health goals also requires
continuously exerting self-control while forgoing an immediately rewarding alternative. To
quantify these subjective costs, we introduced a novel abstinence discounting paradigm and
tested it in a consequential context: nicotine use. Abstinence discounting assessed one’s
preference for larger monetary rewards contingent on maintaining nicotine abstinence versus
smaller, noncontingent monetary rewards that do not require abstinence. Among e-cigarette users
(N = 253; Mage = 28.66, SDage = 4.22, 54.15% female, 45.85% male; 57.71% White, 20.16%
Black, 9.09% Hispanic, 6.32% Mixed), abstinence discounting related more closely and
consistently with nicotine dependence, craving, and cessation motivation while explaining
unique variance in these outcomes beyond delay discounting. These findings support extending
intertemporal choice research beyond the temporal distance of outcomes to consider the
sustained self-control demands required to achieve them.

articles.title: An Open-Source Standardized Pipeline for Equitable Observations of Interactive Behavioral Dynamics: Theory-driven Measurement, Analysis, and Masking
articles.authors: Arkadiusz Białek; Wim Pouw; James Trujillo; Fred Hasselman; Babajide Owoyele; Natalia Siekiera; Joanna Raczaszek-Leonardi; Travis J. Witshire
articles.abstract: Behavioral observation has a longstanding tradition in psychology. However, its reliance on manual coding makes observational methods costly and prone to biases that arise from the inherent limits of coding schemes and from the subjectivity of human raters. Behavioral observation research therefore has drawbacks in terms of applicability, accessibility, reproducibility, and equitability. Computer vision (CV) methods have promise in this regard. In the context of quantifying human movement, CV approaches to pose estimation are becoming increasingly precise and have the benefit of being non-intrusive, reproducible, and low-cost. With such methods, human movement in videos can be processed as multivariate time-series data, offering a basis for a more comprehensive analysis of individual, interpersonal, and social dynamics, opening up the possibility for the widespread study of diverse populations in out-of-lab real-world contexts. Fulfilling such a promise goes beyond technical progress, it requires a theory-driven implementation of new accessible observational methods made equitable to learn. To showcase this promise, we present a CV pipeline with analyses of the temporal dynamics of dyadic interactions, including a cross-cultural investigation of movement fluidity in sibling cooperation during task-focused interactions and longitudinal assessments of infant-caregiver coordination during free-play sessions. The pipeline incorporates a pedagogical computational notebook, pose estimation (YOLOv8), theory-driven linear and non-linear time series analysis, and a CV method for more privacy-aware video data archiving. Together, this pipeline showcases a promising advancement in behavioral observation methods, expanding both who can conduct research and who can benefit from it.

articles.title: The Longitudinal THRIVE study Protocol: Social and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Risk and Resilience in Young People with a History of Childhood Adversity
articles.authors: Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Maximilian König; Pauline Wessels; Hannah Dorsman; Antoinette Haverhals; THRIVE consortium; Peter Bos; Geert-Jan Will; Anne-Laura Van Harmelen
articles.abstract:
Introduction
Childhood adversity (CA) is among the strongest predictors of mental health problems. CA refers to experiences that are likely to require significant adaptation by an average child and that represent a deviation from the expectable environment. CA-related alterations in social and cognitive functioning may result in the thinning of social networks and increases in stressful peer interactions, which subsequently lead to mental health problems. The THRIVE study takes a longitudinal approach to investigate these proposed prospective relationships by examining whether and how social, cognitive, and neurobiological mechanisms interact to shape friendship support, stressful peer interactions, and mental health functioning over time.
Methods and analysis
The ongoing THRIVE study aims to recruit 288 participants aged 18-24 years who retrospectively self-report CA. This longitudinal study comprises six sessions in total. Participants complete an online baseline assessment of mental health, social support, stress experiences, and early life experiences, followed by an in-unit deep-phenotyping session. Assessments include self-report measures, cortisol measures, computerized cognitive tasks, and functional neuroimaging paradigms assessing stress and social evaluation. Participants subsequently complete four online follow-up assessments at 3-month intervals. Using data collected at the in-unit session, we aim to test whether CA is associated with biased emotion processing, blunted feedback learning and enhanced stress responses, and whether social support from peers may moderate these effects. The longitudinal design further enables us to test whether CA contributes to mental health problems through its impact on cognitive functioning, which over time leads to reduced social support and increased social stress. By elucidating how cognitive and social functioning contribute to mental health outcomes following CA, the THRIVE study aims to inform the development of interventions that foster resilience in young people.
Ethics and dissemination
The THRIVE study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee Leiden-The Hague-Delft (NL80017.058.21). The study was co-created with the Augeo Youth Task Force, a panel of young adults with lived experience of CA, who contribute throughout the research process. Findings will be disseminated through scientific publications, conference presentations, preprints, and public engagement activities.

articles.title: Speech Onset Time at Home or in the Lab: The Role of Testing Environment and Experimenter Presence.
articles.authors: Giorgio Piazza; Natalia Kartushina; Christoforos Souganidis; James E. Flege; Clara Martin
articles.abstract: Psycholinguistic research has become increasingly reliant on online experimentation, which has also grown more attractive for studying speech production. However, concerns remain about data quality in online settings and the absence of experimenters to ensure participant engagement. In this pre-registered study, we used two tasks—picture naming and reading aloud—to test whether the lexical frequency effect (Low Frequency words > High Frequency words) on speech onset times can be reliably detected in online environments (run at Home), both with and without experimenter supervision. Participants completed the same tasks under four conditions, varying by Supervision (between-subjects: Supervised vs. Unsupervised) and Environment (within-subjects: Lab vs. Home): Lab-Supervised, HomeSupervised, Lab-Unsupervised, and Home-Unsupervised. Frequency effects emerged across all conditions except Home-Supervised for the reading aloud task, where the effect was in the expected direction but non-significant (~12 ms). All other conditions yielded consistent frequency effects (~17–38 ms), comparable to previous online and lab-based findings. Notably, participants were faster at home than in the lab (~10 ms), and unsupervised settings yielded the largest effect sizes, suggesting that experimenter presence may inadvertently dampen subtle effects, possibly due to increased self-monitoring or reduced comfort. These findings validate the use of online platforms for speech production research and highlight the nuanced influence of supervision on experimental outcomes.

articles.title: Beyond Pre-Post Comparisons: A Comprehensive Effect Size Framework for Intensive Longitudinal Interventions via Time-Varying Modeling
articles.authors: Xiaohui Luo; Yue Liu; Hongyun Liu; Laura Francina Bringmann
articles.abstract: Intensive longitudinal interventions (ILIs), which deliver repeated interventions in people’s daily lives while intensively tracking their psychological states, offer unique opportunities for ecologically valid, real-time, and personalized support. However, there is a striking mismatch between the richness of the data these studies generate and the simplicity of the methods used to evaluate them: evaluations still rely largely on pre-post mean comparisons that collapse dozens or even hundreds of observations per person into a few summary statistics. To resolve this mismatch, we introduce a comprehensive effect size framework based on Bayesian multilevel time-varying autoregressive (TV-AR) models within the generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) approach. The framework organizes effect sizes along four dimensions: subject level (population-average, individual-specific, and between-group), parameter type (mean level, autoregressive effect, and variance), temporal scale (integrated and time-specific), and study phase (active intervention and post-intervention decay). These metrics move researchers beyond whether an intervention works to when effects emerge, plateau, or fade, how the intervention reshapes the dynamics and stability of a process, and for whom it is effective. We demonstrate the framework with data from a mindfulness-based ILI targeting negative affect, in which an intervention and a control group were assessed before and during the intervention, and provide openly available annotated R code and a tutorial. Overall, the framework provides a practical and flexible toolkit for evaluating ILIs, supporting the broader shift toward a more dynamic, process-oriented, and personalized intervention science.

articles.title: Why the body comes first: Effects of experimenter touch on infants’ word finding
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Amanda Seidl; Ruth Tincoff; Christopher Baker; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
The lexicon of 6-month-olds is comprised of names and body part words. Unlike names, body part words do not often occur in isolation in the input. This presents a puzzle: How have infants been able to pull out these words from the continuous stream of speech at such a young age? We hypothesize that caregivers’ interactions directed at and on the infant’s body may be at the root of their early acquisition of body part words. An
artificial language segmentation study shows that experimenter-provided synchronous tactile cues help 4-month-olds to find words in continuous speech. A follow-up study suggests that this facilitation cannot be reduced to the highly social situation in which the directed interaction occurs. Taken together, these studies suggests that direct caregiver-infant interaction, exemplified in this study by touch cues, may play a key role
in infants’ ability to find word boundaries and suggests that words linked with caregiver touches may comprise early vocabulary items.

articles.title: AI-Podcast Misinformation: Testing Active versus Passive Inoculations
articles.authors: Paul McIlhiney; Emily Rebecca Spearing; Ullrich K. H. Ecker
articles.abstract: Realistic, misleading AI-generated audio content is a new threat to digital-media consumers. This study examined the effects of misleading AI-generated podcasts that presented false claims about nanoparticles in sunscreen (Experiment 1; N = 463), or microwaves damaging foods (Experiment 2; N = 500). U.S. participants either received a misleading podcast, misleading article, or a neutral podcast (control). To test interventions, misleading podcasts were preceded by either a passive inoculation explaining how AI-generated information can deceive, an active inoculation that added an educational activity, or no intervention. The podcast and article produced comparable increases in misinformed beliefs. Both inoculations significantly reduced general trust in AI-generated information and attenuated the podcast’s impact on beliefs. Results demonstrate that AI-generated audio can influence health-related beliefs as strongly as text-based misinformation, and that brief AI-source-focused inoculations can mitigate, but not eliminate, its persuasive impact. Findings inform interventions targeting emerging forms of AI-driven misinformation.

articles.title: Integrating science and design in the development of Detour: A mobile intervention for youth smoking cessation
articles.authors: Suhaavi Kochhar; Maartje Luijten; Ken Koontz; Hanneke Scholten
articles.abstract: Digital smoking cessation interventions for adolescents and young adults (AYAs) often either lack a strong evidence base or fail to engage their intended users. Integrating psychological science with design-based methods offers a promising route to interventions, yet the processes behind such integration are rarely reported in detail. In this paper, we describe the development of Detour, a mobile smoking cessation intervention for AYAs, redesigned from an earlier app (HitnRun) using the Bloombox Toolkit to integrate science and design throughout. We describe how six psychological mechanisms including smoking cue devaluation and delay discounting were translated into intervention components. We used an iterative, interdisciplinary process involving behavioural scientists, app designers, and an ongoing youth advisory board. Additionally, we included over 380 AYAs across focus groups, play tests, and qualitative questionnaires. We then reflect on our experience integrating design and science for intervention development and share practical challenges encountered, including budgeting for interdisciplinary teams, retaining youth participants, and regulatory delays. By reporting these processes and challenges transparently, we aim to support other researchers in designing digital health interventions that are both scientifically grounded and engaging for their target users.

articles.title: Designing for Realistic Self-Assessment: Reducing Illusions of Competence in Human–Technology Interaction
articles.authors: Patrick P. Weis; Wilfried Kunde
articles.abstract: Humans frequently overestimate their unaided problem-solving abilities after receiving cognitive support—a bias known as illusion of competence. Such miscalibration harms the ability to seek and sustain support and thus undermines adaptive reliance on technology. In four experiments, we examined how subtle interventions can reduce this bias during technology-assisted problem solving. In Experiment 1, short metacognitive prompts inviting reflection on the contribution of cognitive support abolished the bias. In Experiment 2, the intervention of emphasizing the external origin of the support was tested. The emphasis was implemented by framing the support as coming from a humanlike (a robot face) or a nonhumanlike (a soft-ware window) entity. Both emphases of external origin reduced the bias to a similar extent. Moreover, engaging in unaided problem solving also abolished and even reversed the bias, leading to an illusion of incompetence. We failed to replicate these findings after methodolog-ical refinement in Experiment 3 that included more pronounced external support. When keep-ing refinements but again using less pronounced support, replications succeeded in Experiment 4. Our findings demonstrate that minimal interventions can enhance a problem solver’s meta-cognitive accuracy when receiving cognitive support. We discuss implications for the design of cognitive human-computer interactions that promote realistic self-assessment and thus sus-tainable collaborations.

articles.title: Translation and Validation of the Japanese version of the Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (J-APEQ)
articles.authors: Kaishu Iijima; Hiroto Yamamoto; Yuko Yotsumoto; Shuhei Iimura
articles.abstract: Picky eating is a multidimensional eating behavior that has been studied primarily in children, although it is also observed in adults. The Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (APEQ) was developed to assess multiple dimensions of picky eating in adults, but a validated Japanese version has not been available. The present study aimed to develop and validate a Japanese version of the APEQ (J-APEQ) (Researcher-led translation) and to compare it with a translation generated using generative artificial intelligence (AI-generated translation). The researcher-led translation was completed by 892 Japanese adults, with 210 participants completing the scale again after three weeks. A separate sample of 939 participants completed an AI-generated translation. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original four-factor structure of the researcher-led J-APEQ, and a second-order factor model also showed acceptable fit. The composite score showed adequate internal consistency, while reliability was lower for some subscales, particularly Meal Disengagement and Taste Aversion. Test–retest reliability was moderate, and correlations with food neophobia, disgust, and eating-attitude measures generally supported convergent validity. The AI-generated translation showed a factor structure and reliability broadly comparable to those of the researcher-led translation. Measurement invariance analyses supported configural, threshold, metric, and partial scalar invariance between the two versions. In the present study, however, the researcher-led translation was the version formally validated and established as the Japanese APEQ (J-APEQ), whereas the AI-generated translation was included for comparison. These findings support the use of the J-APEQ for assessing picky eating in Japanese adults and suggest that generative AI may be useful as a tool for psychological scale translation, although human review and validation remain necessary.

articles.title: Material Life Satisfaction Increases Willingness to Engage in Costly Climate Action
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Maien S. M. Sachisthal; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change requires sustained public support for policies and willingness to engage in actions that may incur personal costs. Understanding the social conditions under which citizens are willing to support such measures is important for assessing the feasibility of ambitious climate action. Using data from a large, population-weighted survey of Dutch citizens (N = 22,749) and covariate adjustments informed by directed acyclic graphs, we estimate the effect of different facets of life satisfaction on willingness to contribute 1% of monthly household income to address climate change. We find a strong effect of material life satisfaction: individuals who are very satisfied with their material conditions are more than three times more likely to be willing to contribute than those who are not satisfied at all. In contrast, satisfaction with social life, physical health, and mental health show weak or negligible independent effects on willingness once material life satisfaction and relevant background variables are taken into account. We discuss the implications of our results for the design and acceptability of climate policies that are perceived as placing burdens on households.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: Trust and Intellectual Humility as Necessary Conditions for AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Recently, AI models demonstrated a remarkable ability to facilitate opinion change, a notoriously difficult task between human communicators. Here, we focus on the dispositions that characterize message recipients, specifically identifying trust in AI, intellectual humility (IH), and their interplay as key factors in acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Across two studies with an online British sample (N=294), we replicated findings showing significant attitude change regarding legal immigrants following brief interactions with GPT. Crucially, our findings reveal that opinion change is contingent on higher IH and greater trust in AI, independently and jointly, predicting greater acceptance of counter-attitudinal information. Experimentally capturing the centrality of open-mindedness (IH) and source sensitivity (Trust) highlights how epistemic vigilance constrains AI’s persuasive impact and sheds new light on the persuasion literature by revisiting the role of source credibility. Future research should examine whether these dispositional effects extend to long-term behavioral patterns across broader real-world contexts.

articles.title: Registered Report: Does the valence-dominance model apply to deepfake faces? Validation and its impact on deepfake detection
articles.authors: Gianmarco Convertino; Mara Stockner; Michela Marchetti; Danilo Mitaritonna; Luca Corvitto; Luca Maiano; Lorenzo Papa; Irene Amerini; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was  applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

articles.title: How Employees Experience (Im)balance with W-ICTs: an Ideal Type Analysis of Digital Well-being
articles.authors: Lore Geldof; Ann DeSmet; Alice Verlinden; Elfi Baillien
articles.abstract:
Purpose: The rapid digitalization of work has intensified employees' connectivity to work-related information and communication technologies (W-ICTs), creating both opportunities and risks for digital well-being. While prior research highlights these ambivalent effects, little is known about how employees emotionally experience digital (im)balance with W-ICTs. Hence, we aim to develop a typology detailing such emotional experiences.
Design/Methodology/Approach: Drawing on 40 qualitative interviews (60% female; Mage = 40.25; SD = 9.16), this study abductively develops an experiential typology of digital (im)balance with W-ICT using Ideal Type Analysis. The identified types capture variations in emotional experiences (i.e., affective and cognitive) and digital connectivity processes (DCPs; i.e., interference, boundary blurring, exposure, and time displacement).
Findings: Eight Ideal Types are identified, comprising four experiences of digital imbalance and four experiences of digital balance. The types differ in emotional valence with configurations of DCPs. A comparison of the types show distinct emotional experiences while similar DCPs may occur. This is contextualized in the organisational setting.
Originality: By integrating emotional experiences and DCPs, the typology advances a configurational understanding of employee digital well-being. By contextualizing the types in organizational conditions, the findings suggest that highly connected work environments are not inherently tied to experiences of imbalance.

articles.title: Social readiness and public legitimacy of vaccine mandates: comparative evidence from three countries
articles.authors: Uwana Evers; Joshua Lake; Katie Attwell
articles.abstract: Vaccine mandates are used to increase vaccine uptake during infectious disease emergencies; however, they expose enduring tensions between collective protection and individual autonomy. Existing research treats public opinion toward mandates as a binary – recording only whether people support or oppose them. This study conceptualizes mandate attitudes as comprising two distinct dimensions – perceived public-health protection and concern for rights/autonomy – and examines these in survey data from Australia (N=4,208), France (N=3,858), and Italy (N=3,973). In this framework, mandate legitimacy encompasses both perceived collective benefits and perceived infringements on individual autonomy. Analysis revealed divergent patterns: the protection dimension was more strongly associated with institutional trust and vaccination behavior across all three countries, while rights-based attitudes were more variable. Moreover, trust in health-relevant institutions was more robustly associated with the protection dimension than trust in political institutions or media, but this did not extend uniformly to rights-based attitudes. In France, rights-based attitudes were independent of health system trust; in Italy, rights attitudes were unrelated to national government trust, suggesting rights-based objections operate partly independently of institutional confidence. Feeling compelled to vaccinate against COVID-19 was negatively associated with both dimensions across all countries, indicating coercive vaccination experiences may deplete legitimacy capital available for future mandate deployment. Findings suggest that general mandate approval can conceal substantial rights-based resistance, and that institutional trust is insufficient to reduce rights-based mandate resistance Communication strategies that build health institution trust, minimize coercive framing, and are sensitive to political contexts might sustain the public legitimacy required for effective pandemic preparedness.

articles.title: Narrative Entropy
articles.authors: Devin R Wright; Fritz Breithaupt; Anthony F. Beavers; Jacob G. Foster; Jisun An
articles.abstract: Narrative Entropy Theory (NET) proposes that we inhabit narrative environments: ecosystems of cultures, communities, and personal histories constructed from overlapping stories. Narrative entropy is a dynamic, relational property of these ecosystems: the degree of constraint and uncertainty over the interpretive possibility space available within them. At relatively lower entropy, interpretive activity concentrates around recurrent structures, makes narrative and shared worlds easier to navigate and facilitates shared meaning and experience. At relatively higher entropy, more possibilities remain available, which makes interpretation less anticipable and preserves opportunities for interpretive plurality, perspective-taking, and the generation of new meaning. In this way, narrative environments shape how meaning is interpreted and shared and which experiences and perspectives become available for recognition. NET connects the structure of these environments to cognition, communication, and social coordination while treating narrative as both organized structure and embodied activity. We provide an initial empirical demonstration using 475,716 English-language news articles from sources in 65 countries. We operationalize narrative entropy through topic attention, microframe complexity, and narrative fluency (the compressibility of traversal through narrative networks) and compare these measures with national indices of expressive freedom. All measures covary with these indices in the predicted directions and together account for more than one-third of the cross-national variance in the World Press Freedom Index. Together, these results show that narrative environments leave measurable traces in the artifacts they produce, making their structure empirically tractable for scientific inquiry.

articles.title: Physical endpoint contact enhances visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback in virtual reality
articles.authors: Ryan George King; Guy Wallis
articles.abstract: When reaching for a visually defined target, sensory information not only guides the preparation and execution of the reaching response but also serves as a crucial source of error feedback. Research on visually guided reaching has typically emphasised the contribution of visual feedback to movement preparation and execution.  However, visually guided reaching also depends on non-visual sensory information. Here, we focus on the role of haptic endpoint feedback and visual hand feedback and how they interact to regulate behaviour. Thirty-six participants completed a rapid reaching task using a virtual reality head-mounted display, allowing us to manipulate endpoint haptic feedback and visual feedback of the moving hand. Participants completed a vibrotactile feedback condition, providing vibration feedback to the fingertip upon target touch, and a vibrotactile and physical contact feedback condition, providing additional physical surface contact. On 25% of trials, the virtual hand disappeared after movement initiation. The addition of physical contact led participants to initiate movement earlier, increase movement times, and spend proportionally more time decelerating, resulting in improved endpoint accuracy. Across kinematic measures, the effects of physical contact did not interact with visual hand feedback. Additionally, of six presence and embodiment items, only the item asking whether touch felt like one's own differed between conditions. Overall, these findings suggest physical contact improves visuomotor control beyond vibrotactile feedback alone. However, this advantage appears to be selective, increasing the realism of touch rather than overall presence or embodiment and not compensating for a loss of visual feedback of the hand.

articles.title: Recent Clinical Encounters for Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviours: Disclosure, Assessment, Missed Opportunities, and Implications for Practice
articles.authors: Jennifer Q. P. Nguyen; Glenn A Melvin; David John Hallford
articles.abstract:
Objective: Many individuals who die by suicide have contact with healthcare services in the months preceding their death, making these interactions critical opportunities for identification, intervention, and support. However, little is known about how individuals experiencing suicidal thoughts and behaviours (STBs) perceive recent clinical encounters, including how these experiences are discussed and managed.
Method: Australian adults (N = 266; Mage = 32.9; range = 18-71 years) who had experienced STBs and consulted with a mental health professional within the past two weeks completed an online survey examining suicide-related enquiry, disclosure experiences, clinician responses, and satisfaction.
Results: Psychologists were the most commonly consulted clinicians (49.2%), and 90.8% reported having seen the same clinician previously. Although 95.7% of participants considered discussing their STBs at least somewhat important, only 67.9% reported discussing these experiences with clinicians. Among those who did not discuss STBs, 50.0% reported that they had not been asked. Participants also reported that clinicians more frequently enquired about general emotional wellbeing (80.6%) than directly about STBs (55.3%). Among participants who did discuss STBs, 52.1% reported withholding information, while 46.2% reported feeling hesitant to disclose. Safety planning (36.9%) and follow-up (37.4%) were reported infrequently despite being viewed as important and helpful. Nevertheless, 75.4% reported being satisfied with their recent interactions.
Conclusions: Despite generally positive experiences with these interactions, the findings highlight opportunities to strengthen suicide prevention by creating opportunities to discuss STBs beyond initial clinical encounters, supporting disclosure through compassionate care, and ensuring that suicide-specific care is provided where appropriate following identification.
Key words: suicide; suicidal ideation; suicidal behaviour; disclosure; non-disclosure; clinician-patient communication

articles.title: BoundBase-EN (BBEN): A database of English bound bases in texts for children and young people
articles.authors: Maria Korochkina; Nicola Dawson; Danielle Colenbrander
articles.abstract: Sensitivity to morphological structure is considered a hallmark of skilled reading; however, much of the extant literature has focused on affixation (e.g., -er in teacher) and complex words with free bases (e.g., teach in teacher). This focus has left bound bases (e.g., ceiv(e) in receive) relatively unexplored, despite their prevalence in English and potential importance as a source of morphological regularity in print experience. Using a combination of automated and manual procedures, we developed BoundBase-EN (BBEN), a publicly available database providing lexical statistics and etymological information for 328 English bound bases occurring in texts for readers from age 5 to young adulthood. The BBEN data provide key insights into the distributional properties of these units. First, most bound bases occur infrequently and in a limited number of distinct words, with only a small set accounting for the majority of readers’ exposure. Second, children encounter bound-base words from the earliest years of independent reading, with developmental increases in exposure reflecting greater token frequency (i.e., more encounters with the same words) rather than type frequency (i.e., greater diversity in words containing bound bases). Third, although relatively infrequent overall, many bound-base words occur more frequently than complex words containing free bases, suggesting that they occupy a middle ground in children’s experience of morphological regularities. These findings highlight the importance of investigating bound bases for understanding how morphological knowledge is acquired and processed, and for informing approaches to morphology instruction. The BBEN database provides a foundation for such research.

articles.title: Does This Still Represent Me: Social Media and Narrative Identity Processes in Emerging Adults
articles.authors: Irena Stojković; Marijana Veselinović; Božidar Filipović
articles.abstract: The present study explored how emerging adults experience their social media engagement and how these experiences may be relevant to narrative identity development from the perspective of McLean et al.’s (2007) process model of narrative identity development. Individual semi-structured interviews with 27 emerging adults (19 females, 8 males) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes were developed. The theme Social media as a socially responsive context for self-expression captures perceptions of social media as a context for self-expression, exchange of perspectives, and meaningful interpersonal connections. The theme Selective online self-presentation captures perceptions of social media self-presentation as selective and providing a partial, potentially misleading, representation of a person. The theme Curating the social media profile through reflection on past and present selves describes tension between preserving personally significant memories on social media profiles and removing content that no longer represents how one currently sees oneself. Taken together, the themes suggest that social media represent a distinctive context for situated storytelling in which self-representations are socially negotiated, selectively constructed, and retrospectively curated. The affordances of this context may shape these storytelling processes and autobiographical reasoning, potentially contributing to a greater emphasis on thematic coherence than on temporal and causal coherence.

articles.title: Preschoolers can coordinate with each other to communicate about novel referents
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Robert Zane Sparks; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: Learning language requires learning not only the content of language, but also how to use language to communicate. Iterated reference games provide a window into such skills, requiring sustained interactive communication as participants converge on mutually understandable names for initially novel referents. Some early experiments are interpreted as evidence that 4-5-year-old children cannot converge on the mutually understandable names needed to succeed in an iterated reference game. Here, we revisit young children's referential communicative abilities using a simpler, child-friendly version of the iterated reference game paradigm. Across 4 experiments and 82 pairs of children (N=158), we found that 4-5-year-olds could successfully establish reference with each other. Children were 81% accurate, and they often used descriptions similar to their partner's. These findings suggest that children’s capacity to construct effective referring expressions in novel contexts emerges earlier than previously thought, consistent with the view that children show early pragmatic competence in supportive contexts.

articles.title: Group One Session Treatment: A Feasibility Study in Highly Spider Fearful Youth
articles.authors: Raphael Gutzweiler; Lou Aberfeld; Léonie Rodon; Boris Tolstich
articles.abstract:
Background: One Session Treatments (OST) represent an intensive and efficacious therapeutic modality for the treatment of anxiety disorders. To date, research has been predominantly focused on individual OST in adults. Research on group OST with children and adolescents is scarce. The objective of the present study is to examine the feasibility of a group OST for highly spider fearful children and adolescents, and to conduct an initial evaluation of this treatment.
Methods: A total of 19 children and adolescents (M = 11.95 years, SD = 2.66) participated in the group OST. We assessed fear of spiders using questionnaires, a clinical interview, and a behavioural approach task. Furthermore, an assessment of disgust sensitivity was conducted. Assessments were administered prior to, at the end of (post), and three months following (FU) the group OST.
Results: Participants reported a high reduction in levels of spider fear (Hedges' g = 2.00 (post), g = 1.7 (FU)), increase in behavioural approach, and full remission (in 84% of cases). Participants, their caregivers, and therapists rated overall moderate to high improvements. No effects were found regarding disgust sensitivity. Group OST effects remained stable during the 3-month FU-interval.
Implications: Group OST in spider fearful children and adolescents provided evidence for feasibility and efficiency.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Social Sharing of Emotion: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Sarah Taylor O'Brien; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Sooyeon Kim; Peter Koval; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos
articles.abstract: After experiencing an emotional event, people almost always talk to other people about their experience. People generally believe this process—labelled social sharing of emotion—is beneficial, but empirical findings on the outcomes are mixed. We argue that underlying these mixed findings is an issue with the conceptual clarity of social sharing. In pursuit of conceptual clarity and in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we conducted a scoping review to map how social sharing has been defined and operationalized in the literature. Our review included 99 articles, including 128 studies, empirically investigating social sharing of emotion (sourced from PsychInfo (Ovid), ProQuest Dissertations and Theses Global, PsyArXiv, and PubMed). From these articles, we identified common features of researchers’ definitions and operationalizations of social sharing, highlighting what researchers deem central to the process. We found large heterogeneity in how social sharing has been conceptualized, which may contribute to the mixed findings on sharing thus far. For instance, we identified 16 unique features of social sharing in researchers’ definitions, 11 unique features in self-report study operationalizations, and 10 unique features in manipulation study operationalizations. Based on our findings, we propose a new consensus definition of social sharing, outlining necessary and sufficient features of the process. In all, this review elucidates a common behavior that is gaining relevance in a world with more ways to connect with each other than ever before.

articles.title: How Meaning Shapes a Rule: Neural Signatures of Morphological Learning and Generalization
articles.authors: Marianne Azar; Alec Marantz
articles.abstract: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. In language, we apply it to connect what words mean to what they are made of, such as their suffixes. This is a morphosemantic relation, and it helps us process words we already know and easily acquire new words by composing their meaning. How is this relation acquired, and how does it manifest into generalization for understanding new words? In this study, we investigated the brain basis of these questions through an English-based artificial language study, where learners read sentences to learn a suffix-meaning relation of new words like “thinkle”. Words were either meaningful (places or things) or had no clear meaning. Each suffix family had majority and minority meaning words that participants had to keep track of for testing. For meaningful words in training, we found that higher performance scores predicted higher selective engagement in the left inferior frontal gyrus, specifically the pars triangularis and pars opercularis. In testing, both learned and generalized words, both increased lateral prefrontal cortex engagement. Meanwhile, words with no clear meaning had a much more diffuse brain engagement, recruiting bilateral temporoparietal regions. This resembles the processing of abstract words from previous literature. We found no difference between majority and minority meaning words, especially with the variance in participants’ performance strategies, but found differences in what predicted significant brain activity based on strategy difference. This study grounds itself in the reality of word and affixal semantics with previous research on language learning and universals. Ultimately, it lends a learning paradigm that resembles natural language learning across many languages to carefully investigate its brain basis, while addressing an understudied aspect of rule generalization: ambiguity.

articles.title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Research in Aphasia: An AI-Assisted Scoping Review and Semantic Network Analysis
articles.authors: Mengyang Qiu; Siena Sun; Sara NassrElgrgawi; Zirui Feng
articles.abstract:
Purpose: A shared view of artificial intelligence (AI) research in aphasia is needed to locate related work across clinical and computing publications. This scoping review mapped research topics and connections, AI method families over time, and reported evaluation and participant characteristics relevant to clinical applicability.
Method: Seven sources were searched for publications from January 2010 through June 2026. Two large language models (LLMs) independently screened records and extracted information from publication abstracts. Disagreements within and across LLMs were manually reviewed and resolved. To check screening accuracy, three human reviewers independently screened a sample without seeing model responses. Semantic network analysis of the abstracts identified research communities and connecting studies.
Results: LLM-assisted screening identified 412 primary studies. Its decisions agreed with the human majority on 91% of 145 sampled records. Network analysis identified 12 communities, with partial separation between clinical and computing publications and general separation between post-stroke aphasia and primary progressive aphasia studies. Deep learning and generative AI first appeared in clinical and computing publications in the same respective years and represented larger proportions of computing publications. Abstracts often lacked key evaluation and participant information: only 28 abstracts (7%) reported independent model testing, 21 (5%) clinical evaluation, and 34 (8%) aphasia severity.
Conclusions: The map provides entry points for exploring related research, and the workflow offers a foundation for future evidence syntheses in communication disorders. Clearer reporting of evaluation and participant characteristics could improve communication across disciplines and help readers identify relevant publications.

articles.title: Motivation to Act and Social Connection Sustain  Everyday Climate Change Conversations
articles.authors: Ovidia Stanoi; Alyssa Hannah Sinclair; Diego A. Reinero; Kirsten Lydic; Michael Mann; Danielle Cosme; Emily B. Falk
articles.abstract: Public concern about climate change is high, yet most Americans rarely talk about it. This project investigated the social, cognitive, and emotional factors that motivate or prevent climate change conversations in everyday life. Across three studies using cross-sectional surveys (N = 2,804), a qualitative elicitation survey (N = 202), and longitudinal daily diary data (N = 1,487), we found that most people want to talk more about climate change but often refrain due to anticipated conflict, emotional discomfort, and perceived goal misalignment. When conversations occurred in daily life, however, they were generally pleasant and likely to be sustained when people focused on motivation to act and emotional closeness. Notably, experiences of conflict, negative emotions, and dismissal were relatively infrequent and did not reduce willingness to re-engage, contrary to common expectations. Together, these findings point to incorrect expectations about the social and emotional consequences of climate change conversations as barriers to dialogue.

articles.title: Popular nonfiction can durably shift politically relevant attitudes—and so can a much shorter AI summary
articles.authors: Joshua Paul White; Adam J. Berinsky; James Patoriza; David Gertler Rand
articles.abstract: Can reading a chapter of popular nonfiction shift politically relevant attitudes among resistant partisans, and, if so, can an AI-generated summary do so just as effectively? In a preregistered experiment, N = 555 Republicans were randomized to read “The Cyber Sleuth” by Geraldine Brooks—a profile of IRS cybercrime investigators from Michael Lewis’s Who Is Government?—or a control text, and further randomized to either the full text (∼5300 words) or a much shorter AI-generated summary (∼1400 words). Reading “The Cyber Sleuth” produced wide-ranging attitude change relative to control: IRS favorability increased substantially (d = 0.62), with spillover to civil-service favorability (d = 0.37) and opposition to DOGE-led workforce reductions (d = 0.40). These effects remained significant two months later (ds 0.14–0.19). Strikingly, the AI-generated summary produced effects statistically indistinguishable from the full text. Popular nonfiction, and an AI summary thereof, can be an effective tool for politically relevant attitude change, even on a polarized, partisan issue.

articles.title: LLM-Generated Social-Desirability Ratings for Forced-Choice Questionnaire Construction: A Preregistered Downstream Validation
articles.authors: Yui Furukawa; Kyosuke Bunji; Kensuke Okada
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly produce evaluative judgments, but rating-level human–model agreement does not establish whether they can replace human inputs in a downstream task. Using HEXACO personality items as a case study, we conduct a preregistered three-stage validation of whether LLM-generated social-desirability ratings can serve as inputs to forced-choice scale construction, a psychometric task that requires costly human ratings. In Stage I, three LLMs served as raters of item-level social desirability for sentence- and adjective-format items, with human ratings serving as references. In Stage II, human- and LLM-based ratings were entered into the same constrained optimization procedure. In Stage III, 400 participants completed the resulting forms, and latent trait estimates were compared using graded Thurstonian item response theory. LLM ratings showed strong item-level correspondence with human ratings (sentence: r = 0.942–0.963; adjective: r = 0.979–0.980), but optimized forms showed partial item overlap and sparse exact pair overlap. Despite these design differences, LLM-based forms produced latent trait estimates that closely matched those from human-based forms (mean r = 0.815 for sentence items and 0.768 for adjective items). These results support the conditional use of LLM-generated ratings as scalable construction inputs while showing why downstream validation is necessary.

articles.title: What Race Means for Health among Black Americans: How Microaggressions Shape Self-Efficacy and Readiness for Behavior Change
articles.authors: Amanda Almond
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives: Persistent racial disparities in cardiovascular health among Black Americans reflect not only structural inequities in the United States, but also the racialized meanings of cardiovascular disease reproduced through public and private health communication. Drawing on ecological systems theory, this research examines how beliefs linking race and cardiovascular disease are reinforced through routine clinical interactions and how these meanings shape health behavior change. Method: Across two experimental mixed-methods studies, a model integrating ecological, social–cognitive, and behavior-change frameworks was tested. In Study 1 (N = 374), health-message framing was experimentally manipulated to examine effects on self-efficacy and decisional balance while controlling for prior experiences of racial microaggression in medical contexts. Study 2 (N = 589) extended this work by testing whether conceptualizations of race as biological/genetic and social/political moderated these effects. A subset of participants (n = 57) voluntarily provided narratives of racially charged healthcare experiences, which were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize quantitative findings. Results: Racial microaggressions from health professionals disrupted self-efficacy and decisional balance for cardiovascular health behaviors. Endorsement of biological versus social race beliefs moderated these effects, shaping both their magnitude and direction. Qualitative findings revealed how everyday clinical interactions reproduce racialized meanings of disease risk and personal control. Conclusions: These findings identify clinical communication as a consequential site where racial meanings of disease are constructed and psychologically internalized, influencing motivation for health behavior change. Addressing biologically essentialist framing in healthcare may therefore be critical for strengthening self-regulation and reducing cardiovascular disparities among Black Americans.

Keywords: racial microaggressions; health communication; self-efficacy; decisional balance; Transtheoretical Model; ecological systems theory; racial essentialism; cardiovascular health disparities

Public significance statement: How health professionals and public campaigns talk about race matters for behavior change. This research shows that subtle racialized cues in medicine can weaken Black patients’ sense of control and readiness to take preventive action. Training clinicians to avoid biological essentialist framing may improve patient engagement and help reduce cardiovascular health disparities.

articles.title: The Quiet Window–Challenge Window Framework: A Conceptual Framework for Habit Formation During GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy
articles.authors: Holly R Hull; Melanie Rae Lenius Meister; Laura E Martin; Molly M. Fain; Sarah Crawford; Debra Sullivan; Alexandra R. Brown; Johanna G. Finkle
articles.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have transformed obesity treatment by producing substantial weight loss while altering appetite, food-related cognition, and eating behaviors. Although current clinical recommendations emphasize dietary quality, adequate protein intake, physical activity, and behavioral support during GLP-1RA therapy, they primarily focus on what behavior strategies should accompany treatment rather than when they may be most effective. Emerging evidence suggests that the cognitive and behavioral effects of GLP-1RA therapy are dynamic, creating periods during which healthy habits may be more readily established and later tested. We propose the Quiet Window-Challenge Window Framework, a conceptual model that reframes behavioral opportunity during GLP-1RA therapy as a dynamic process. The Quiet Window represents a temporary period of reduced food-related cognitive burden that facilitates habit acquisition, whereas the Challenge Window reflects increasing cognitive and environmental demands during which newly established habits are tested. A central hypothesis is that durable behavior change depends on the progressive transfer of behavioral regulation from pharmacologic support to resilient, self-sustaining habits through repeated practice, increasing automaticity, and subsequent testing under greater behavioral demands. We further propose that Quiet and Challenge Windows operate across multiple time points, including broader treatment phases and recurring weekly states within weekly dosing intervals. The framework generates testable hypotheses regarding food-related cognition, habit formation and resilience, and adaptive behavioral interventions. By conceptualizing behavioral opportunity as dynamic, this Framework shifts the focus from whether behavioral interventions should accompany GLP-1RA therapy to when they are most likely to promote durable behavior change.

articles.title: A Latent Oscillator Measurement Model to Simulate Emotional-Expression Score Dynamics in Video
articles.authors: Aleksandar Tomašević; Hudson Golino; Alexander P. Christensen
articles.abstract:
Facial-expression classifiers convert video into multivariate time series of scores with measurement
error from classifiers, videos, and recording conditions. Empirical score series cannot establish whether
the score channels reflect a smaller set of latent expressive processes or whether an analysis would recover
those processes. We introduce the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a data-generating
model that separates latent dynamics, time-varying activity, and a factor-analytic observation model.
The latent processes are damped, undamped, or amplifying linear oscillators. LOMM generates bounded
scores or continuous indicators. Study 1 used four-fold cross-fitting with scores from 100 MAFW videos
to calibrate LOMM and evaluate generated series on held-out videos. Median plausibility and coverage
were 0.970 and 0.920 for LOMM, versus 0.510 and 0.370 for a calibrated static logistic-normal generator.
Study 2 tested whether Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis (DynEGA), static EGA, GraphicalVAR,
and GIMME recovered a known dimensional structure from continuous indicators generated by LOMM.
At 100 observations per clip, with failed or timed-out fits counted as incorrect, correct-dimension
recovery was 0.939 for DynEGA, 0.884 for static EGA, 0.777 for GraphicalVAR, and 0.176 for GIMME.
Replacing the common fixed initialization with independent stationary starts for stable dimensions and
bounded independent starts for amplifying dimensions reduced recovery for DynEGA, static EGA, and
GraphicalVAR. The primary initialization was optimistic relative to this alternative. LOMM provides
a controlled test of whether an analysis recovers a specified latent structure before score patterns are
interpreted psychologically.

articles.title: Taking the speaker’s perspective? Investigating quantifier and implicature processing in an AI-language training paradigm using EEG-VR
articles.authors: Maria Spychalska; Ludmila Reimer; Marjolijn Dijkhuis; Peter Hagoort
articles.abstract:
Interpreting speaker meaning requires taking into account the speaker’s epistemic perspective, i.e., their access to relevant information. The extent to which listeners integrate this perspective during comprehension is known as the perspective-taking problem. We present the first EEG study to investigate the role of perspective-taking in the processing of quantifiers and scalar implicatures. Using immersive virtual reality, we asked participants to assist an AI, represented by a virtual agent, in learning to use quantifiers appropriately. Critically, the agent had limited access to the reference domain compared to the participant.

Our results show that when the speaker’s information access is restricted, listeners initially process the semantic content of quantified statements from an egocentric perspective. Effects of the speaker’s perspective emerge only later, reflected in a sustained anterior negativity. For pragmatically ambiguous sentences containing ``some", we observe neither an effect of speaker perspective nor evidence for scalar implicature processing. We argue that contexts requiring consideration of the speaker’s knowledge primarily support Gricean, weak implicatures, which are computed relatively late as post-propositional inferences.

articles.title: All BANG, little buck: Basic psychological needs are weakly linked with video gaming behavior
articles.authors: Nick Ballou; Tamás Andrei Földes; Matti Vuorre; Thomas Hakman; Kristoffer Magnusson; Andrew K Przybylski
articles.abstract: Psychological theories of media use often assume that subjective motivation affects observable behavior. Using video games as a test case, we examine this assumption by pairing repeated self-reports of motivation with objective digital trace data at scale. Across two datasets comprising tens of thousands of hours of gaming behavior, we test predictions derived from self-determination theory and the Basic Needs in Games (BANG) model, which posit that autonomy, competence, and relatedness experiences drive engagement. Study 1 (preregistered) analyzes 11k daily observations from 555 U.S. players with 30 days of multi-platform digital trace data. Study 2 (exploratory) examines 102k sessions from 9k PowerWash Simulator players, linking in-game experience prompts to behavioral logs. In both studies, need satisfaction was robustly associated with subjective states but showed weak or null associations with short-term gaming behavior, including subsequent play, session length, and return latency, across extensive preregistered and robustness analyses. These findings reveal a substantial motivation–behavior gap and suggest that SDT-based accounts may overestimate the role of need satisfaction in explaining when or how much people play. Data and code are available under a CC0 license at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18352505.

articles.title: Selective reductions amid global increases in neural information dynamics jointly track self-dissolution in meditation
articles.authors: Daniel Andrew Atad; Pedro A. Mediano; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein; ‪Yair Dor-Ziderman‬‏; Henrik Röhr; Yoav Schweitzer; Ohad Nave; Stephen Fulder; Aviva Berkovich-Ohana
