articles.abstract: The sense of self is fundamental to experience, yet its neural basis remains unresolved. Contemplative traditions and empirical evidence suggest it can be voluntarily dissolved while retaining awareness, offering a window onto this question. We combined magnetoencephalography with in-depth phenomenology in long-term meditators (N=45, mean 3,832 practice hours) who reliably modulated self-boundaries across rest, self-maintenance and self-dissolution. Meditation broadly increased entropy and information transfer, yet selective reductions characterized self-dissolution. Reduced posterior-medial high-beta entropy and within-cingulate information transfer differentiated dissolution from maintenance. Information transfer reductions from occipital, cingulate, limbic, and subcortical regions, alongside orbitofrontal entropy stabilization, correlated with dissolution phenomenology. Combined with posterior-medial high-beta power reductions, these correlates explained 52% of dissolution depth variance, yet only information transfer predicted held-out participants. We propose selfhood relies on distributed processes that can be reconfigured in meditation through relaxed priors, gated bottom-up evidence, and stabilized evaluative dynamics, distinct from global disruption during psychedelic ego-dissolution.

articles.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a higher distribution of web surveys was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles.title: Humanlike AI May Strengthen Women’s Agreement With Sexist Stereotypes
articles.authors: Sterling Williams-Ceci; Rachel Minkowitz; Lior Zalmanson; Michael MACY; Mor Naaman
articles.abstract: AI can influence societally-consequential attitudes by generating biased arguments – but can it influence our attitudes without changing its arguments at all? In four experiments (N = 2,762), we show that the mere presence of humanlike features in an AI chatbot influences women to more strongly accept ideologically-compatible sexist stereotypes, biases that often resist influence and have societal harm. This influence operates indirectly by increasing “mind perception” – the belief that AI is conscious and thinking – which increases perceptions of its trustworthiness. Our contribution is that anthropomorphism’s influence extends beyond increased trust toward AI itself, impacting women’s broader attitudes about their competence and status. This influence happens when women are attentive during conversations with AI. As developers add more anthropomorphic features to AI, the harms of stereotypes it repeats will increase for vulnerable groups – but making AI appear less humanlike can mitigate this risk.

articles_hidden.title: Genetic Evidence Linking Prefrontal Surface Area to ADHD, Major Depression, and Smoking Initiation
articles_hidden.authors: rui wang; Yifan Du; Yunkai Yang
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), major depressive disorder (MDD), and smoking behaviour exhibit substantial comorbidity and evidence of sequential occurrence. However, the shared upstream neurodevelopmental structural basis underlying this psychiatric–addiction cascade remains poorly understood.
Methods: This study applied a high-dimensional imaging-genetics framework. First, an exploratory Mendelian randomization (MR) screening was conducted across 3,935 UK Biobank imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) to prioritize candidate brain structural targets. Subsequently, univariable MR, multivariable MR (MVMR), and serial mediation analyses were used to characterize the potential temporal and causal cascade, with MRlap applied to account for potential sample overlap and weak instrument bias. Finally, Bayesian colocalization with expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and functional network annotation were integrated to explore potential molecular mechanisms.
Results: High-dimensional screening prioritized left rostral middle frontal gyrus (rMFG) surface area as a core upstream structural phenotype. Genetically predicted larger left rMFG surface area showed consistent directional evidence of association with lower risks of ADHD, MDD, and smoking initiation. MVMR analyses showed that the conditional direct association between left rMFG surface area and smoking initiation was substantially attenuated and was no longer statistically detectable after adjustment for psychopathological liability, although limited conditional instrument strength warranted cautious interpretation. Exploratory MRlap-adjusted pathway analysis suggested a substantial relative contribution of the prespecified sequential pathway, with the product of path coefficients corresponding to an exploratory estimate of approximately 65.51% of the estimated total effect. Bayesian colocalization (PP.H4 = 0.911) and functional mapping further suggested BDNF-AS and neurodevelopment-related modules as potential molecular mechanisms.
Conclusions: Structural developmental vulnerability of the prefrontal cortex does not appear to relate to smoking initiation through an independent direct pathway. The association between genetically predicted left rMFG surface area and smoking initiation may be partly consistent with a pathway involving ADHD and MDD; however, this interpretation remains exploratory because of limited conditional instrument strength and the pairwise nature of the pathway analysis. These findings provide a neuroimaging-genetics perspective on cross-diagnostic comorbidity and suggest a potential role for shared neurotrophic regulatory mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Attentional Spreading within Form-Based Perceptual Groups: An ERP Study
articles_hidden.authors: Tetsuko Kasai; Kei Kobayashi
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research has shown that spatial attention can spread to to-be-ignored objects that share similar shapes with objects at attended locations during relatively late stages of visual processing (Kasai et al., 2011). Such attentional spreading may be associated with perceptual grouping by shape similarity. However, this possibility remains unclear, partly because other grouping factors may have been confounded in the previous study. The present study aimed to examine the time course of attentional spreading associated with shape similarity, while distinguishing shape similarity from collinearity. Participants were required to sustain their attention to one visual field and respond to infrequent target shapes (circles or squares) presented at the attended location. The stimuli consisted of rapidly presented pairs of ovals or rectangles arranged bilaterally, with the two objects differing in luminance contrast and width. Behavioral performance was impaired for rectangle pairs compared with both oval pairs and dissimilar pairs, suggesting that attentional allocation to the attended location was affected by geometric relations between objects. Time-resolved electrophysiological measures further showed that similar-shape pairs (ovals or rectangles) reduced the lateralized attention effect around 260 ms after stimulus onset, suggesting attentional spreading based on shape similarity. This effect was also evident around 300 ms for rectangle pairs, which additionally involved collinearity. These findings suggest that geometric relations among spatially separated objects shape how attention is guided across space and time.

articles_hidden.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles_hidden.abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

articles_hidden.title: The Environmental Includes the Social: On the Psychological Structure of Altruistic and Biospheric Values
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Eric Neef; Quinn J Hundgen; Siegmar Otto; P. Wesley Schultz
articles_hidden.abstract: A substantial body of research has discussed the close relationship between altruistic (i.e., human-oriented) and biospheric (i.e., nature-oriented) motivations. Some researchers posit that they reflect a single, other-oriented construct, while others have shown discriminant validity between the two. Using values as representations of motivation, we reconcile these conflicting positions. Building on and extending the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern, we propose that biospheric values inherently encompass altruistic values. We provide support for the proposed extended Inclusion Model across a series of studies: an exploratory analysis (Study 1: N = 222, U.S. sample), a pre-registered study (Study 2: N = 791, U.S. sample), and a large-scale secondary data analysis (Study 3: N = 85,796; 52 countries). We find that, across much of the world, individuals who hold strong biospheric values also tend to hold strong altruistic values. However, holding strong altruistic values does not likewise imply holding strong biospheric ones. Biospheric and altruistic values predicted humanitarian outcomes similarly, whereas biospheric values predicted environmental outcomes better than altruistic values did. Using bifactor modeling in line with the Inclusion Model resolves interpretational challenges arising when treating both values as unidimensional (i.e., lack of discrimination) or correlated (i.e., suppression). Bifactor results suggest that effects previously attributed to biospheric values may partly reflect their altruistic core. Interventions can reach broader audiences by appealing to altruistic motivation, and interventions targeting environmental motivation may also tap into altruistic motivation. Future work should determine the boundaries of this model, further explore global heterogeneity, and test its practical implications.

articles_hidden.title: Altered Self-Other Distinction in Motor and Cognitive Domains in Individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder: Evidence from a Multi-Site Behavioral Study
articles_hidden.authors: Ekaterina Pronizius; Celine De Meulemeester; Nita Bislimi; Sarah Kathryn Fineberg; Ingmar Heinig; Martin Horký; Inga Niedtfeld; Magdalena Helísková; Pavla Horká Linhartová; Thea M McAfee
articles_hidden.abstract: Self–other distinction (SOD), defined as the ability to separate self- from other-related mental representations, has been proposed as a core mechanism in borderline personality disorder (BPD), yet experimental evidence remains limited. In this preregistered, multicenter study (Austria, Belgium, Czechia, Germany, USA), we assessed motor SOD (Automatic Imitation Inhibition Task, AIT) and cognitive SOD (Visual Perspective-Taking, VPT) in 290 adults (131 BPD, 159 healthy controls), alongside a Stroop-based inhibitory control task. Overall, individuals with BPD showed slower and less accurate performance across tasks. In the AIT, BPD exhibited reduced motor SOD relative to healthy controls, reflected in increased imitative interference. These effects were robust to covariate adjustment and not explained by demographic or clinical factors. In the BPD sample, symptom severity was neither associated with motor SOD performance nor interindividual differences in self-reported childhood maltreatment. In the VPT task, the BPD group showed greater egocentric bias than controls, with effects varying depending on covariate inclusion (e.g., ADHD symptoms, age, cognitive control). Within the BPD group, childhood maltreatment moderated the association between symptom severity and VPT egocentric bias, such that greater childhood maltreatment and greater symptom severity were associated with increased bias. Overall, findings indicate selective, context-dependent alterations of SOD in BPD, characterized by heightened imitative interference and increased egocentric bias rather than a global deficit. Early adversity appears to shape variability in cognitive SOD in BPD.

articles_hidden.title: Intergenerational differences and inheritance of marriage between born “around 1975” and “after-1995” groups based on China
articles_hidden.authors: Jingxi Zheng; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract: Marriage is a union under socialised norms, the typical model being monogamy. It provides for the smooth development of society and a perennially active economic market. The globalised rise in late marriage and divorce rates is to some extent a reflection of life choices and attitudes towards marriage. China is a densely populated country, and after the one-child policy, most families has a pyramidal structure; in 2021, the Chinese government officially enacted the three-child policy, with the aim of stimulating and encouraging people to have more children. However, with the rapid development of the economy, modernisation and industrialisation, there are dynamic changes of individuals’ consideration. The target group for this study is parents who have experienced a change in fertility policy who born around 1975, and their children, the millennials born after 1995. Seven pairs of families were recruited to join the study through snowball sampling. The study used a qualitative approach, with volunteers first completing a demographic questionnaire; semi-structured interviews allowed participants to explore and consider in depth, and asynchronous interviews compensated for the fact that some participants were unable to have simultaneous one-to-one communication online. The researcher forms four themes: the importance of marriage, love and cruelty in marriage, opposite sex kinship and mate choice, and women in marriage. The analysis concluded that there are indeed similarities and contradictions in intergenerational perceptions of marriage, as well as differences between individuals and family units. Inheritance is mainly in the identification of marital behaviour and marital and family pressures, and differences revolve around the two generations' starting points for marriage and attitudes to non-mainstream marriage trends. However, parental influence on children is also externalised into acting styles such as reinforcement, correction, and avoidance to spousal choices due to the unique patterns of the individual internalised system.

articles_hidden.title: The Impact of Puppetry on Pro-Social and Anti-Social Behaviours: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kenneth Gear; Samuel Bennett
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examines the potential benefits and barriers to the utilization of puppets within behaviour intervention of children during their pre-operational stage of development. It presents a  systematic qualitative review of studies that either aim to reduce antisocial behaviour or develop pro social behaviour. Works included educational and clinical settings and development of pro social behaviours such as inclusion and sharing, and reduction of anti-social behaviour such as refusal to comply and aggressive behaviours. The literature was searched using scholarly databases, with additional articles sourced from snowball method of similar reviews. Papers were included based on specific selection criteria and multiple validity and reliability measures. The wider field of research regarding puppetry within behaviour highlighted the overlap of socio-cognitive factors with the psychological principles and concepts of modeling, shared cognition, mediation and social influence being present among studies. From the review, utilizations of puppetry differed and overlapped among studies with modeling, mediation, performance and pedagogy all being utilized to develop and/or reduce behaviours. With majority of studies predominantly exploring the development of pro social behaviour, no significant differences between processes in reduction or development of behaviour were determined. Key themes among all studies were (1) internalization and interaction, (2) direct communication, (3) indirect communication, (4) play and indirect therapy, and (5) rehearsal and imitation. Benefits highlighted were the strengthened communication and dual development of three-party relationships in the sense that facilitators and researchers gained greater insight of participants’ perspective via indirect and direct communication, and vice versa. Though all studies reported positive behavioural change, there are barriers regarding the assessment of behavioural change and determination of purpose and intent.

articles_hidden.title: Epigenetic mechanisms of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review of Human and Preclinical Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: June Kang; JeYoung Jung
articles_hidden.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) produces clinical and behavioural effects persisting weeks to months beyond stimulation. This persistence is typically attributed to LTP- and LTD-like synaptic plasticity, yet short-lived synaptic events alone cannot explain it; epigenetic mechanisms, the leading candidate substrate, have never been systematically evaluated. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PMC to June 2026 (2,089 records; 1,941 de-duplicated). Twenty-two studies were eligible: ten human, ten preclinical, and two invasive cervical-VNS studies retained for sensitivity analysis. Among 18 interventional studies, 17 reported significant epigenetic change (94%; p = 1.45×10⁻⁴), driven by the controlled animal tier (10/10; p = 0.002); the human stream alone (5/6) was non-significant (p = 0.22). Adjusting for publication bias, the pooled signal held under a moderately conservative null (p₀ = 0.7, p = 0.020) but not a strongly conservative one (p₀ = 0.8, p = 0.15). Effects spanned histone modifications, DNA methylation, non-coding RNAs, and epigenetic enzymes. Histone acetylation was the most compelling pathway, supported by causal pharmacological rescue in rodent rTMS and tDCS models. DNA methylation showed an "epigenetic homeostat" pattern, normalising stress-induced aberrations at promoters including BDNF and COMT. Non-coding RNAs formed the largest stream, with circulating miR-146a-5p recurring across rTMS trials. BDNF emerged as a convergent node, also predicting rTMS response via baseline methylation and circulating microRNAs. Coverage is skewed: rTMS and tDCS dominate, tVNS is sparse, tACS/tRNS uninvestigated. NIBS is consistently associated with epigenetic remodelling across mechanisms and species, positioning chromatin regulation as a primary substrate for durable neuromodulatory after-effects.

articles_hidden.title: Antecedents of ecospirituality across cultures
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Ira Billet; Adam Baimel
articles_hidden.abstract: The idea that humanity and nature are spiritually connected—ecospirituality—is a core aspect of cultural and religious worldviews around the world. Sociocultural factors, like religion, urbanization, and socioeconomic status, are hypothesized to shape people’s spiritual connections with nature, yet there are no systematic cross-cultural surveys of ecospirituality that can speak to these hypotheses. We present the results of a study assessing the associations between ecospirituality and these three sociocultural factors using a cross-cultural sample of religious individuals from 15 countries spanning the 5 major world religions (N = 11,186) and a sample of religious and non-religious individuals from the United States (N = 3,329). The overall pattern of results suggested that greater religiosity, urbanization, and socioeconomic status contribute to greater ecospirituality across cultural and religious contexts. Results in the sample of individuals in the United States largely departed from the results found across other countries in the cross-cultural sample, even other Western majority-Christian societies. This research contributes to our understanding of how sociocultural factors that are rapidly changing in many parts of the world may shape people’s connections with the natural environment.

articles_hidden.title: Disentangling between- and within-person effects of HIV PrEP and treatment attitudes on condom use and bacterial STIs among sexual minority men
articles_hidden.authors: Trevor Adam Hart; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Yangqing Deng; Syed Noor; David M. Moore; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Daniel Grace; Nathan Lachowsky; Joseph Cox; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling
articles_hidden.abstract: HIV treatment attitudes and HIV PrEP are associated with sexual behavior that elevates the risk for bacterial STIs (B-STIs) among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Using a longitudinal multi-site study (Engage Cohort Study, 2017-2024), we modelled direct and indirect within- and between-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on condomless anal sex (CAS) and incident B-STIs among 1863 HIV-negative GBM. We modelled up to four years of follow-up visits using multi-level mediation analysis, with CAS as a mediating variable between HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs. We found direct within-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs, such that participants were more likely to report incident B-STIs at time points if they reported using PrEP and being more optimistic about HIV treatments; there were no indirect within-person effects through CAS. In contrast, we found both direct and indirect between-person effects. Specifically, participants who reported more PrEP use or who were more optimistic about HIV treatments over the course of the study were more likely to report incident B-STIs. Further, these effects were partially mediated by CAS. Given that we found within-person PrEP use is associated with increased CAS and STIs, and the general increase in adoption of PrEP over time, there is a need to expand biomedical intervention programs for B-STIs prophylaxis by integrating them with social and informational interventions about B-STIs risks, especially for GBM who use HIV PrEP.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamics of Perceived Rejection in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: ZhaoXuan Shang; Haya Fatimah; Marina Bornovalova; Lijuan Wang; Fallon Rachael Goodman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Interpersonal rejection is typically studied using trait questionnaires or in laboratory settings, while its temporal dynamics that may characterize important individual differences are often overlooked. This study examined perceived rejection in daily life as a dynamic process and its specificity from negative affect.

Method: 89 community adults, including 46 with DSM-5 Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), completed a 28-day EMA protocol with five prompts per day, yielding 9279 observations after data screening. Dynamic structural equation modeling was used to estimate equilibrium (typical level), inertia (persistence over time), innovation variance (magnitude of momentary perturbations), and stationary variance (overall within-person variability) for perceived rejection.

Results: Perceived rejection dynamics were associated with negative affect dynamics. After controlling for the corresponding negative affect components, SAD diagnosis and several interpersonal vulnerability measures (e.g., separation anxiety) remained associated with perceived rejection dynamics. When SAD diagnosis and interpersonal vulnerabilities were considered together, separation anxiety was uniquely associated with higher equilibrium, greater inertia, and greater stationary variance, whereas SAD was uniquely associated with greater log innovation variance; need to belong and rejection sensitivity were additionally associated with higher equilibrium.

Conclusions: Perceived rejection appears to reflect a distinct interpersonal dynamic process beyond negative affect. Within this process, a person’s typical level of perceived rejection, momentary perturbations, the persistence of deviations from the person’s typical level, and overall variability showed different patterns of association with SAD and interpersonal vulnerabilities, suggesting that these dynamic features capture different aspects of perceived rejection.

articles_hidden.title: Not all effort is equal: Invested and demanded effort in nicotine abstinence
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Wahlers; William Hart; Oh-Ryeong Ha; Katie Garrison; Seung-Lark Lim
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Understanding the connection between perceived effort and nicotine abstinence requires recognizing not only how much effort people anticipate exerting, but why they anticipate exerting it. The Invested and Demanded Effort Model (IDEM) provides a framework for distinguishing between perceptions of effort associated with favorable and unfavorable psychological conditions for abstinence.

Method
E-cigarette users between the ages of 21 and 35 in the United States were recruited via Prolific (N = 253; Mage = 28.66, SDage = 4.22, 54.15% female, 45.85% male; 57.71% White, 20.16% Black, 9.09% Hispanic, 6.32% Mixed). We assessed anticipated invested and demanded effort toward nicotine abstinence (adapted Invested and Demanded Effort Scale [IDES]), states that make quitting feel difficult (e.g., e-cigarette dependence motivation, craving), goal-directed states that support quitting (e.g., cessation motivation), and abstinence-related traits (i.e., trait self-control, self-efficacy).

Results
Anticipated invested effort was associated with greater goal-directed states that support quitting including cessation motivation, cessation confidence, and willingness to bear the cost of abstinence whereas anticipated demanded effort was associated with greater states that make quitting feel difficult including e-cigarette dependence motivation, behavior, and craving and less willingness to bear the cost of abstinence. These findings were not attributable to confounding with trait self-control and self-efficacy.

Conclusions
Anticipated effort had no universal connection with abstinence-related states but depended on whether effortful control is attributed to one’s volition irrespective of self-control demands (invested effort) or the demands of abstinence (demanded effort). These findings bolster IDEM and extend its relevance to self-control contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Carrying the Hidden Stone: Mapping "The Sisyphean Quad" in Pre- and Posttrauma Discourses and Its Application
articles_hidden.authors: Swarnendu Karmakar
articles_hidden.abstract: This article introduces the Sisyphean Quad, a framework conceptualizing trauma as recursive and multidimensional across psychological, social, ethical, and existential domains. The model identifies four interlocking constructs: Sisyphean Burden (enduring moral, emotional, existential weight), Sisyphean Curve (cyclical fluctuations, nonlinear progression, unpredictable rhythms), Sisyphean Reflex (automatic survival responses, defense mechanisms, ingrained coping patterns bypassing awareness), and Sisyphean Paradox (tension between coping and preservation of identity). The recursive tightness of these constructs is captured by the Tono Factor (τ), approximated empirically by the Tono Index (τ^) via the Tono Scale (rating recurrence frequency, reflex rigidity, distress intensity, and recovery latency). To apply the model, this article also introduces the Triangular Model of Sisyphean Discussion integrates logotherapy for meaning; psychoanalysis for Burden, Curve, and Reflex; and Cognitive–Behavioral Pattern Interruption for resolution restructure of the paradox and future occurrence. Analyzing trauma across neurological, cognitive, behavioral, existential, cultural, and narrative layers, the article develops an ontologically stacked, interdisciplinary model, the first of its kind. Clinically, the Quad distinguishes maladaptive recurrence from meaningful return, guiding therapeutic dialogue when clients feel trapped in repeating patterns; reducing τ (and τ^) becomes the goal of intervention, loosening the cycle without erasing it. This theoretical and metatheoretical contribution introduces the Sisyphean Quad as a first universal account of trauma’s recursive architecture, where recurrence becomes not a failure but a gentle invitation to reenter life with renewed meaning and coherence.

articles_hidden.title: Developing a treatment pathway to reduce violence risk in psychosis:  from risk assessment to complex intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Whiting; Belinda Lennox; Seena Fazel
articles_hidden.abstract: Violence perpetration is an important adverse outcome for psychiatric services to reduce. Clinical services for psychosis, such as Early Intervention in Psychosis services, represent a key opportunity for prevention, but this is challenging without specialist expertise and resource for violence risk assessment and management. One innovation to address this is a scalable clinical prediction tool for violence, OxMIV, which has been developed using contemporary statistical approaches and been found to be both feasible to use and more accurate than clinical judgement alone in these settings. However, assessing risk does not reduce violence unless it leads to effective interventions being offered more consistently to those who are most likely to benefit. Evidence-based, population health approaches for linking individual risk estimates to intervention pathways have been successfully implemented elsewhere in medicine. Here we adopt such an approach for assessing and reducing the risk of violence in psychosis, presenting a framework for using OxMIV to support decision-making around allocating resources for further assessment and offering interventions that address modifiable risk factors. To develop, implement and test the effectiveness of such clinical pathways, assessments of risk and linked interventions should be studied together as complex healthcare interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Kudos to CUDOS: Resurrecting Mertonian Principles to Remedy Politicized Science
articles_hidden.authors: Cory J Clark; Medhini Urs
articles_hidden.abstract: Science is the most effective system humans have developed to understand reality. Like all systems, it is flawed and subject to bias and error. Reforms such as the Open Science movement seek to address these issues by institutionalizing long-standing Mertonian norms (communalism, universalism, disinterestedness, organized skepticism), helping scientists escape their biases and discover truth. However, other actions within scientific institutions have introduced ideological and political values into the truth-seeking domain, including harm-based censorship, DEI policies, positionality statements, and endorsements of political candidates and positions, among others. These developments can deprioritize epistemic quality and decrease public trust in science. Because the politicization of science arising within the academy has occurred primarily from one direction (i.e., left-wing), some strategies to counteract this bias have been to prioritize ideological/political diversity in hiring, or to encourage scientists to stay away from weighing in on political issues altogether. We argue that these well-meaning solutions to the problem of politicization compounds non-epistemic values in science, thereby risking further loss in public trust. Effort should be directed to restoring Mertonian norms that historically underpinned scientific credibility so that epistemic rigor can be improved and the issues of politicization can be solved without introducing more politics.

articles_hidden.title: Priority Maps, Featureful Processing, and the Superior Colliculus
articles_hidden.authors: Wayne Wu; Neeraj J. Gandhi; James P. Herman
articles_hidden.abstract: The priority map has been used to explain how locations are prioritized for attention and behavior. Priority maps provide a test case for how computational models and neural data can be integrated. Focusing on the superior colliculus (SC) as a paradigm neural substrate for priority maps, we raise two questions: (1) What does priority mean computationally? (2) Since priority maps are featureless, how can this be integrated with recent work on feature coding in SC? We argue that the priority map remains computationally unclear because the nature of priority remains unsettled. Given emerging evidence for “featureful” coding within SC, we challenge the priority map’s featureless assumption as applied to SC and suggest an alternative: a featureful priority matrix where feature dimensions remain distinctly represented.

articles_hidden.title: The Cognitive Science of Maria Montessori.
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Desirée Di Paolo
articles_hidden.abstract: Maria Montessori is among the most globally influential figures in the history of education, yet she remains almost entirely absent from the history of science. This paper argues that her absence is unwarranted, and that her work is best understood not as pedagogy but as the empirical investigation of cognitive development by a scientist trained in the positivist and evolutionary milieu of late nineteenth-century Rome. Drawing on Italian-language sources and untranslated early publications, we reconstruct her scientific formation, in particular her relationships with the anthropologist Giuseppe Sergi and the experimental psychologist Sante De Sanctis. We believe that these relationships gave her a theory of cognitive development structured around three irreducible and simultaneous dimensions: individual variation, the designed material environment, and the socio-cultural context. The prepared environment, the central contribution of her method, was designed to make these dimensions explicit and tractable, and maps with notable precision onto frameworks that cognitive science has formalised only recently. We then ask why this scientific dimension of her work has gone so consistently unseen, identifying three historical and contingent causes: a communicative style bent by financial and political necessity, systematic losses in translation, and the structural exclusion she faced as a woman in the scientific institutions of her time. We close with the case of Jean Piaget, whose sustained exposure to Montessori's method, and subsequent formalisation of a developmental theory that diverged from hers on precisely the points where later research has moved back in her direction, offers the sharpest illustration of what the misreading has cost.

articles_hidden.title: A World-Model Theory of Trait Anxiety
articles_hidden.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Joel G. Thomas; Noa Yadid; Dafna Yavetz
articles_hidden.abstract: Computational psychiatry has sought the mechanisms of anxiety in domain-general biases in learning and planning, and found small, inconsistent effects. We argue this is because trait anxiety is not a bias in how a person learns any task but a property of the person's world model, namely the beliefs they hold about threat, control, and the self in particular domains, and the strategies that bring those beliefs to bear on a situation. We formalize a world model as comprising causal knowledge, an intrinsic reward function, available actions, and internal strategies, and build a minimal generative model in which each has a concrete role in explaining common trait anxiety behaviors. Most importantly, the model inverts the usual place of generalization. Instead of asking whether a task's findings generalize to real-world conditions, it models how far a person's real-world beliefs generalize to the task, and treats the computational parameters of learning and planning that a task measures as contingent on that generalization. Simulations demonstrate how, within tasks similar-enough to the domains of core anxious beliefs, avoidance behavior and anxious thought can arise in qualitatively distinct ways by virtue of world model components. We review prior attempts to relate trait anxiety to computations of learning and planning using our model, and argue that, to advance the field, future studies should personalize cognitive tasks based on threat-related world model content.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Attributed Innateness Beliefs Moderate the Heritability of Psychological Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Jern
articles_hidden.abstract:
People vary in how strongly they believe their psychological traits are innate. Using a 
twin/sibling design (N = 5,844; 1,043 MZ and 2,607 DZ families), I tested whether such 
beliefs moderate the heritability of 11 traits spanning sexuality, personality, attitudes, and 
health behavior. Innateness beliefs significantly moderated heritability for all traits: 
individuals who considered a trait more innate showed higher heritability for that trait. The 
effect was more trait-specific than indicative of a general essentialist tendency and largely 
driven by the individual's own belief rather than shared familial or genetic factors 
(religiosity and risk-taking were partial exceptions). A stringent sensitivity analysis reduced 
the number of significant traits from 11 to 6, indicating that for some traits the moderation 
may at least partly reflect a confound between extreme trait scores and innateness beliefs. 
The low heritability of innateness beliefs is consistent with largely non-genetic beliefs 
gatekeeping the expression of genetic variation.

articles_hidden.title: Relational generalization through memory integration: building knowledge beyond direct experience
articles_hidden.authors: Lainey Costa; Cheyna Warner; Dagmar Zeithamova
articles_hidden.abstract: Memory allows us to remember the past but also form complex knowledge combining information obtained across time. As a key example, relational generalization helps us infer new information by connecting related information acquired separately (AB & BC, therefore AC). Associative inference across arbitrary associations of visual objects has been the most fruitful paradigm, but how it relates to real-world knowledge acquisition is unclear. A more naturalistic paradigm is self-derivation of knowledge, assessing the ability to integrate two related, real-world facts to infer a novel fact. However, because of the rooting in verbal material and semantic memory, it is unclear to what degree the two paradigms assess a common underlying process. Here we tested the degree to which an individual's self-derivation performance can be predicted from their general verbal retrieval abilities and a standard associative inference task with arbitrary object pairs. Results showed that associative inference and verbal fluency separately positively predicted self-derivation of knowledge. Associative inference predicted self-derivation even after controlling for individual differences in associative memory strength. Finally, we found that resistance to interference in the associative inference paradigm may serve as an alternative measure of memory integration. These findings demonstrate that self-derivation of knowledge and associative inference are underpinned by the same process of memory integration across experiences and reinforce the validity of both laboratory measures to assess relational generalization. More broadly, they show that the knowledge humans form depends not only on what they encode, but also on how effectively they integrate across memories.

articles_hidden.title: A triadic model of bilingual shared reading:  Contributions of the book, parent, and child in shaping dual language use
articles_hidden.authors: Marissa Castellana; Christine Potter; Viridiana L. Benitez
articles_hidden.abstract: This study proposes and tests a triadic model of shared reading in bilingual contexts. Sixty-two Spanish-English bilingual parents (92% mothers, 88% Latino) and children (M=3.86 years, 51.6% male) read an English-only Monolingual book and bilingual Codeswitching book with Spanish words embedded in English text. Both parents and children produced more Spanish and codeswitching when sharing Codeswitching vs. Monolingual books, and dyads’ Spanish use was positively correlated while reading both books. These findings reveal that books, parents, and children all make meaningful contributions to the learning opportunities available during shared reading, consistent with the proposed triadic model. This framework can inform a deeper understanding of shared reading interactions that include diverse language experiences and environments.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking and predicting physical task failure using machine learning
articles_hidden.authors: Darias Holgado; Juan Eloy Arco; Priscilla Bartschi; Daniel Sanabria; Nicolas Place
articles_hidden.abstract: Task failure during sustained exercise is often defined mechanically as the inability to maintain a prescribed force, yet cessation may reflect a developing decision to disengage. This study characterized the temporal dynamics of this process and tested whether imminent task failure could be anticipated from multimodal signals. Twenty-three healthy adults performed a sustained isometric knee extension at 20% maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) until task failure. During exercise, auditory probes required participants to indicate whether, since the previous probe, they had thought about or felt the need to stop. Neuromuscular function was assessed before and immediately after exercise, and seven subjective dimensions were reconstructed using Temporal Experience Tracing. Probe-level data were entered into ridge-penalized within-participant Cox proportional hazards models using physiological-behavioral, subjective, and full feature sets; discrimination was quantified with Harrell’s C-index. Participants reached failure after 549 ± 336 s. The first “yes” response occurred at 45% of individual task duration, showing that disengagement-related thoughts preceded failure. Force output remained stable, whereas knee-extensor EMG increased; MVC force, voluntary activation, and 100-Hz doublet amplitude decreased post-exercise, confirming central and peripheral fatigue. Cox models ranked probes by proximity to failure above chance in all participants. The experiential (C-index = 0.988 ± 0.003) and full models (0.984 ± 0.002) outperformed the physiological-behavioral model (0.882 ± 0.014; p < 0.001) and anticipated failure ~50–54 s before cessation. Perceived physical fatigue, mental fatigue, frustration, reduced motivation, EMG activity, and “yes” responses were the main contributors. Task failure reflects a cumulative, multimodal process rather than physiological failure.

articles_hidden.title: Disentangling between- and within-person effects of HIV PrEP and treatment attitudes on condom use and bacterial STIs among sexual minority men
articles_hidden.authors: Trevor Adam Hart; Paolo Aldrin Palma; Yangqing Deng; Syed Noor; David M. Moore; Terri Haochuan Zhang; Daniel Grace; Nathan Lachowsky; Joseph Cox; Shayna Skakoon-Sparling
articles_hidden.abstract: HIV treatment attitudes and HIV PrEP are associated with sexual behavior that elevates the risk for bacterial STIs (B-STIs) among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM). Using a longitudinal multi-site study (Engage Cohort Study, 2017-2024), we modelled direct and indirect within- and between-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on condomless anal sex (CAS) and incident B-STIs among 1863 HIV-negative GBM. We modelled up to four years of follow-up visits using multi-level mediation analysis, with CAS as a mediating variable between HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs. We found direct within-person effects of HIV treatment attitudes and PrEP use on incident B-STIs, such that participants were more likely to report incident B-STIs at time points if they reported using PrEP and being more optimistic about HIV treatments; there were no indirect within-person effects through CAS. In contrast, we found both direct and indirect between-person effects. Specifically, participants who reported more PrEP use or who were more optimistic about HIV treatments over the course of the study were more likely to report incident B-STIs. Further, these effects were partially mediated by CAS. Given that we found within-person PrEP use is associated with increased CAS and STIs, and the general increase in adoption of PrEP over time, there is a need to expand biomedical intervention programs for B-STIs prophylaxis by integrating them with social and informational interventions about B-STIs risks, especially for GBM who use HIV PrEP.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion Recognition From AI-Generated and Human Faces: Performance, Mental Health, and Demographic Diversity
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew J Vowels; Laura Marika Vowels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Facial emotion-recognition tasks are widely used to investigate social-cognitive differences across mental health conditions, but their
scientific value depends on the faces used to measure performance. Established photographic databases are difficult and expensive to
expand, and many provide little ethnic diversity. AI-generated faces offer a more representative, flexible, and scalable alternative,
provided they capture the same clinically relevant individual differences as photographs of human faces. We compared 161
photorealistic AI-generated faces with 72 images from FACES, an established human-photograph set. Prolific participants contributed
83,206 valid trials; 77,238 trials covering the six shared emotions entered the primary comparison (accuracy \textit{n} = 1,047; response
time \textit{n} = 1,046). AI-diverse expressions were recognised more accurately (89.12\% vs.\ 81.72\%) and faster (2.29 vs.\ 2.64 s) than
FACES expressions, while AI-diverse and AI-White performance did not differ significantly. The AI task retained the individual differences needed for research: lower accuracy on both sources was associated most consistently with psychotic-like experiences and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, with magnitudes aligned with previous literature. AI-diverse and FACES accuracy correlated at \textit{r} = .56, and corrected split-half reliability was .70 and .60, respectively. Women were more accurate than men; participant ethnicity was unrelated to performance. Higher AI accuracy indicates that the expressions were clear; it does not show general psychometric superiority, possibly because very easy items can compress differences among high performers. The combination of clear expressions, comparable symptom sensitivity, and broader representation shows that generative AI can modernise a core social-cognition research tool while making stimulus design more controllable, expandable, and shareable.

articles_hidden.title: Visual, Vocal, and Verbal Markers of PTSD: A Parallel Affective Computing Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Yuanyuan Yang; Daiil Jun; Brett Welch; Allison Sylvia; Joel Gregory Sprunger; Jeffrey M. Girard
articles_hidden.abstract: Current PTSD assessment methods often compromise diagnostic precision for scalability, limiting clinical effectiveness. We propose a digital task-shifting framework that utilizes computational techniques to enhance assessment capacity while preserving clinician judgment. We implemented two structured trauma-activation tasks (trauma account and impact statement) via telehealth to elicit disorder-relevant behavioral signals, then quantified PTSD-related behaviors across modalities: verbal, vocal, and visual. Parallel unimodal statistical analyses prioritized interpretability. Comparing 49 individuals with PTSD and 44 trauma-exposed controls isolated PTSD-specific effects. Bayesian generalized linear mixed models revealed significant main effects of group across all modalities with group-by-task interaction effects specifically in verbal and vocal modalities. These findings demonstrate digital task-shifting can capture clinically meaningful variations in PTSD within a scalable framework, complementing traditional assessment methods. Strong interaction effects indicate context-dependent shifts and constrained stylistic patterns across modalities. This approach provides objective indicators of distress to potentially support clinical assessments and research via telehealth.

articles_hidden.title: Some Things Do Last Forever: The Stability Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans develop fixed beliefs, even though the world is constantly changing. Drawing on Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, this paper proposes a generative hypothesis about a crucial source of these fixed beliefs: they are triggered when information is encoded as part of a concept’s central form – a unitary structure within every concept that stores a compressed subset of its information and gives that information default influence in cognition. In Experiment 1, participants endorsed the strong belief that form properties of familiar categories will be present in category members forever. In Experiment 2, participants exhibited the same strong belief for form properties of newly learned categories. In both cases, they rejected this strong belief for non-form properties. These findings indicate that central forms may play a significant role in the fixation of beliefs within different domains – such as functional fixedness, stereotyping, and fixed mindsets – suggesting a universal mechanism for the development of belief fixation. The substantial benefits of this belief fixation to the cognitive system are also discussed.

articles_hidden.title: The influence of visual manipulations on behavioural, physiological and perceptual responses in the heat:  A multi-experiment, mixed methods approach
articles_hidden.authors: Harry Mayes; Liam Satchell; Martina Navarro; Daniel Muller; Finlay Morgan; Juan Ignacio Badariotti; Danny White; Mike Tipton; Zac Schlader; Soichi Ando
articles_hidden.abstract: Thermal perception is essential for human survival through its influence on behavioural thermoregulation. Existing literature suggests that thermal perception can be altered by simple visual manipulations, but this has not been empirically investigated using more contemporary immersive tools such as virtual reality or during exposure to high ambient environments. We tested the hypothesis that visual manipulation, using virtual reality (VR), would alter thermal perception during both rest and exercise in ambient temperatures above ≥ 35 °C. Across three separate experiments, participants cycled at a fixed intensity in 35 °C (experiment 1, n=16), rested in 40 °C (experiment 2, n=12), or completed a fixed-RPE protocol in 35 °C (experiment 3, n=12). Participants completed three visits for each experiment; a ‘hot’ VR environment, a ‘cold’ VR environment, and No VR environment. A single, participant-blind, block randomised controlled, cross-over design was employed. Key outcome measures were thermal comfort, thermal sensation, behavioural thermoregulation, and thermophysiological variables. Additionally, participants were interviewed to explore their perceptual experience in depth, and this added insightful data about their experiences. Visual manipulation had no effect on thermal sensation, thermal comfort, behavioural thermoregulation or any other thermophysiological variables (all p > 0.05). It is concluded that visual manipulations using virtual reality do not alter thermal perceptual, behavioural thermoregulation or thermophysiolological variables during rest or exercise in the heat, but interview data suggest participants believed the VR environments had more of an effect than elucidated quantitatively. These novel findings provide evidence that the hue-heat hypothesis may only exist in thermoneutral environments, further research should confirm this in other (e.g. cold) environments.

articles_hidden.title: China–US Differences in Attributions of AI Consciousness and Moral Status
articles_hidden.authors: Ali Ladak; Nick Corvino; David Moss; Bradford Saad; Jeff Sebo; Matti Wilks; Lucius Caviola
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite AI’s global reach, little is known about how laypeople outside Western contexts think about whether AI systems can be conscious—capable of subjective experience—or whether they could have moral status—warranting moral consideration. In a preregistered main and replication study, we compared such attitudes among laypeople in China and the US (main sample: N = 820; replication sample: N = 910). Across a range of measures, Chinese participants were more open to AI consciousness and moral status than US participants. For example, a larger proportion of Chinese than US participants judged it in-principle possible that AI could be conscious (86.3% vs. 39.6%) and have moral status (89.1% vs. 54.0%). While both countries, on average, leaned against current AI systems being conscious, Chinese participants’ average ratings were higher than US participants’. Chinese participants also, on average, rated a hypothetical future AI system—an exact digital copy of a human brain with a physical body—as having comparable consciousness and moral status to a chimpanzee, while US participants, on average, rated the same system close to an ant. These differences may reflect more positive general attitudes towards AI and greater animism (measured by the belief that non-living things can have a spirit or soul) in China than in the US. Despite these diverging attitudes, participants in neither country supported protecting advanced AI systems at the expense of humans or their own country. Yet participants in both countries supported international cooperation regarding conscious AI, pointing to an opportunity for collaboration in global AI governance.

articles_hidden.title: Ensuring quality in research, 'Authorship Effect' & Conflict of Interest. Response submitted to BMJ Mental Health in response to 'Clinician perspectives on the utility and acceptability of OxSATS: a qualitative study of a novel structured suicide risk assessment tool
articles_hidden.authors: Leah Quinlivan; Alastair Cockburn; Karen Lascelles
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper is a response to the recent BMJ Mental Health publication, 'Clinician perspectives on the utility and acceptability of OxSATS: a qualitative study of a novel structured suicide risk assessment tool.’1 We outline several methodological limitations, including a dissonance between the participants’ responses and the study conclusions, recruitment, reflexivity, and conflict of interests. We conclude with highlighting the importance of scientific standards and academic integrity in producing trusted, unbiased, good quality research.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical Foundations for Estimating Conditional and Score-Related Standard Errors of Measurement
articles_hidden.authors: Wilco Emons
articles_hidden.abstract: Measurement uncertainty is typically expressed by the standard error of measurement (SEM). However, the SEM provides only a global measure of precision and may obscure important differences in precision at different latent trait levels. Several methods have been proposed for estimating trait-related (conditional) standard errors of measurement (CSEM). Even though CSEM estimators have been available for decades, surprisingly little research has systematically examined their shared underlying conceptual principles and their sampling properties. This paper fills this gap. First, different conceptualizations of conditional measures of precision and accuracy are explored. Second, a general framework for estimating CSEMs within the framework of classical test theory is developed. Third, the sampling properties of CSEM estimators (bias, variance, and accuracy) are studied using simulations. The paper concludes with general recommendations and suggestions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: Dual-Task Interference Elicits Reactive Adjustments in Neural Correlates of Performance Monitoring
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Löschner; Marco Steinhauser
articles_hidden.abstract: Interference in dual-tasking poses a challenge both for task performance and for effective performance monitoring. The question emerges whether the brain copes with such interference not only reactively but also proactively by engaging adjustments in anticipation of interference. The present study investigated how two key correlates of performance monitoring, the error-related negativity (Ne/ERN) and the error positivity (Pe), adjust to interference in dual-tasking. In a Psychological Refractory Period paradigm, participants completed two tasks separated by a long or short stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA). Next to the actual SOA in a trial, we manipulated the expected SOA in blocks of trials by varying the frequency of short and long SOAs. This allowed participants to form expectations regarding the occurrence of dual-task interference, thereby creating conditions under which proactive adjustments to performance monitoring would be advantageous. While expecting short SOAs led to a proactive slowing of the first task in line with capacity-sharing accounts of dual-tasking, neural correlates of performance monitoring indicated a reactive but not proactive adjustment for the Pe. Following an erroneous response on the first task, the Pe was reactively reduced and later reappeared after the correct response of the second task, a pattern previously labeled adaptive rescheduling. For the Ne/ERN, no clear evidence for either a reactive or a proactive pattern emerged. Taken together, these findings suggest that performance monitoring adjusts reactively to dual-task interference in order to prevent interference between temporally overlapping processes while maintaining effective performance monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: The impact of cognitive hints on mathematical problem solving: A webcam-based eye-tracking study
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Boros; Marzena Binkiewicz; Agnieszka Glica; Artur Pokropek
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates the impact of cognitive hints on mathematical problem-solving performance and the role of individual learner characteristics in engaging with hints, while simultaneously evaluating the technical feasibility of webcam-based eye-tracking with a single calibration session for large-scale learning analytics. Utilizing a webcam-based eye-tracking approach, we recorded the gaze patterns of 5th-grade students (n = 134) as they solved mathematical tasks across four thematic sets. The study employed a within-subject design with rotated thematic sets and on-demand access to step-by-step hints. Data were analyzed using Linear Mixed Models (LMM) to account for the nested structure of the observations. A key methodological objective was to determine whether lower-quality webcam data, which can be easily gathered at scale without compromising participant privacy, can still reliably support the analysis. Findings indicate that while hints have a negligible effect on high-performing students, they significantly reduce the knowledge gap for students with lower initial ability levels. Furthermore, a significant learning effect was observed for subsequent tasks within the same thematic set. Despite the inherent noise in webcam-based data, the eye-tracking metrics explained a substantial part of the variance between experimental conditions. We found that students with higher levels of math anxiety and intrinsic motivation exhibited significantly longer total fixation time on hints once accessed and a lower overall fixation count in this area. Additionally, female students demonstrated a general tendency for higher visual engagement with hint areas, regardless of whether they chose to open them.

articles_hidden.title: The effects of increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information on implicit and explicit evaluations: A replication and extension of Rydell et al. (2007)
articles_hidden.authors: Benedek Kurdi; Ming Ma; Nicholas Surdel; Melissa J. Ferguson; Jeremy Cone
articles_hidden.abstract: Rydell et al. (2007) documented a dissociative pattern of updating such that implicit (automatic) evaluations changed continuously, whereas explicit (controlled) evaluations changed asymptotically in response to increasing amounts of counterattitudinal information. The present project consisted of two preregistered experiments (total N = 1,090). In Experiment 1, implemented as a close replication, implicit evaluations changed asymptotically, whereas explicit evaluations changed continuously, thus deviating from the original result. In Experiment 2, designed as a test of boundary conditions, neutral statements were omitted from the learning phase, and implicit evaluation measurement was improved. Here, implicit and explicit evaluation change were both asymptotic. These results demonstrate that the functional trajectories of evaluative updating are highly variable across independent investigations. Given that these divergent patterns are challenging to reconcile with any single existing account, they underscore the value of grounding future research in quantitative models of learning.

articles_hidden.title: Sex-Differences in the Relationship between Methamphetamine-Use Experience and Spatial Memory in Non-Treatment Seeking Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Alisha Schaefer; Hyeon Jung Heselton; Hillary Schwarb
articles_hidden.abstract: Methamphetamine remains a public health concern in the United States, and its use has been associated with detrimental effects on memory. More specifically, spatial memory deficits after methamphetamine exposure have been heavily researched in the rodent literature and sex-differences have been reported. However, the effects of methamphetamine on spatial memory in human studies remain underinvestigated and sex differences have not been considered. The current study recruited 30 community-dwelling people with recent or current methamphetamine-use experience, and 30 without methamphetamine-use experience people matched on sex and age. All participants completed a computerized spatial reconstruction task where they studied arrays of randomly positioned objects and then, after a short delay, attempted to reconstruct the remembered study array. Accuracy for both the general spatial arrangement and specific object-location bindings as well as various types of spatial-errors were evaluated. Data indicated that both groups were able to remember global features of the task similarly (i.e., the general spatial arrangement). However, large group differences were evident when specific object-location associative binding was assessed. These group differences were driven by males such that males, but not females, with methamphetamine-use experience were significantly impaired at remembering specific object-location pairings. Together, these findings underscore the need to further characterize spatial memory deficits in people with methamphetamine-use experience as such impairments may have detrimental effects on everyday function and spatial navigation. Furthermore, these findings emphasize the need for sex-balanced samples when studying spatial memory in this population, thus affording the opportunity to investigate possible sex differences.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion recognition in neurotechnology: A scientific and technical fact check
articles_hidden.authors: Marie Luise Schreiter
articles_hidden.abstract:
Consumer neurotechnology systems that are claimed to be able to infer human emotions from facial expressions, voice, and physiological signals are increasingly deployed in domains such as marketing, education, human resources, and mental health.  As these systems have moved beyond clinical and research settings into consumer markets, their purported capacity to infer users’ internal states has become increasingly relevant to everyday life. More recently, emerging neurotechnologies have extended these claims by suggesting that emotional states can be detected directly from neural data using artificial intelligence, thereby bypassing outward behaviour altogether. These technologies are often promoted on the premise that emotions can reliably be measured objectively, enabling more precise, efficient, and equitable decision-making. However, the scientific and technical foundations underlying these claims remain contested.
In this article, we examine the scientific basis and methodological reality underlying claims regarding emotion classification in neurotechnology. We will evaluate the basic assumptions that are embedded in emotion recognition claims: That 1) emotional states can be objectively and reliably inferred from bodily or brain data and 2) emotional states are associated with stable and sufficiently specific behavioural, physiological, or neural signatures that permit reliable inference and 3) recordings from forehead, in-ear devices or consumer EEG in the form of headbands, glasses, or earbuds can deliver technically good-enough signal to inform about the internal emotional states of an individual user. 
Based on current findings, we are sceptical about claims regarding consumer emotion recognition systems. These systems currently face fundamental conceptual, empirical, and practical limitations. We conclude that the current enthusiasm surrounding AI-based emotion recognition reflects an overconfidence in the objectivity of data-driven systems as well as current technological capabilities. A more realistic appraisal of the technical state of the art and transparent discussions of limitations of these technologies is necessary, particularly when they are deployed in high-stakes contexts or in vulnerable groups. Clarifying these limitations is essential for responsible development, evaluation, and governance of emotion recognition in neurotechnology.

articles_hidden.title: The role of spontaneous strategy use in younger and older adults' visuospatial memory
articles_hidden.authors: Gerard Campbell; Rebecca Hart; Richard John Allen; Claudia Christina von Bastian; Melanie Rose Burke; Mario Parra Rodrigues; Victor Kenji Medeiros Shiramizu; Louise A. Brown Nicholls
articles_hidden.abstract: Spontaneous strategy use may contribute to age-related changes in visuospatial memory. We aimed to establish which strategies are associated with young and older adults’ working memory and long-term memory performance, using ecologically valid stimuli. Across four experiments, we investigated younger (18–37 years; total N = 192) and older (63–85 years; total N = 192) adults’ strategy use when remembering coloured objects within everyday virtual scenes. Participants attempted to recall object-colour or object-location bindings from working memory. In-task spontaneous strategy use was also comprehensively assessed via theory-driven, repeated Likert scale probes. Participants subsequently completed an incidental or intentional long-term memory task assessing item (objects only) and associative memory (object-colour/object-location associations) for the working memory task stimuli. All experiments revealed age-related deficits in working memory and long-term memory, although item long-term memory exhibited smaller effect sizes than associative long-term memory. Regarding strategies, younger adults used verbal coding to a greater extent than older adults, who generally exhibited a reduced strategy repertoire. Importantly, verbal coding was consistently associated with better working memory performance. Regarding object-colour associations, using semantic strategies was associated with better intentional, but not incidental, long-term memory, showing the importance of task foreknowledge in strategy selection. For object-location binding, verbal coding was positively related to both incidental and intentional long-term memory. Object-colour associations may therefore be more amenable to strategic semantic encoding than locations. The findings highlight that strategy use is associated with age effects in visuospatial memory and have implications for developing strategy-based interventions to improve visuospatial memory.

articles_hidden.title: Developing a treatment pathway to reduce violence risk in psychosis:  from risk assessment to complex intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Whiting; Belinda Lennox; Seena Fazel
articles_hidden.abstract: Violence perpetration is an important adverse outcome for psychiatric services to reduce. Clinical services for psychosis, such as Early Intervention in Psychosis services, represent a key opportunity for prevention, but this is challenging without specialist expertise and resource for violence risk assessment and management. One innovation to address this is a scalable clinical prediction tool for violence, OxMIV, which has been developed using contemporary statistical approaches and been found to be both feasible to use and more accurate than clinical judgement alone in these settings. However, assessing risk does not reduce violence unless it leads to effective interventions being offered more consistently to those who are most likely to benefit. Evidence-based, population health approaches for linking individual risk estimates to intervention pathways have been successfully implemented elsewhere in medicine. Here we adopt such an approach for assessing and reducing the risk of violence in psychosis, presenting a framework for using OxMIV to support decision-making around allocating resources for further assessment and offering interventions that address modifiable risk factors. To develop, implement and test the effectiveness of such clinical pathways, assessments of risk and linked interventions should be studied together as complex healthcare interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Duration-Dependent Bias and Variability in Short-Interval Time Reproduction: Evidence for Separable Timing and Control-Related Mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Aliza Naseer; Elena Gorbunova
articles_hidden.abstract: Time-reproduction performance can reflect both systematic distortions in temporal estimates and variability in the response used to express those estimates. The present study examined whether these aspects show different patterns across short target durations and participant groups. Sixty-seven HSE University students initially completed a PsychoPy-based time-reproduction task; five were excluded for insufficient valid trials, leaving 62 participants (40 International, 22 Russian). Participants reproduced five target durations (1.4, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, and 2.6 s). Performance was quantified using signed error, absolute error, and coefficient of variation (CV). Signed error showed a strong duration effect, F(4, 240) = 78.35, p < .001, ηp² = .566, whereas neither the group effect, F(1, 60) = 3.74, p = .057, nor duration × group interaction, F(4, 240) = 1.26, p = .285, was significant. Shorter intervals were over-reproduced and longer intervals under-reproduced, consistent with central tendency. Absolute error showed effects of group, F(1, 60) = 8.86, p = .004, ηp² = .129, duration, F(4, 240) = 2.50, p = .043, and their interaction, F(4, 240) = 3.60, p = .007, ηp² = .057. CV likewise showed effects of group, F(1, 60) = 10.57, p = .002, ηp² = .150, duration, F(4, 240) = 18.27, p < .001, ηp² = .233, and duration × group, F(4, 240) = 6.55, p < .001, ηp² = .098. The findings indicate that directional bias and response variability provide non-equivalent information about temporal reproduction. The behavioural results are compatible with contextual calibration of temporal estimates and with additional influences on response consistency, but they do not identify specific cognitive or neural mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: The Unequal Selves Model: How Children Develop Self-Views in an Age of Economic Inequality
articles_hidden.authors: Eddie Brummelman
articles_hidden.abstract: Economic inequality is on the rise globally. How do children form self-views in an age of economic inequality? I offer a developmental model—the Unequal Selves Model—addressing this question by bridging insights from the psychological, educational, and sociological literatures. To support the model, I draw on qualitative, observational, survey, experimental, and intervention research, including cross-cultural studies, with a broad focus on childhood and adolescence (ages 4–18). The model identifies three pathways. Specifically, in contexts of economic inequality, children make social comparisons with worse- or better-off others (comparative self), face socioeconomic stereotypes (stereotyped self), and imagine their futures while receiving few opportunities for upward social mobility (disillusioned self). As a result, children from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds may come to see themselves as less worthy, deserving, competent, and capable of growth, while children from socioeconomically advantaged backgrounds may develop excessive achievement pressure. These gaps may widen in contexts with greater economic inequality and have downstream consequences (e.g., for mental health and academic achievement). The model informs theory and practice by positioning children’s self-views not as merely personal afflictions but as reflections of broader structural conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Subgroup Relationships and Individual Differences  in Musical Synchronization
articles_hidden.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Chihiro Honda; Davide Lionetti; Pieter-Jan Maes; Marcelo Wanderley; Caroline Palmer
articles_hidden.abstract: Musicians demonstrate strong auditory-motor synchronization abilities during group performance, although most empirical studies have examined only solo or dyadic performance. We investigated musical synchronization in four-person groups performing simple and complex rhythms. Each musician's spontaneous production rate for familiar melodies provided individual difference measures of intrinsic rhythms. Participants were randomly assigned to quartets and synchronized their drumming while they performing rhythms based on Binary or Ternary Meters in Simple (1:1 isochronous) and Complex (2:3 polyrhythmic) Rhythm conditions. An unexpected perturbation cue instructed members to switch to the opposite meter, from Ternary to Binary or vice versa. Simple rhythms yielded greater synchrony and shorter relaxation times for returning to stable synchronization following perturbations than Complex polyrhythms. History-dependent effects, reflecting carryover from previous states, were observed when musicians switched between Ternary and Binary rhythms. Quartets with larger individual differences in spontaneous production rates had longer relaxation times to achieve stable coordination. Social interaction ratings indicated greater perceived relationship toward the dyadic partner than toward the four-person group in the Complex Rhythm condition, but not in the Simple Rhythm condition, consistent with in-group (partner) and out-group (group) roles. These findings were largely consistent across North American and European testing sites, suggesting that group and subgroup relationships generalize across sites.

articles_hidden.title: Better Safe Than Sorry? Risks and Benefits of Neuroticism in Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Larissa Lucia Wieczorek; Eva Bleckmann; Solomiia Myroniuk; Bertus F. Jeronimus; Sanne Booij; Jenny Wagner; Albertine Oldehinkel
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroticism is known for detrimental outcomes, but it may also serve beneficial functions in adolescence, where avoiding and protecting oneself from threats becomes crucial. We examined potential benefits of neuroticism based on longitudinal data of two samples of Dutch adolescents, one population (n = 2229, 51% female) and one clinic-referred (n = 543, 34% female) sample. Neuroticism was measured with parent-ratings of the temperament dimensions fear and frustration and used to predict a diverse set of outcomes in the domains lifestyle choices (e.g., substance abuse) and social resources (e.g., social skills) between ages 11 to 19. High neuroticism conveyed heightened risk but four key observations refine this picture: (1) higher fear related to more social skills and prosocial behavior among adolescents in the clinic-referred sample; (2) fear generally related to fewer risks than frustration; (3) controlling for childhood adversity (e.g., low socioeconomic status, parental divorce) removed links between fear and most detrimental outcomes; (4) both fear and frustration were consistently associated with parent-rated social behavior problems, while other associations varied across neuroticism scales and measurement points. Altogether, we provide initial evidence that, under certain conditions, neuroticism can be beneficial in adolescence, especially among vulnerable individuals and in the social domain.

articles_hidden.title: Safety, Compatibility and Reconnection: Understanding Restorative Nature Through the Lens of Chronic Low Back Pain
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Smith; Kayleigh Wyles; Patricia Schofield; Sam William Hughes
articles_hidden.abstract: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is a pervasive and debilitating condition that is often resistant to conventional pain management strategies. This has driven a growing interest in novel psychosocial approaches, such as the use of restorative nature-based environments as part of pain self-management strategies. However, many assumptions regarding restorative nature spaces are based on the perspective of healthy individuals. A population living with cLBP may conceptualise or identify restorative nature spaces differently, given such factors as risk of reinjury or physical limitations. Two focus groups were conducted with a cLBP group (n = 7, Mage = 55.57, 6 females) to explore what a restorative outdoor nature space means through the lens of chronic low back pain. Thematic Analysis generated four Themes (Safety, Confidence, and Control; Embodied Capability; Reclaiming Self Beyond Pain; and Engagement with Living Nature).
