The present study highlights the necessity of inclusion of lived experience and perspective when discussing how best to incorporate restorative nature spaces into pain self-management or green social prescribing frameworks for the chronic pain community. Future research can build upon the present research to codesign tailored nature-based interventions for people with a lived experience of chronic pain.

articles_hidden.title: Norms for a German version of the Phenomenological Control Scale: Measuring the capacity for creating and controlling experience
articles_hidden.authors: Moritz Schiltenwolf; Marie Luise Schreiter; Peter Lush
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to create experiences which misrepresent reality and thereby meet strategic goals is a stable trait that varies substantially in the general population. The capacity for such phenomenological control can be measured by response to imaginative suggestions for a variety of experiences, for example, hallucination in various modalities, amnesia, paralysis or motor actions which are experienced as involuntary. Here we present norms for a German translation of the Phenomenological Control Scale (PCS;  Lush et al., 2021).  Data were collected from a representative sample of native-German speakers (N=299) using a single-session online screening procedure. We show that the translated scale is psychometrically sound, and in line with the results of the original scale in terms of mean scores, distribution and internal consistency. All analyses, code, data, materials and the full questionnaire script are made freely available. Other researchers in the field of psychology are welcome to access and encouraged to use the German norms for the Phenomenological Control Scale (PCS-GER), for example, to assess the degree to which trait phenomenological control may be involved in other psychological effects.

articles_hidden.title: AI-based detection of suicidal ideation in text: model development and evaluation for a student mental health chatbot
articles_hidden.authors: Lotenna Olisaeloka; Leonard Ruocco; Richard Munthali; Melissa Vereschaagin; Yuqian Zhuang; Angel Wang; Tiana Mori; Chris Richardson; Kristen Hudec; Daniel Vigo
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Conversational digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) require mechanisms for recognizing expressions of suicidal ideation (SI) and initiating appropriate safety responses. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection approaches could provide a scalable safeguard; but systems designed for real world deployment must consider accuracy alongside computational efficiency, transparency, and appropriate response pathways. 

Methods: We developed a lightweight SI-detection system for integration into Minder, a mental health chatbot intervention for students. The detection pipeline combined a fine-tuned Sentence-BERT (SBERT) encoder with a nonparametric, anchor-based decision layer. The encoder was trained on 220,833 sentence-level text samples from public social media datasets. Fine-tuning used partial unfreezing and Batch-All Triplet Loss, with three configurations (Light, Medium, Heavy) compared on a development set. Each text input was encoded as 768-dimensional embeddings, then compared, using cosine similarity, against an expert-curated reference set of statements spanning suicidal ideation, intent, planning, and method. Inputs exceeding a development-set threshold were flagged as containing SI. The selected model was evaluated on a held-out test set and benchmarked against four open-weight generative language models under zero-shot prompting. 

Results: The Light fine-tuning configuration was selected for its strong performance and better preservation of the embedding space’s broader semantic structure. On the held-out test set, it achieved precision 0.91, recall 0.92, specificity 0.92, F1 0.91, and accuracy 0.92. A stricter threshold raised precision to 0.98 but lowered recall to 0.34. This trade-off informed a proposed workflow in which high-confidence detections trigger an immediate supportive response and crisis resources, while intermediate scores prompt clarification and re-evaluation. The system performed comparably to Phi-4 (accuracy 0.93, F1 0.92) while using roughly one-eighteenth of its storage and fewer than one-hundredth of its parameters. 

Conclusion: These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of a computationally efficient, domain-grounded approach for SI detection in informal text. Keeping the decision logic separate from the encoder makes the system auditable and allows the flagging criteria to be inspected and iteratively refined. Prospective evaluation using contextually representative chatbot conversations is required before deployment, including assessment of missed disclosures, user acceptability, and clinical governance.

articles_hidden.title: Constructing Composite Scores for Multidimensional Educational Assessment Batteries: Evaluating Alternative Psychometric Models in K–12 Reading Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Tongtong Zou; Jon Weeks; Jason D. Yeatman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Educational assessment batteries often measure constructs that are conceptually multidimensional yet sufficiently coherent to support interpretation through a single summary score. While the literature on essential unidimensionality has primarily focused on individual scales, less attention has been given to how multidimensional assessment batteries can be represented by a composite score, particularly in developmental contexts where construct shift and structurally missing assessments pose additional challenges. This study examines the construction of an essentially unidimensional composite score using the Foundational Reading Skills Assessment Suite from the Rapid Online Assessment of Reading (ROAR) as an empirical example.

Four alternative modeling approaches were evaluated, including a unidimensional Rasch model with fixed guessing parameters (1PL-G), a three-parameter logistic model (3PL), a bifactor model, and a Projective IRT model. The resulting composite scores were compared with respect to model fit, score agreement, measurement precision, reliability, external validity, and robustness to varied assessment combinations across developmental stages.

Results indicated that although multidimensional models provided improved statistical fit, the resulting composite scores were highly consistent across modeling approaches and demonstrated comparable validity evidence. Furthermore, the composite scores exhibited stable measurement properties across developmental stages and were generally robust to variations in assessment composition, supporting the interpretation of a common underlying reading construct despite meaningful differences among subskills. Consequently, the choice of composite model should be guided by the intended use of the score and the trade-offs among model complexity, measurement precision, interpretability, and operational feasibility rather than by model fit alone.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Equivalence Testing with the Updated TOSTER R Package
articles_hidden.authors: Aaron R Caldwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of methodological guidance, researchers continue to misinterpret non-significant results as evidence for the absence of an effect. Equivalence testing via two one-sided tests (TOST) provides a principled alternative, but adoption remains limited by software accessibility and lack of training. The TOSTER R package, originally developed by Lakens (2017), made TOST accessible to experimental psychologists. This paper describes a major update to the package that expands its scope with (1) a unified t-test interface supporting both equivalence and minimal effect testing, (2) a simplified hypothesis testing interface returning standard R objects, (3) tools for computing and testing standardized effect sizes and correlations, (4) robust and resampling-based alternatives including bootstrap and permutation tests, (5) equivalence testing for ANOVAs, and (6) power analysis and sample size planning. Each capability is demonstrated with worked examples. TOSTER is also available as a jamovi module for researchers who prefer a graphical interface.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Up:  Accessible Approaches for Improving Measurement Practices in Psychological Science
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Feld Strand; Violet Aurora Brown
articles_hidden.abstract: The conclusions psychologists draw are only as sound as the measurements they are based upon. Despite the foundational role of measurement in psychological science, many areas suffer from insufficient attention to measurement practices. Although improving measurement practices is widely recognized to be important work—indeed, reliability and validity are taught in introductory psychology courses at the high school and college level—psychometrics has a reputation of being inaccessible to those without formal training. This paper provides a framework to facilitate asking and answering questions about measurement, with the goal of providing researchers without formal training in psychometrics with an accessible entry point to evaluating the measurement tools in their research area. Specifically, we present four questions that researchers can pose of the literature to guide careful evaluation of the measurement landscape in their subdiscipline, focusing on issues related to reliability, validity, and variability in task administration and scoring. In each section, we provide examples of nonempirical and empirical work that can either be conducted in a standalone study or incorporated into ongoing research projects.

articles_hidden.title: Impact of the proportion of emotional faces on ensemble perception of group emotion.
articles_hidden.authors: MOURGUES; Guillaume T. Vallet; Simon Rigoulot
articles_hidden.abstract: In everyday life, we frequently interact with crowds with  faces showing various emotional expressions. Ensemble coding allows the visual system to efficiently extract average group emotion in groups  of faces. However, this process is biased as emotional intensity of the group is often overestimated. This amplification effect is reported to increase as a function of group size. Yet, it remains unclear whether this effect is driven only by the number of faces or could be influenced by another factor, the proportion of emotional faces in the group. The present study tested whether the amplification effect is driven by group size or the proportion of emotional faces within the group. Emotional valence (anger vs. happiness) was also manipulated as a potential influence of the amplification effect. Twenty-one participants estimated the average emotion intensity in groups of 4, 8, or 16 male faces, with 25%, 50%, or 75% of faces showing either happiness or anger. The amplification effect was operationalized as the proportional estimation error between the actual and estimated proportion of emotional faces. The results showed that larger groups were associated with greater amplification than small groups, that amplification increased when the proportion of emotional faces was higher, and that it was consistently stronger for anger than for happiness. These findings suggest that amplification may not depend only on group size, but also on the proportion of emotional faces, and that valence could modulate this effect. Together, the results highlight the role of structural and emotional factors in shaping how people perceive group emotions.

articles_hidden.title: Episodic Health Behavior: A Cognitive Event-Based Perspective on Health Behavior Change
articles_hidden.authors: Darko Jekauc; Jeffrey M. Zacks
articles_hidden.abstract: Health behavior research has generated extensive knowledge about motivational and volitional determinants of behavior, yet it often treats behavior as an aggregate outcome rather than specifying the unit through which action is cognitively organized and enacted. This paper introduces episodic health behavior as health-relevant action represented and regulated as discrete behavioral episodes. Drawing on research in event cognition, we define behavioral episodes as temporally bounded and contextually situated units of action with specific initiation conditions, unfolding trajectories, and end states that can be prospectively anticipated, enacted, and retrospectively experienced. We argue that this framework addresses a structural mismatch between aggregate measurement and the episodic organization of behavioral enactment. The episodic perspective reframes core phenomena in health psychology: the intention-behavior gap reflects temporal and contextual misalignment between momentary intentions and behavioral opportunities, planning specifies actionable episode representations, habitualization increases efficiency in the initiation of recurrent episodes, and behavior change can be understood as a transformation in the frequency, regularity, and stability of episodic chains. The framework provides a theoretical rationale for intensive longitudinal designs, event-contingent assessment, within-episode measurement, and phase-sensitive interventions, particularly for recurrent health behaviors. It also identifies boundary conditions concerning participant burden, measurement reactivity, missing data, and analytic complexity.

articles_hidden.title: Consciousness at the Edge of Death: Dark Retreat, Near-Death Experience, and Generative Brain Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Miller; Zach Buck; Alex Zhu; Andrew Holecek
articles_hidden.abstract:
Near-death experiences (NDEs) and advanced contemplative practices such as dark retreat are frequently reported to involve vivid inner imagery, encounters with non-ordinary agents, moral insight, and panoramic life reviews. Despite growing empirical interest, these experiences remain theoretically fragmented across neuroscience, psychology, and religious studies. In this paper, we develop a unified computational account of NDEs, dark-retreat phenomenology, and Tibetan Buddhist bardo (“between two, gap” often glossed as “transitional process”) models using the active inference framework.
We argue that these experiences arise from lawful generative dynamics that emerge when sensory input is radically attenuated, action relevance collapses, and autobiographical self-models lose precision. Under these conditions, the brain enters a regime of offline inference in which deep priors governing identity, value, and meaning become available for revision. In extended darkness, previously unconscious processes may be brought into the light of consciousness, allowing the practitioner to relate to them rather than from them. Life review is interpreted not as episodic memory replay, but as hierarchical compression and reweighting of autobiographical information under conditions of severe constraint. Archetypal and deity-like figures are interpreted as agentive generative hypotheses that stabilize cognition when narrative selfhood can no longer organize experience, helping to explain their cross-cultural recurrence and exceptional salience.
Dark retreat is examined as a trainable analogue of the dying process (a form of bardo yoga) that allows these dynamics to unfold gradually rather than catastrophically, on the practitioner’s terms rather than on death’s involuntary and non-negotiable terms. Integrating phenomenological reports, contemplative theory, and predictive-processing models, we show how moral salience, karmic imagery, and self-transcendent insight can emerge without invoking metaphysical assumptions. Taken together, this framework reframes experiences at the edge of death as principled reorganizations of generative self-models, offering a tractable scientific account of meaning-making under maximal uncertainty and self-evidencing across increasingly refined levels of self-modeling.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamics of Perceived Rejection in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: ZhaoXuan Shang; Haya Fatimah; Marina Bornovalova; Lijuan Wang; Fallon Rachael Goodman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Interpersonal rejection is typically studied using trait questionnaires or in laboratory settings, while its temporal dynamics that may characterize important individual differences are often overlooked. This study examined perceived rejection in daily life as a dynamic process and its specificity from negative affect.

Method: 89 community adults, including 46 with DSM-5 Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), completed a 28-day EMA protocol with five prompts per day, yielding 9279 observations after data screening. Dynamic structural equation modeling was used to estimate equilibrium (typical level), inertia (persistence over time), innovation variance (magnitude of momentary perturbations), and stationary variance (overall within-person variability) for perceived rejection.

Results: Perceived rejection dynamics were associated with negative affect dynamics. After controlling for the corresponding negative affect components, SAD diagnosis and several interpersonal vulnerability measures (e.g., separation anxiety) remained associated with perceived rejection dynamics. When SAD diagnosis and interpersonal vulnerabilities were considered together, separation anxiety was uniquely associated with higher equilibrium, greater inertia, and greater stationary variance, whereas SAD was uniquely associated with greater log innovation variance; need to belong and rejection sensitivity were additionally associated with higher equilibrium.

Conclusions: Perceived rejection appears to reflect a distinct interpersonal dynamic process beyond negative affect. Within this process, a person’s typical level of perceived rejection, momentary perturbations, the persistence of deviations from the person’s typical level, and overall variability showed different patterns of association with SAD and interpersonal vulnerabilities, suggesting that these dynamic features capture different aspects of perceived rejection.

articles_hidden.title: An Integrative Somatic Approach to Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy:  Theoretical Foundations and Biological Mechanisms
articles_hidden.authors: Devon Christie; Manesh Girn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) has demonstrated transdiagnostic efficacy across a range of psychiatric conditions and is increasingly conceptualized through third-wave cognitive–behavioral frameworks. These frameworks, including Contextual Behavioral Science (CBS) and the psychological flexibility model, emphasize processes such as cognitive insight, belief revision, and narrative meaning-making as central to therapeutic change in PAT. While valuable, they often under-specify the embodied, autonomic, and relational dynamics that patients and clinicians frequently identify as central to both therapeutic benefit and potential risk

In this paper, we introduce Integrative Somatic Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy (ISPAT), a process-based framework that extends psychological flexibility by explicitly centering interoceptive processing, autonomic nervous system regulation, and co-regulated relational presence as core mechanisms of change in psychedelic-assisted therapy. Drawing upon complexity science, trauma-informed somatic psychotherapy, and contemporary neurobiological models of psychedelic action, ISPAT conceptualizes the human psyche as an embodied, relational, and dynamic adaptive system. 

Within this framework, psychedelics are understood as controlled perturbations that temporarily relax rigid patterns of cognition, affect, interoceptive-autonomic functioning, and interpersonal relating. ISPAT articulates how somatic awareness, autonomic regulation, and relational safety can scaffold psychological flexibility across preparation, medicine, and integration phases, helping guide psychedelic-induced reorganization toward coherence rather than fragmentation. By expanding PAT beyond cognicentric formulations, ISPAT offers a scientifically grounded and clinically actionable framework for understanding how psychedelic pharmacology interfaces with embodied and relational processes to shape therapeutic outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: As life happens: Prospectively studying the temporal dynamics of autobiographical and collective narratives
articles_hidden.authors: Ziming Cheng; Öykü Ekinci; Samuel Fynes-Clinton; William Fisher; Karl Szpunar; Buddhika Bellana; Donna Rose Addis
articles_hidden.abstract: Autobiographical and collective experiences both contribute to memories for lifetime periods, but how these narratives evolve over time remains unclear. The COVID-19 pandemic allowed us to prospectively track the development of these narratives as a new lifetime period unfolded. Across nine surveys conducted during 2020-2021, participants wrote pandemic “chapters” for their autobiography and for a history book. We used natural language processing (NLP) to track measure features of lifetime period narratives. First, Automated Autobiographical Interview Scoring and Structural Topic Modelling provided evidence of distinct mnemonic representations: autobiographical narratives contained more episodic detail and personal topics, while collective narratives focused more on public topics. We also found differences between narrative types in how the use of personal and public topics changed over time. Second, Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) quantified the semantic similarity between pairs of narratives, providing evidence of increasing integration between autobiographical and collective narratives, and that both types of narratives remained anchored to the origin narrative for the lifetime period. Intersubject similarity analyses on USE data revealed that pairs of narratives from participants residing in the same region (European Union, North America and United Kingdom) had slightly higher similarity that different-region pairs. Interestingly, different-regions pairs showed steeper increases over time suggesting that despite initial differences, the pandemic gave rise to a shared narrative representation across regions. Our prospective method provides insights into how autobiographical and collective narratives converge and stabilize as a lifetime period is being lived – effects impossible to investigate from a fully retrospective standpoint.

articles_hidden.title: Age-Related Cognitive Slowing and Wrong-Target Errors on the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality Across the Adult Lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiotis Kourtesis; Katerina Denaxa; Lydia Asimakopoulou; Christina Anastasopoulou; Petros Roussos; Maria Roussou; Ion Beratis; Chrysanthi Nega
articles_hidden.abstract: Age-related differences in cognitive test performance must be characterised for each assessment format before scores can inform individual interpretation. This cross-sectional study examined age-related differences on the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), an immersive adaptation of the Trail Making Test, across the adult lifespan. Specifically, it examined whether completion time and wrong-target errors increased with age, whether the age association differed between Parts A and B, whether it was linear or accelerated at older ages, whether it held within each of three adult developmental periods, namely early (19–39 years), middle (40–59 years) and late (60–90 years) adulthood, and which of the exported and derived scores carried the age signal. The sample comprised 230 healthy adults aged 19–90 years (131 women). Part-level mixed-effects models with participant random intercepts tested the linear, quadratic and part-specific age terms; age-band and age-balancing robustness analyses followed, together with a comprehensive, multiplicity-controlled examination of all 26 TMT-VR scores and a direct comparison of their age associations. Older age was strongly associated with longer completion time and moderately with more wrong-target errors on both parts. The associations were linear across the adult range on the modelled scales, with no evidence of acceleration at older ages, and the completion-time slope per decade was of similar size within each developmental period. The completion-time Age × Part interaction was not clearly supported; the absolute Part B minus Part A difference grew with age while the B/A ratio did not. This is compatible with proportional slowing across parts, without establishing equivalent slopes or an absence of executive ageing. Error-adjusted time, which combines duration with correctness, was among the most age-related scores at every level, but it correlated .99 with completion time and its age association was no stronger, making it an economical summary rather than additional evidence in healthy adults. Sex and education were unrelated to the outcomes beyond age; mean selection distance varied too narrowly across participants for an age association to be detectable. Completion time, error-adjusted time and wrong-target errors are therefore the TMT-VR scores on which age referencing should build.

articles_hidden.title: EFFECTS OF SELECTED PSYCHOLOGICAL SKILLS INTERVENTION ON SELF-CONFIDENCE AMONG BENDEL INSURANCE FOOTBALL CLUB PLAYERS
articles_hidden.authors: Celina Abayomi; F. M. Adeyeye; Adewunmi C. M.
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The study was designed to establish the effectiveness of selected psychological skills interventions in improving self confidence among Bendel Insurance Football Club players. To guide the study, one research question and one corresponding hypothesis was raised and  formulated. 
Methods: The study adopted a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design. The population comprised players of Bendel Insurance Football Club. The sample consisted of 49 players aged between 19 and 26 years. Data collected using Athletic Self-Confidence Scale were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics involving Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) at the 0.05 level of significance.
Findings: The findings of the study revealed significant improvements in psychological characteristics of involving self-confidence of players in the experimental group compared with the control group which indicated that the intervention significantly increased players' self-confidence of players. The study concluded that selected psychological skills interventions are effective in enhancing self-confidence of Bendel Insurance Football players, which is necessary for improved competition performance. Consequently, it was recommended among others that football clubs should incorporate structured psychological skills training programmes into their routine training schedules to ensure that mental preparation that builds self-confidence receives the same level of attention as physical, technical, and tactical training.

Keywords: Athletic Self-Confidence Scale, Bendel Insurance Football Players, Psychological Skills Intervention, Self-Confidence.

articles_hidden.title: ADHD and Creativity: Contribution of ADHD Trait Dimensions and an Exploration of Other Contributing Factors
articles_hidden.authors: Han Fang; Anouk Scheres; Lisa I. Horstman; Emma L.M. Laan; Mats N.J. Akkermans; Eva Hermans; Rutger Carelse; Anne M. den Dulk; Martine Hoogman
articles_hidden.abstract: ADHD is associated with impairments but also strengths like creativity. How inattentiveness and hyperactivity-impulsivity contribute to creativity, and how potential factors influence and contribute to the link, remain unclear. This study examined the unique contribution of inattentiveness and hyperactivity-impulsivity to creativity (divergent thinking and creative achievement) and explored the influences of novelty seeking, extraversion, persistence, hyperfocus, and self-restraint in these associations across two independent studies. Data were obtained from two independent university student samples (n = 158, n = 122) via online testing. Divergent thinking was assessed using the Alternate Uses Task; creative achievement, ADHD traits, and potential influencing and contributing factors were measured through self-report questionnaires. Inattentiveness and hyperactivity-impulsivity correlated with creativity in both samples: hyperactivity-impulsivity was the stronger predictor. Among all the potential contributing factors, only hyperfocus accounted for part of the association between inattentiveness and creative achievement. Our findings indicate that hyperactivity-impulsivity is the dominant ADHD trait dimension in the association with creativity. Hyperfocus accounted for part of the associations between inattentiveness and creative achievement, suggesting it may be a factor contributing to this association. Understanding positive phenotypes associated with neurodevelopmental conditions can optimize psychoeducation, reduce stigma, and improve the quality of life for those affected.

articles_hidden.title: Cox versus Discrete-Time Models in Behavioral Research: A Simulation Study of Predictive Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Hyungjun Park; Mike W.-L. Cheung
articles_hidden.abstract: The Cox proportional-hazards model is the standard for survival prediction, although discrete-time models are often recommended as an alternative in behavioral research. Discrete-time models theoretically handle the proportional-hazards assumption and tied events better, but whether this theoretical advantage translates to better predictions under behavioral-research conditions has not been systematically tested. The present study compared six survival prediction models (Cox, elastic-net Cox, gradient-boosted Cox, random survival forest, logistic hazards, and multi-task logistic regression) via simulation under all combinations of sample size, number of time points, event rate, and hazard distribution. Each model's predictive performance was evaluated by the concordance index, mean absolute error, and integrated Brier score. Results on the concordance index and mean absolute error were broadly comparable across all six models in every condition tested. Results on the integrated Brier score showed that the Cox-family models consistently performed worse than the discrete-time models and random survival forest, although this was attributed to how the Cox-family models estimate baseline hazards, not how they handle the proportional-hazards assumption or tied events. Overall, concerns about the proportional-hazards assumption and tied events overstate the case against the Cox model. The Cox model remains a reasonable default for prediction, with discrete-time alternatives favored when probabilistic calibration matters; whether the calibration advantage is substantial enough to justify the additional implementation effort remains unclear. Possible directions for future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: A scoping review of community engagement and implementation outcomes for approaches  to adapt mental and behavioral health evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic youth
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Tschida
articles_hidden.abstract:
Mental and behavioral health evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic youth are commonly adapted for use in community-based settings and, more increasingly, with community-engaged  research methods (Stahmer et al., 2005). However, it is unknown which adaptation method, including what level of community engagement, may be most effective and feasible for (1) enhancing the fit of mental and behavioral health EBPs with autistic client needs in a community 
service context and, (2) improving implementation and intervention outcomes (Dickson et al., 2021). Using the Model for Adaptation Design and Impact (MADI; Kirk et al., 2020) and the Continuum of Community Engagement in Research (Key et al., 2019), this scoping review aimed to fill this research gap by assessing approaches to adapt mental and behavioral health EBPs for autistic youth served in community-based settings from existing literature. Data sources included PsycInfo, PubMed, and Web of Science. Article eligibility criteria included (a) reported in English, (b) describes EBP adaptation, (c) includes children with autism spectrum diagnoses and/or their caregivers, and (d) considers community-based mental and behavioral health settings. Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines, an initial literature search (n = 349) was followed by title and abstract screening (n = 230), full text review (n = 121), and data charting and analysis (n = 37). Frequencies were obtained for MADI and the Continuum of Community Engagement in Research domains reported and assessed across studies. Qualitative content analysis also was used to yield more nuanced descriptions of each adaptation approach and related context, feasibility, and empirical support (Graneheim & Lundman, 2004). Context 
surrounding adaptation, common factors for feasible and effective adaptation methods, and two effective and feasible exemplar methods to were identified. Overall, this scoping review contributes to science found at the intersection of autism research, implementation science, and community-engaged research. Further, it has the potential to inform and improve efforts to adapt and implement EBPs in community-based settings and consequently improve wellbeing among 
autistic youth and their families.

articles_hidden.title: Transcranial ultrasound stimulation as a tool to causally modulate the human hippocampus
articles_hidden.authors: Craig McFarland; Miriam Klein-Flugge; Helen Barron; Valentina Mancini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Non-invasive brain stimulation has, until recently, had limited effect on deep brain circuits critical for memory. Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising tool to address this limitation. By delivering spatially focused acoustic energy, TUS enables targeted modulation of deep brain structures such as the hippocampus. TUS therefore provides new opportunities to causally modulate activity in neural circuits important for memory.
Objective: This perspective discusses how TUS provides a potential methodological advance for human memory research, examining the mechanistic basis of the technology, emerging empirical evidence, and outstanding interpretative and technical limitations.
Methods: We synthesise human and animal TUS studies targeting hippocampal and other memory-relevant circuits, compare TUS with alternative brain stimulation approaches and discuss potential clinical applications for TUS in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and medial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE).
Results: TUS provides a tool to modulate activity in deep circuits that have been inaccessible to other forms of non-invasive brain stimulation. Human TUS studies to date document changes in neurochemistry, functional connectivity, and memory-relevant behaviour. Moreover, clinical studies in AD and mTLE report memory improvement and seizure reduction, respectively. To guide future work, we outline five critical considerations: uncertain directionality of effects, individual differences in delivered acoustic dose, state-dependence of outcomes, evidence of lasting synaptic modification, and standardisation of protocols.
Conclusions: TUS holds promise for studying and enhancing human memory. Realising this potential will require concurrent neuroimaging or electrophysiology to verify target engagement, and close attention to individual differences in dose and brain state, together with cross-laboratory standardisation.

articles_hidden.title: Social Isolation and Ambition: A Two-Wave Correlational Study of School Ostracism and Goal Abandonment in High-Achieving Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Aleksandr Anikeev
articles_hidden.abstract: Independent student research project examining the relationship between chronic school peer ostracism and thoughts of abandoning ambitious personal goals in high-achieving adolescents. Across two independent samples (Wave 1, N = 82, CIS-based Co-founder ecosystem; Wave 2, N = 35, international communities), we find a robust positive correlation between school ostracism and goal-abandonment ideation (pooled N = 117; r ≈ 0.61). A formal Baron-Kenny mediation analysis supports full mediation through school burnout. This OSF project contains the manuscript, anonymized Wave 2 data, and a reproducibility analysis script.

articles_hidden.title: Critical Perspectives Towards Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and How They Contribute Towards ADHD Attitudes Among Related Interest Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Naomi Dodgson; Carolynn Hare; Renee Leow-Guerville; Rachel Mack; Katarina Jovanovic; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract:
From its earliest conceptions, some have challenged the concept of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) as pathologization of normal childhood behavior. In this study we aimed to examine how different conceptions of ADHD contribute to attitudes towards ADHD. We asked participants about whether they felt ADHD was a Disability, a Scientific or Social Construct, and whether they viewed ADHD through the medical model and social model of disability. Additionally, we collected a measure of attitudes towards ADHD and misconceptions about ADHD. Three ADHD interest groups participated: people with ADHD (n=232), parents of ADHD people (n=79), people who work in an ADHD-related field (n=172), and members of the public (n=134; total N=536). We found that having ADHD, being a parent of an ADHD child, and working in and ADHD-related field all predicted more positive attitudes and lesser endorsement of the ADHD-related misconceptions. Knowledge about ADHD was the most consistent predictor for positive attitudes. The social construct view of ADHD was associated with more negative attitudes towards ADHD, and greater endorsement of ADHD-related misconceptions. Viewing ADHD as a disability was inconsistently associated with an improvement in attitudes (ADHD and professionals groups only), and inconsistently with a reduction of misconceptions (parent and public groups only). We conclude that examining ADHD as a social construct or through the social model of disability may not be an appropriate tool for stigma reduction for ADHD. 

Keywords: ADHD, Neurodiversity, Disability, Social Model of Disability, Social Constructs

articles_hidden.title: Shared Dimensions, Divergent Patterns: Multidimensional Well-Being Among Cultural Majority and Minoritized Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu; Jozefien De Leersnyder
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents adapt constantly to their social environments, which can support certain functions while limiting others. In intercultural contexts, adolescents share institutions but hold different social positions and cultural references. Consequently, similar overall well-being scores can mask entirely different combinations of health, relationships, and material conditions—a limitation of single total scores. Well-being and acculturation research approach this problem differently. Well-being research provides broad theories but typically focuses on global indicators within Western majority samples, while acculturation research studies adaptation in intercultural contexts but primarily examines minorities and separates psychological adjustment from sociocultural competence. Researchers currently lack a common multidimensional framework to capture well-being variations among adolescents sharing an intercultural environment. We addressed this gap in 1,385 Belgian-majority and Turkish–Moroccan minoritized adolescents using exploratory and multigroup factor analyses, which supported a broadly comparable five-domain structure. This demonstrates that a common framework can apply across groups while accommodating meaningful differences in how well-being is experienced and organized. Item-level differences formed a mixed profile rather than a consistent advantage for either group. Cross-sectional Gaussian graphical models revealed differences in overall edge-weight structure and global strength, with greater aggregate connectivity in the Turkish–Moroccan network, though no individual edge difference survived correction. Across both groups, the strongest associations clustered within domains alongside cross-domain links. These findings suggest that adolescent well-being is better understood as a multidimensional system than as a single score: shared dimensions can coexist with different profiles and relational organization. Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these patterns reflect contextual conditions, cultural orientations, or their interplay.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring cultural and individual differences in the hierarchy of moral concern: Evidence from student samples across 41 cultural groups
articles_hidden.authors: Işıl Ayça Akkuş; Charlie R Crimston; Kelly Kirkland; Brock Bastian; Bastian Jaeger
articles_hidden.abstract: Disagreement about the rights and protections owed to different individuals underpins many important historical and current debates (e.g., on the abolishment of slavery, the feminist movement, abortion, and environmental protection). Recent work on moral concern (i.e., the subjectively felt moral obligation to consider an individual’s welfare and interests) has uncovered a seemingly robust hierarchy. For example, people extend most moral concern toward family and friends, followed by ingroup members (e.g., a co-worker), outgroup members (e.g., a foreign citizen), the environment (e.g., a coral reef), and, lastly, criminals (e.g., a murderer). However, these studies were all conducted in a few countries from the Anglosphere, raising doubt about the cross-cultural generalizability of the results. We analyzed a data set with 6,665 participants recruited from 41 cultural groups to explore cultural and individual variation in the hierarchy of moral concern. We find that (1) on average, across the 41 cultural groups, 11 of the 13 rankings in the typical hierarchy of moral concern replicated, pointing to substantial cultural similarities; (2) countries that are culturally more similar to the reference sample from the initial U.S. study showed a more similar hierarchy; (3) some rankings (e.g., prioritizing family and friends over human ingroups) replicated more often than others (e.g., prioritizing human outgroups over the environment) across countries; and (4) both cultural and individual differences were largest most pronounced examining people’s concern for non-human animals and the environment.

articles_hidden.title: Theorising arts engagement as a health-promoting behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Daisy Fancourt; Robert West; Andrew Steptoe; Sharifa Abdulla; Naoki Kondo; Pier Luigi Sacco; Agustin Ibanez
articles_hidden.abstract: Arts engagement encompasses a diverse range of human creative practices ubiquitous in every human culture. This Perspective advances a conceptual argument for classifying arts engagement as a health-promoting behaviour, drawing on evolving health behaviour theories and ontological definitions and models. We balance theoretical critiques against this conceptualisation (namely normative instrumentalist and dual valence arguments) alongside accumulating empirical evidence for its value, drawing on experimental and epidemiological research demonstrating associations and causal effects across psychological, cognitive, physiological, and social outcomes. We consider the practical opportunities that could emerge from integrating arts engagement into behavioural monitors, applying behaviour change frameworks, and formalising classification within behaviour change ontologies. Finally, we explore future research directions that a health behavioural framing suggest, include cross-cultural epidemiology, ecological momentary assessment, biomarker integration, exposome-informed models, and One Health frameworks.

articles_hidden.title: Loneliness and alcohol use in alcohol use disorder: A longitudinal within-person analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Anja Kräplin; Michael A Rapp; Jan Luca Wiedenhöft; Gianna Spitta; Louisa Diallo; Shuyan Liu; Tobias Banaschewski; Andreas Heinz; Fabian Arntz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Alcohol use is a major public health concern and a leading cause of preventable disease and death worldwide. Loneliness has been identified as a psychosocial risk factor associated with negative mental health outcomes such as increased alcohol use and alcohol-related problems through stress-relieving or self-medication processes. In turn, alcohol use may exacerbate loneliness through social and interpersonal consequences. Our goal was to examine the longitudinal dynamics of these factors in a population with alcohol use disorder (AUD).
Methods: Data were drawn from the Collaborative Research Center Transregio (TRR) 265 longitudinal cohort study, which included adults with AUD who were assessed across four waves with 4 months in-between waves. Alcohol use was measured by frequency, quantity, binge drinking of alcohol, and the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT). Subjective loneliness was assessed using the UCLA Loneliness Scale. Dynamic panel models were used to examine within-person associations over time. Gender and age were tested as moderators.
Results: Analyses revealed no evidence that loneliness predicts subsequent alcohol consumption frequency, quantity, or binge drinking episodes. However, elevated loneliness was associated with lower subsequent AUDIT scores. This relationship was significantly moderated by baseline age, specifically, the negative association was more pronounced among older birth cohorts. In contrast, alcohol use did not significantly predict subsequent loneliness across any indicator. No evidence of gender interactions was observed.
Conclusions: The relationship between loneliness and alcohol use appears asymmetric rather than bidirectional, characterized primarily by fluctuations in problematic drinking rather than consumption levels in an AUD sample over four waves with four-month intervals. Diverging from self-medication hypotheses, loneliness was associated with fewer alcohol-related problems, particularly among older adults. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between alcohol consumption and alcohol-related problems and of using within-person approaches to understand their dynamic interplay.

articles_hidden.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles_hidden.title: Effectiveness of Culturally Adapted Group CBT for ADHD Among Indian University Students: A Large-Scale Comparative Study from Greater Noida
articles_hidden.authors: Kadim Lovakumari; Tosendra Dwivedi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) persisting into adulthood is associated with significant academic and functional impairment among university students in India. However, culturally adapted, scalable psychological interventions remain limited.
Objective:   To evaluate the effectiveness of a culturally adapted 26-session group CBT compared to a supportive academic group for university students with ADHD.
Methods:  IEC-approved study (Ref: IEC/IILMU/PSYCH/2026/01, dated 15 March 2026) included 674 university students (21-26 years) meeting DSM-5-TR criteria from Greater Noida. Allocated to Group CBT (n=337) and Supportive Academic Group (n=337) based on counselling centre availability. Primary outcome: CAARS. Secondary outcomes: NIMHANS Battery. Assessments at baseline, post-intervention (12 weeks) and 3-month follow-up. Intent-to-treat analysis with LMM, MLE. Written informed consent obtained.
Results:  LMM revealed significant Group × Time interactions for all outcomes. CBT showed greater reductions in inattention [F(2,1344)=268.42, p<.001, d=2.31, 95% CI 2.12-2.50, 41.6% reduction] and hyperactivity-impulsivity [F(2,1344)=189.76, p<.001, d=1.58] and improvements in executive function [F(2,1344)=312.55, p<.001, d=1.18, 21.0% increase]. Gains maintained at 3-month follow-up. Mean attendance 89.3%, fidelity 92%, no adverse events.
Conclusions:  Culturally adapted group CBT is effective, feasible and scalable for Indian university students with ADHD and may be implemented in university counselling settings.
 Keywords: ADHD, group CBT, executive function, university students, India, culturally adapted

articles_hidden.title: What are the merits of identifying as neurodivergent? Assessing the effects of neurodiversity labels on the evaluation of and stigmatizing attitudes towards people exhibiting autistic traits.
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Schlier; Maya Kaiser; Laura Jungnitz; Milena Sophia de Bruin; Luc Weilandt; Marie Ballhause; Felix Strakeljahn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
With the neurodiversity movement gaining traction, people with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and other diagnoses have begun self-identifying as neurodivergent and report that this manner of disclosure boosts their self-esteem and well-being. However, little is known about how self-labelling as neurodivergent changes public perception about the people self-labelling as neurodivergent. This study explores how neurodiversity labels influence stigmatizing and empowering public perceptions of people displaying ASD-typical characteristics.

Methods
In a three-armed online-experiment, 1215 participants received a text-vignette describing a male adult with everyday life challenges typically associated with ASD. The man was either labelled as neurodivergent/neurodiverse, autistic, or not labelled. Participants then rated the described man in terms of social, general, and self-regulation competencies and answered questionnaires on stigmatizing and empowering beliefs about the presented person and/or people like him.

Results
In the neurodiversity-label and no-label conditions, ratings on social competencies and emotional stability were higher than in the autism condition. The crucial stigmatization components blame and desired social distance were significantly lower in the neurodiversity- and autism-label conditions than in the no-label condition.

Conclusion
Across all public perception outcome categories, using a neurodiversity label provided the optimal balance of benefits. This highlights how self-identifying as neurodivergent (rather than by one’s diagnosis) may be a way to circumvent some public stigma when disclosing one’s challenges and warrants further investigation into the generalizability and stability of such effects.

articles_hidden.title: Mediators and moderators of the relationship between maternal childhood adversity and offspring´ outcomes during early childhood: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Rabasa Serrano; Sandra Doval; Belén Fernández; Marta Giménez-Dasí
articles_hidden.abstract:
Maternal adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) can lead to intergenerational effects beginning in the earliest stages of offspring development. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined the biopsychosocial pathways linking maternal ACEs to offspring outcomes from birth to age 3. The systematic review evaluated both mediators and moderators of these associations, whereas the meta-analysis focused exclusively on mediation effects. A total of 41 studies were included in the systematic review and 26     in the meta-analysis, covering publications up to September 2025. 
Findings indicate that maternal mental health—including distress (c’ = 0.045, 95% CI: 0.011–0.086), depression (c’ = 0.020, 95% CI: 0.010–0.033), and anxiety (c’ = 0.018, 95% CI: 0.009–0.030)—emerged as the most robust and consistent mediator. Other mediators, such as physical health problems, parenting style (c’ = 0.011, 95% CI: 0.003–0.020), and broader psychosocial factors (c’ = 0.014, 95% CI: -0.001–0.034), showed more variable or context-dependent associations when integrating evidence from both the review and the meta-analysis. The systematic review also identified several biological moderators of intergenerational risk, including child sex, age, markers of cellular aging, and genetic factors. 
Taken together, these findings underscore the complex pathways through which maternal ACEs influence offspring development and highlight maternal mental health as a key target for early identification and intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Harmonizing Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) in Mental Health Research and Services: A Delphi Study on an EMA Core Item Set
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Rauschenberg; Annette Brose; Joshua M Smyth; Peter Kuppens; Peter Wilhelm; Inez Myin-Germeys; Harald Baumeister; Christine Knaevelsrud; Pascal-M. Aggensteiner; Patrick Bach
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) captures experience and behavior as they occur in daily life, yielding intensive longitudinal data that are well suited for modeling within- and between-person processes and outcomes. However, heterogeneity in EMA items across studies hampers comparability, data aggregation, and reproducibility.
Objective: To establish expert consensus on an EMA core item set, a standardized set of momentary variables from which comparable phenotypic indicators can later be derived. This minimum item set aims to be broadly applicable yet concise enough for use in large-scale research consortia and routine care while maintaining minimal completion time and assessment burden, adopting a nested structure (i.e., minimum core, extended core, add-on modules).
Methods: A Delphi study was conducted with support from an international expert panel (J.S., P.K., I.M-G., P.W., M.L.) and 50 invited EMA experts from the German Center for Mental Health (DZPG). Candidate items were derived from prior work, the international expert panel, as well as a narrative review. The items were iteratively refined between Delphi rounds based on aggregated ratings and expert comments. They were assigned to one of three layers – the minimum core, extended core, or add-on modules – according to their degree of generality, the minimum core comprising the most broadly applicable items. A priori consensus was set at ≥75% endorsement. Rating stability and qualitative agreement informed revisions. Experts additionally reported on current methodological EMA practices (e.g., sampling frequency, study duration).
Results: The EMA core phenotype was established in three rounds. Participation was n=41 in Round 1 (82%), n=43 in Round 2 (86%), and n=40 in Round 3 (80%). Of 69 initial item candidates, 37 partly revised items remained in the three-tiered structure. The finalized EMA minimum core (7 items) comprises four affect items, one item on social context, and two items on positive and negative events. The EMA extended core includes 5 additional items (total 12) on affect, social context, and activities. Completion time for both the minimum and extended core remains low. More specific items (e.g., self-esteem) are reserved for more specific EMA add-on modules.
Conclusions: The consensus-derived DZPG EMA core phenotype provides a consented, ready-to-use item set that balances information yield with minimal assessment burden. By harmonizing EMA assessment across studies, it facilitates comparability, data pooling, and reproducible research while supporting integration into large-scale digital mental health assessment and intervention pipelines. The EMA core will be maintained as a living, versioned measure. Ongoing initiatives include a prospectively specified, multi-study validation program of items, systematic variation of design and assessment procedures (e.g., answering formats), as well as cross-cultural adaptation of the EMA core phenotype.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric Properties of the Swedish version of the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ) in a mixed trauma sample – a comprehensive evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Kristina Bondjers; Albin Granlöf; Josefin Sveen; Filip K. Arnberg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. The International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ) is the most widely used self-report measure of ICD-11 PTSD and Complex PTSD (CPTSD), but its psychometric properties have not been evaluated in a Swedish context, and few studies have examined its properties as a screening tool against clinician-assessed PTSD and CPTSD. 
Methods. In a Swedish adult trauma-exposed sample (N = 276), we examined internal consistency, test–retest reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, and the latent structure of the standard 12-item ITQ and an extended item pool with the 22-item developer version (D-ITQ) using confirmatory factor analysis. In a subsample assessed with the International Trauma Interview (n = 248), we evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of ITQ scores and algorithms and compared pattern of subscale scores across clinician-assessed diagnostic groups.
Results. Reliability was good for the ITQ total, PTSD, and DSO scores but low for affective dysregulation (α = .53). Factor models for the standard ITQ produced inadmissible solutions, with affective dysregulation and difficulties in relationships empirically inseparable (r = 1.09). The D-ITQ had no improper estimates but global fit remained inadequate and the two factors stayed highly correlated. ITQ sum score thresholds showed high overall accuracy, but levels of specificity were low on ≥ .80 sensitivity for PTSD. Algorithm-based classifications showed high specificity but modest sensitivity for PTSD and low positive predictive value for CPTSD. Subscale profiles matched ICD-11 expectations, with negative self-concept showing the largest divergence between PTSD and CPTSD cases. 
Conclusions. The Swedish ITQ is reliable and valid for symptom assessment and screening but is best complemented by clinical assessment. Persistent difficulty separating DSO factors, together with the two-item factors, suggests that a version of the ITQ with more items would be valuable for future research on the ICD-11 constructs.

articles_hidden.title: ‘Why me?’ - The influence of perceived fairness of climate policies on adoption intentions of high impact climate actions across cultural contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Mario Herberz; Tobias Brosch; Claudia R. Schneider
articles_hidden.abstract: The unresolved question of how efforts to reduce carbon emissions should be fairly distributed across society constitutes a major hurdle to widespread cooperation on climate change mitigation. While perceived fairness has been established as a key characteristic of broadly supported climate policies, its affective underpinnings and its relevance for individual-level adoption of climate actions, as well as the added value of addressing fairness concerns in climate policies remain understudied. Here, we investigate the association between the perceived fairness of governments promoting the adoption of high impact climate actions and adoption intentions, the affective processes involved in fairness judgments, and the extent to which two climate policies addressing perceptions of unfairness succeed in increasing intentions to adopt climate actions. Across three pre-registered studies conducted in Switzerland, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom (Ntotal = 1063) we demonstrate that perceived fairness positively predicts adoption intentions, and this more strongly so than the perceived impact of climate actions. We found anger, psychological reactance, and lack of enthusiasm to be affective correlates of lower perceived fairness. Reducing the cost of adopting high impact climate actions and mandating societies’ highest emitters to reduce their carbon emissions to increase self-interested and distributional fairness, respectively, successfully increased adoption intentions. Evidence on potential moderators of these effects remained largely inconclusive. While practical challenges in the study of the behavioural effects of climate policy design remain, systematically accounting for inequalities and perceived unfairness seems to be key to the widespread adoption of high impact climate actions.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluation Frameworks for Gambling Harm Reduction: A Rapid Evidence Review of Outcome Measurement Approaches for Assessing Interventions in the UK.
articles_hidden.authors: Ryan Statton; Imogen Martin; Phoebe Weston-Stanley; Sokratis Dinos; Colin Walsh; James Close
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Current intervention trials for gambling harm reduction are dominated by Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) based approaches, usually measured by clinically-related outcome tools such as the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI). To understand the broader ecosystem of intervention and measurement beyond this, we systematically review current outcome assessment for gambling harm reduction interventions (excluding CBT) in the UK and other comparable regulatory markets. 
Design 
A pre-registered rapid evidence review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, an approach well suited to areas with policy and regulatory relevance. 
Methods and Outcomes
Keyword searching (e.g. “gambling AND treatment AND reduction AND efficacy”) was conducted on Scopus, PsycInfo, and Medline with additional grey literature searches. Screening criteria identified publications that reported non-CBT gambling harm reduction interventions, published in English, conducted within the UK or other comparable regulatory market, using adult (18+) population. Publications were assessed for the type of intervention reported and approaches to measurement and assessing efficacy of interventions. Records were appraised with Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and analysed through Critical Interpretive Synthesis. 
Results 
Thirty nine records were identified that met inclusion criteria. Several trends were observed. First, a default to clinical measures (e.g. PGSI being 18/39 records), indicating a continued reliance on pathology derived approaches to harm reduction. Secondly, though many interventions were holistic, and used holistic outcome measures, their definitions of harm reduction were lacking, or relied on the default to pathology. Thirdly, there was a trade-off between validated and bespoke outcome measures, making comparison challenging. 
Conclusion 
Overall, there was generally a disconnect between the mechanism that interventions sought to work on (being largely psychosocial) and their outcome measures (gambling behaviour/ cessation). Future work should generate a clear definition of harm reduction informed by lived experience. To enable such complex outcome measurement, a core outcome set should be developed, as has been previously achieved for drug and alcohol harm research.  Following this, a shared “harm and recovery” tariff could allow different, validated measures to interoperate within such a core outcome set.

articles_hidden.title: Timing Is Everything: Modeling the Temporal Dynamics of Suicidal Ideation
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Segundo Pena Loray; Julian Rubel; Juan Martín Gómez Penedo; Miriam Ina Hehlmann; Tobias Steinbrenner; Jay Lawrynowicz; Wolfgang Lutz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Suicidal ideation (SI) is a critical clinical concern, yet most predictive approaches rely on static or aggregate measures that overlook its session-to-session dynamics. This study aimed to improve next-session SI prediction by integrating dynamic item-level data and identifying the clinical features that contribute most strongly throughout treatment. Methods: 
Data from 2,045 outpatients were analyzed across the first 10 sessions. A transformer-based time-series model was trained to predict next-session SI using prior-session item-level scores and was compared against a static elastic-net baseline. SHAP values were calculated to quantify feature contributions at both group and individual levels. Results: The dynamic model significantly outperformed the static baseline (average R² = .95 vs. .12), and performance remained improved even without autoregressive inputs (average R² = .24). While prior-session SI was consistently the strongest predictor, depressive affect, hopelessness, meaning in life, and anxiety-related symptoms also provided significant predictive value. SHAP analyses further revealed temporal fluctuations and patient-specific patterns in influential features. Conclusion: Dynamic, interpretable models using item-level data substantially enhance short-term SI prediction. These findings provide clinical insights into which symptoms are most relevant for specific patients at different times, supporting more responsive and personalized suicide risk monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Emotional Crying as a Dynamic Multilevel Regulatory Process: A Scoping Review and Integrative Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Giaquinto
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of research, emotional crying remains an insufficiently integrated phenomenon, with its biological, cognitive, and interpersonal functions often investigated independently. This scoping review maps the existing literature on emotional crying and proposes a multilevel conceptual model of crying as a context-dependent regulatory process. Fifty-seven studies were included (44 primary studies and 13 theoretical or review papers). Evidence was organized according to both crier and observer perspectives, revealing a multilevel architecture linking antecedent appraisals, physiological regulation, neural mechanisms, cognitive representations, and interpersonal communication. Across studies, crying was associated with experiences of helplessness, emotional overload, and meaning-making, while also functioning as a social signal capable of influencing support-related responses and interpersonal dynamics. Observer-focused research further indicated that the effects of visible tears depend strongly on contextual, relational, and interpretative factors. Overall, these findings suggest that crying is better understood as an emergent multilevel regulatory process rather than as a simple emotional discharge. The proposed framework highlights dynamic interactions among biological, cognitive, and social systems that shape internal regulation and organism–environment exchanges. Within this perspective, emotional crying can be interpreted through the Thermodynamics of Mind framework as a process involving hierarchical transitions between mental states. Ultimately, this model integrates intrapersonal and interpersonal accounts of crying while providing a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical investigation.

articles_hidden.title: A priori power analysis for ANOVA interaction effects with the anovapowersim R package: a short introduction
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles_hidden.abstract: Although power analysis has become increasingly accessible over time, researchers still find it challenging to compute power for complex ANOVA interactions. anovapowersim is an R package that enables users to easily specify between, within, and mixed interactions of varying complexity and simulate power based on a target effect size. This tutorial provides a short introduction to the package's core functionality, along with worked examples and sample R code.

articles_hidden.title: How Many Factors Underlie the WAIS-5? Evidence From the Australian and New Zealand Standardization Sample.
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles_hidden.abstract:
The latent structure of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Fifth Edition (WAIS-5) is the subject of recent psychometric debate. Although the publisher's initial confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported a theoretically derived five-factor model, a recent independent evaluation of the US standardisation sample found that complementary exploratory and confirmatory analyses favoured a hierarchical four-factor representation. The present study examined whether these findings could be independently replicated using the published WAIS-5 Australasian standardisation sample (N = 677).
Exploratory factor analyses were conducted using principal axis factoring with Promax rotation, followed by Schmid-Leiman transformation and model-based reliability and dimensionality analyses. Confirmatory analyses compared competing oblique, higher-order, and bifactor models evaluated in the US sample.
Factor-retention procedures did not support the proposed five-factor structure. Exploratory analyses consistently recovered four interpretable factors corresponding to Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, and Processing Speed, with Visual Spatial and Fluid Reasoning failing to emerge as distinct latent constructs. Confirmatory analyses identified the same higher-order (4h3) and bifactor (4b3) models as the preferred representations of the data. Model-based reliability analyses indicated a dominant general factor with smaller contributions from the broad cognitive abilities. Despite modest differences in model parameters, the central conclusions closely replicated those of the US sample.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on early adversity and resting-state EEG from infancy to adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Haleigh M. Brown; Emma Hart; Josué Rico-Picó; Kathryn N. Gray; Man Chen; Sonya V. Troller-Renfree
articles_hidden.abstract: Early adversity is theorized to alter brain activity detectable via resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), positioning it as a scalable tool in creating a global biomarker of brain health. Yet, the consistency of the association between adversity and EEG across the pediatric literature is unclear. We systematically reviewed 34 papers (N = 4245 EEG recordings) and meta-analytically synthesized 19 papers (N = 2669 EEG recordings, 228 effect sizes) on the association between early adversity and resting-state EEG power. Using a Correlated and Hierarchical Effects Model, we found a small, yet robust association (r = −0.086, 95% CI [−0.132, −0.040]) that withstood sensitivity analyses, publication bias correction, and was comparable for both correlational and randomized controlled trial designs. We found power (absolute, relative) significantly moderated the association, though adversity type, frequency band, resting-state EEG procedure, developmental life stage at EEG, and study design did not. The systematic review revealed a similar pattern of findings while also highlighting inconsistent reporting practices. This robust but modest effect suggests adversity is measurably linked to brain activity. However, with substantial unaccounted for heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting practices, EEG's promise as a scalable biomarker will depend as much on methodological standardization as on further biological characterization.

articles_hidden.title: Memories of a shameful episode: Multiple access routes towards understanding self-memory integration
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Lukaschewski; Rebekka Heinen; Emil Eva Rosina; Carlos Alexandre Gomes; Frans Schalkwijk; Kristina Liefke; Oliver T. Wolf; Albert Newen; Nikolai Axmacher
articles_hidden.abstract: Shame, a self-conscious emotion, plays a crucial role in understanding the interplay between autobiographical memory and the self. Self-incongruent memories—particularly those eliciting shame—are often difficult to integrate with the self and may persist in a distressing and fragmented format. At the same time, it remains unclear how phenomenological, semantic, and behavioral access routes to autobiographical memory uniquely capture the effects of interventions and provide complementary insights into how such memories are represented and transformed. Here, we investigated the effects of a novel experimental shame-induction procedure and subsequent manipulations aiming to reduce self-incongruence. Healthy participants (N = 75) were instructed to sing a difficult song in front of a committee providing negative social feedback; salivary cortisol levels and subjective ratings indicated successful induction of shame and psychosocial stress. Participants were then assigned to self-affirmation, reframing, or control conditions. Phenomenological analyses revealed no significant group differences. By contrast, participants in the self-affirmation condition mentioned “not remembering” less often, produced semantically more similar narratives, used more negative emotion words (trend), and showed better recall for central objects from the shameful scene. Participants in the reframing condition produced more semantic jumps per sentence, indicating a less linear recall structure. Correlational analyses revealed associations across semantic, phenomenological, and object-memory variables. Finally, an exploratory factor analysis identified three representational profiles reflecting emotionally elaborated recall, a shame-prone defensive style, and a structural–behavioral dimension. These findings support a model of multiple access routes to autobiographical memory and highlight their convergence and divergence.

articles_hidden.title: Studies reporting bodily feedback effects on motivation have poor evidentiary value: a critical review and z-curve analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles_hidden.abstract: The embodied view of cognition holds that cognitive and emotional processes are grounded in our bodily experiences and physical interactions with the world. In line with this view, embodied motivation studies have purported to show that enacting motivation-related postures, expressions, and actions can elicit or modulate their corresponding motivational states. While theory-building reviews on the topic have accepted these studies’ conclusions at face value, a closer reading of key articles reveals several statistical issues that cast doubt on their veracity. The present review shows that evidence for bodily feedback effects on motivation relies on: (1) studies using multiple measures of motivation, and dismissing results from those that do not support hypotheses, (2) analytical degrees of freedom inflating the false positive rate, and (3) reviews on the topic interpreting non-significant hypothesis tests as if they were significant. Supporting this analysis of the literature, a z-curve on 52 significant results reported across 18 articles indicated little, if any, evidentiary value, with a dismal estimated replicability rate of 22%. In sum, there is little credible evidence that bodily postures modulate motivational states.

articles_hidden.title: Estimating Effects of Time-Varying Special Education Regimes Using Targeted Maximum Likelihood
articles_hidden.authors: Bryan Keller; Lindsey Liu; Yingqi Huan
articles_hidden.abstract: Longitudinal treatments are common in social science research but are often reduced to ever-versus-never exposure indicators that obscure their time-varying nature. This study shows how causal questions can be clarified by defining treatments through explicit intervention regimes rather than collapsed summaries. We introduce this framework by linking the longitudinal setting to single-time-point causal inference and extending it to time-varying exposures, sequential identification assumptions, and estimation using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). We also address practical challenges, including missing data and positivity violations. Using data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study, Kindergarten Class of 1998-1999 (ECLS-K), we examine the effect of special education participation on 5th-grade mathematics achievement. Comparing static and dynamic regimes, we find meaningful differences: always-treated versus never-treated contrasts yield the largest negative estimates, while rule-based dynamic regimes produce substantially smaller effects. These results highlight the importance of well-defined interventions for interpreting longitudinal treatment effects.

articles_hidden.title: Lifetime Engagement in the Activities of Parenthood (LEAP): Capturing personal transformation and the thinking and feeling work of parenthood across the lifespan
articles_hidden.authors: Katia Manariti; Caroline Gurvich; Edwina R Orchard; Sharna Jamadar
articles_hidden.abstract: Parenthood contributes to lasting changes in brain structure, function, and cognition, with emerging evidence suggesting a neuroprotective effect against cognitive ageing. Long-term environmental complexity is a recognised contributor to cognitive reserve. We recently proposed that the enduring cognitive and emotional demands of parenthood represent a unique form of environmental complexity. However, the absence of a well-defined construct capturing lifetime engagement in parenthood limits our ability to examine its impact on the parental brain. This qualitative phase of a mixed methods study examines how parents conceptualise the cognitive demands of caregiving across the lifespan, providing a conceptual foundation for the Lifetime Engagement in the Activities of Parenthood (LEAP) scale. Twenty-nine parents (21 mothers, 8 fathers) participated in one of five focus groups exploring the psychological and environmental demands of parenthood. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist framework. Three themes were developed: thinking work, feeling work, and personal transformation, each enduring and evolving from the peripartum period into late life. Taken together, these findings position lifelong engagement in parenthood as a form of environmental complexity that may influence normative ageing and contribute to cognitive reserve in late life.

articles_hidden.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI).
