In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles_hidden.title: The Implicit Trait Function: Effectiveness as a Function of a Trait-Driven Antecedent Disposition
articles_hidden.authors: Stijn Schelfhout; Femke Timmerman; Eva Derous
articles_hidden.abstract: An implicit trait policy (ITP) comprises of a form of general domain knowledge (GDK), for which a worker’s knowledge of effectiveness interacts with (trait-driven antecedent) dispositions like agreeableness. Through this interaction, an ITP succeeds in predicting and explaining effective work behavior. Studies therefore use an ITP as a validation mechanism in research that aims to predict and explain future work behavior like situational judgement tests (SJTs). Currently, ITP literature still debates the nature and the validity of the ITP concept, while also pointing towards methodological problems in the field. The present study introduces the implicit trait function (ITF) that transforms the dimension of a trait-driven antecedent disposition into the dimension of effectiveness, for both workers as well as behavioral responses. Proactive and retrospective applications of this function demonstrate that an ITP exhibits ample levels of construct-related validity, provided that the measuring instrument, the measurement scoring key, and the subsequent ITP calculations are properly facilitated. The ITF thus renders a comprehensive framework that not only integrates key contributions from the ITP literature but also addresses contemporary challenges within the field.

articles_hidden.title: Collaboration, Creation, & Imagination: Exploring the Effects of Co-Imagination on Divergent Thinking
articles_hidden.authors: Zoe Fowler; Clin KY Lai; Roger Beaty; Brendan Bo O'Connor
articles_hidden.abstract: Creativity is essential in adaptively navigating the challenges of the future. While creativity research reveals the complex ways social context can influence creative outcomes, research on how we imagine the future has only just begun to explore imagination as a collaborative process (i.e., collaborative imagination, or co-imagination). How does collaborative imagination influence creative cognition? Across two studies (N = 162), we assess how imagining the future collaboratively rather than individually influences engagement in divergent thinking during imagination. This work quantified divergent thinking by measuring the semantic distance between all words spoken by a given participant in the narrative (i.e., Divergent Semantic Integration, or DSI). Study 1, run with university students in-lab, found no significant effects of collaborative imagine vs. individual imagine tasks on DSI scores. Exploratory analyses including social connection found that participants in the co-imagine condition had significantly higher DSI scores, though this model also revealed social connection related negatively to DSI scores. Study 2, run over video call with Prolific participants, did not replicate these findings. Together, these studies consider underexplored questions at the intersection of collaboration, imagination, and creativity, and provide tools for future research to investigate creative cognition in co-imagination.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring Up:  Accessible Approaches for Improving Measurement Practices in Psychological Science
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Feld Strand; Violet Aurora Brown
articles_hidden.abstract: The conclusions psychologists draw are only as sound as the measurements they are based upon. Despite the foundational role of measurement in psychological science, many areas suffer from insufficient attention to measurement practices. Although improving measurement practices is widely recognized to be important work—indeed, reliability and validity are taught in introductory psychology courses at the high school and college level—psychometrics has a reputation of being inaccessible to those without formal training. This paper provides a framework to facilitate asking and answering questions about measurement, with the goal of providing researchers without formal training in psychometrics with an accessible entry point to evaluating the measurement tools in their research area. Specifically, we present four questions that researchers can pose of the literature to guide careful evaluation of the measurement landscape in their subdiscipline, focusing on issues related to reliability, validity, and variability in task administration and scoring. In each section, we provide examples of nonempirical and empirical work that can either be conducted in a standalone study or incorporated into ongoing research projects.

articles_hidden.title: Toward a Formal Theory of Cognitive Effort: Application of Linear Control Theory to a Simple Cognitive Model of Controlled Processing
articles_hidden.authors: Clay B. Holroyd
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive effort is a defining feature of cognitive control but theories about its origin and purpose have long been controversial. Recently, it has been proposed that cognitive effort can be understood using linear control theory, a mathematical formalism developed in the engineering literature to control dynamical systems. On this view, effort levels reflect the energy required by the cognitive control system to support representational states that deviate from the intrinsic dynamics of the cognitive system. Although this approach has been used to characterize the energy landscape of neural networks abstracted from the human structural and functional connectome, it has yet to make contact with neurocomputational models of cognitive control. Here we demonstrate the potential of this approach by applying LCT to a classic computational model of cognitive control, and discuss its broader significance in the context of other models of cognitive effort and future studies that can test the theory.

articles_hidden.title: Interference in Long-Term Memory: Competition between Intentionally and Incidentally Acquired Memory Traces Leads to Forgetting
articles_hidden.authors: Melinda Sabo; Şahcan Özdemir; Anna Lena Mantei; Daniel Schneider
articles_hidden.abstract: Forgetting is a fundamental feature of human memory, yet questions remain about how long-term memories become vulnerable to interference. While previous work has focused on exploring interference between intentionally encoded long-term memories, it is less clear to what extent incidentally acquired long-term memories can also disrupt intentionally encoded ones. We address this question across two experiments (total N = 88). Participants encoded object-location associations into long-term memory. Afterwards, they completed a working memory task in which the same objects reappeared in the same or shifted locations (60° or 120°), or were absent, before a final long-term memory test. Results indicated that the interference induced via the working memory task impaired long-term memory retrieval, and that this effect was driven by swap errors. Occasionally, participants accidentally reported the task-irrelevant working memory location instead of the long-term memory one, indicating that they incidentally transferred the working memory task information to long-term memory. Experiment 2 sought to investigate the mechanisms underlying interference. Results showed that both maintenance and testing in working memory disrupted long-term memory, with the combination of maintenance and testing producing the strongest effects. These findings demonstrate that incidentally acquired long-term memories, especially those that underwent maintenance and testing in working memory, can disrupt intentionally encoded long-term memories.

articles_hidden.title: Novel perspectives on the affect regulation hypothesis of substance use: Introduction to special issue
articles_hidden.authors: Jonas Dora; Andrea M Wycoff; Jack Waddell; Andrea Howard; Kevin Michael King
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: The affect regulation hypothesis, the proposition that people use substances to manage how they feel, has organized addiction science for decades, yet empirical support varies markedly across methods. This special issue was assembled to examine the hypothesis through novel theory, rigorous empirical tests, and synthesis of existing evidence. Method: We introduce twelve contributions spanning theoretical proposals, (placebo-)controlled laboratory experiments, ecological momentary assessment (EMA), and longitudinal, cross-sectional, and qualitative designs. The studies address alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, and gambling across various populations, including recently suicidal psychiatric patients, pregnant adults, sexual and gender minority young women, Black men, and treatment-seeking individuals. We organize the contributions into five themes: affect regulation as a person-level vulnerability, laboratory tests of the hypothesis, real-time tests of negative reinforcement, studies of positive reinforcement, and an extension beyond substances. Results: Across contributions, no simple global verdict emerges. Within-person negative reinforcement was evident in some operationalizations, populations, and contexts but not others; positive affect and its dysregulation were more consistent correlates of use than negative affect; motive-response associations were substantially driven by expectancies; and affect regulation extended to gambling. Findings frequently diverged by substance and by timescale of measurement. Conclusions: The evidence summarized here supports not a refutation but a refinement of the hypothesis; one in which positive affect is at least as central as negative affect, and populations, timescales, expectancies, and context matter substantially.

articles_hidden.title: Personality dysfunction is an excellent marker of general psychopathology, particularly internalizing symptoms but less so for externalizing: A commentary on Martin, Kuer, & Sellbom
articles_hidden.authors: Josh Miller; Nathaniel Luke Phillips; Ashmita Ghosh; Leigha Rose; Donald R Lynam
articles_hidden.abstract: Martin and colleagues examined the separability of personality dysfunction (PF) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) using clinician ratings and self-reports in a sample of 289 adults receiving community-based mental health treatment. Using both confirmatory factor and bifactor analyses, the authors found that a general factor splitting across both BPD and PF best accounted for their variance. The authors concluded that PF and BPD “represent the same underlying construct,” with only modest unique variance left in BPD thought to be artifacts of its conceptualization in the DSM. In this commentary, we argue two basic points. First, there is simultaneously ample evidence that PF is an excellent marker of psychopathology writ large and comparatively little evidence that it will successfully delineate personality disorders from other forms of psychopathology, as has been suggested. Second, there is growing evidence that PF is a better marker of internalizing than externalizing forms of psychopathology. Without modification to the conceptualization and assessment of PF, we believe that current (and forthcoming) diagnostic models of personality disorder unduly focus on internalizing, distress-based presentations, which potentially exclude more purely externalizing forms such as (grandiose) narcissism and antisocial/psychopathic personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: The Description–Experience Gap in Loss Aversion
articles_hidden.authors: Nuno Busch; Thorsten Pachur
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans make different decisions under risk when they acquire information about their options through experience than when they learn it from a summary description. Research on this description–experience gap has largely focused on differences in probability weighting—for instance, how low-probability events are reflected in people’s decisions. Here, we show that the gap manifests much more broadly and also occurs with regard to the influence of outcomes. Specifically, we investigated how description- and experience-based decisions differ in loss aversion—the tendency for loss outcomes to have a greater impact on choice than equivalent gain outcomes. We first conducted a meta-reanalysis synthesizing raw data of all available datasets that directly compared description- and experience-based decisions involving mixed-domain lotteries (88,409 choices in total across N_Desc = 439 and N_Exp = 468). The results indicate that loss aversion, measured with cumulative prospect theory (CPT), is more pronounced in experience-based than in description-based choices. We then replicated this description–experience gap in loss aversion in a large-scale experiment with preregistered methods (19,435 choices by N_Desc = 202 and N_Exp = 202) tailored to address potential limitations of the studies included in the meta-analysis, and also showed the gap in an analysis that does not depend on estimating a latent loss aversion parameter. An analysis of the experience-based choices with a reinforcement learning model suggests that a possible mechanism for the apparently higher loss aversion in decisions from experience could be asymmetric learning after positive versus negative prediction errors during experiential sampling.

articles_hidden.title: From Friend to Foe: Stereotypes of Dogs are Ambivalent
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay Palmer; Remy Frost; Sophia Ruppel; Anamarie C Johnson; Andrew Johnson; Clive DL Wynne
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on animal stereotypes often lacks nuance, focusing on animals broadly rather than specific subgroups or contexts. In Study 1, 172 participants listed stereotypes about Dogs, Aggressive Dogs, and Friendly Dogs in open-ended responses. We identified 17 themes for Dogs (e.g., “good companions”), 15 for Aggressive Dogs (e.g., “dangerous to children”), and 20 for Friendly Dogs (e.g., “affiliative”). In Study 2, we examined stereotype endorsement, policy support, and how related belief systems influenced endorsement. Using items created from Study 1 responses, 305 participants rated their personal endorsement of stereotypes (Dogs, Friendly Dogs, or Aggressive Dogs). We found that greater belief in stereotypes about Dogs and Aggressive Dogs decreased support for policies to improve welfare, and only stereotypes about Aggressive Dogs predicted increased support for restrictive policies. We found that beliefs in essentialism and dominance theory consistently predicted greater stereotype endorsement.

articles_hidden.title: Ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Gaurav Mahajan; Caroline J Charpentier; Valentin Guigon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Computational research depends on complex, linked operations. In cognitive neuroscience, these operations often combine multiple data types, specialized toolboxes, custom scripts, and changing computing environments. Open science practices, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) principles, and data standardization have improved how research objects are shared and described. However, they do not guarantee that the same analysis can be rerun to reconstruct the original result. This limitation becomes more consequential as AI-assisted coding tools are accelerating code development, with the potential to strengthen good practices, but also to amplify weak ones. Related problems have long been addressed in software engineering and machine learning operations through practices that make code, data, environments, and execution steps traceable. Drawing from these practices, we present ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience. We emphasize simple, low-cost decisions that can be implemented early and scaled as
projects become more complex.

articles_hidden.title: Engagement begins at recruitment: Comparing videoconference verification to passive online screening for participant retention and study engagement
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Howard; Johanna Peetz
articles_hidden.abstract: Researchers who conduct studies online increasingly struggle with fraudulent respondents, programmable bots, inattention or carelessness, and ineligible impostors. This study tested whether participants in a longitudinal intervention study who were recruited using videoconference eligibility verification—meeting participants one by one on Zoom to verify their identities—were more engaged in the study tasks and showed better longitudinal retention. Using existing data from a sample of Canadian young adult women (N = 1,257), we compared participants who were screened via videoconference to participants who were passively screened (i.e., possessed valid email addresses) and participants who were pre-screened members of a commercial participant platform (Prolific.com) on seven measures of retention and six measures of engagement with study tasks. Results showed that videoconference verified participants had better rates of study initiation and retention, with over 90% completing all study waves. However, we found no meaningful differences between recruitment streams as a function of time to survey completion, engagement with the study’s intervention activities, or honest responding. Videoconference eligibility verification may be a practical tool for recruiting participants likely to remain enrolled in longitudinal research and limit attrition.

articles_hidden.title: How Self-Location Predicts the Degree and Quality of the Felt Sense of Connection
articles_hidden.authors: MARIE SESTER; Glenn Hartelius; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality—specifically the felt sense of connection—remains underexplored. This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world. We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location. Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, self-expansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection. Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making. In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic. These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.

articles_hidden.title: Foreboding Amid Prosperity: Phantom Anxiety Theory and Abstract Pessimism
articles_hidden.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles_hidden.abstract:
The analyses drew on 38 independently conducted international surveys involving more than half a million respondents. The results demonstrate that higher national levels of human development, as indexed by the Human Development Index (HDI), are associated with more pessimistic expectations about the future. Leading theories of optimism/pessimism, negativity, threat processing, resource loss, and the determinants of hope predict patterns that are inconsistent with the empirical findings.
This article posits the existence of endogenous anxious arousal analogous to the vigilance observed in prey animals. Such vigilance promoted survival in the environments that shaped the human nervous system but is evolutionarily mismatched to the modern world. Phantom anxiety theory predicts the observed effect—abstract pessimism—and specifies the conditions under which it should intensify; both predictions are supported by the data. The hypothesis of endogenous anxious arousal in humans also offers a new perspective on anxiety disorders and the evolutionary origins of sapientization.

articles_hidden.title: Exposure-Blind Resilience: A Scoping Review of Resilience, Recovery, and Adaptation in Israel After October 7
articles_hidden.authors: Adrian Mendelson; Yossi Levi-Belz; Yael Segal Elbak; Dalia Moallem; Rinatia Maaravi-Hesseg; Ziv Ben-Zion
articles_hidden.abstract: After the October 7, 2023, attack and the prolonged war that followed, research on resilience, recovery, and adaptation in Israel expanded rapidly. We conducted a prospectively registered scoping review of 147 peer-reviewed quantitative publications drawn from 125 independent samples to examine how resilience and adaptation were conceptualized, which resources were associated with favorable outcomes, and what evidence supported protective mechanisms. No publication operationalized resilience relative to the adversity participants experienced. Instead, resilience was predominantly measured as a self-reported capacity, and adaptation was most often inferred from low symptom levels rather than preserved functioning or broader positive adjustment. Personal resilience and individual psychological resources showed comparatively strong associations with favorable outcomes. However, the reliance on self-report resilience measures limits the interpretation of these associations as effects of distinct resources. Belonging showed a more consistently favorable pattern in a smaller literature, whereas findings for social support, family resources, and collective resources were less consistent. Formal tests of adversity-buffering effects were uncommon, predominantly cross-sectional, and indicated context-specific rather than general protection; prospective evidence regarding mechanisms was similarly sparse. No randomized trial tested a resilience-promoting intervention against a non-active comparator. The literature, therefore, identifies numerous correlates of favorable outcomes but provides substantially less evidence about when these resources constitute resilience or alter adaptation in the face of adversity. Future research should prioritize exposure-sensitive definitions, multidimensional outcomes, longitudinal designs, and temporally ordered tests of mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Electrophysiological signatures of statistical segmentation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Liesa Ravijts; Isabella Toselli Prequero Sbrocco; Brent Vernaillen; Rodrigo Dal Ben; Débora de Hollanda Souza; Louisa Bogaerts
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning (SL), the ability to extract regularities from continuous sensory input, is widely studied using segmentation in embedded pattern learning (EPL) paradigms. Different electrophysiological measures, including event-related potentials (ERPs), steady-state responses (SSRs), and event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs), have been proposed as neural signatures of statistical segmentation. However, the extent to which these measures provide consistent evidence remains unclear. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of EEG and MEG studies to assess the evidence for these signatures in the current literature. After screening 635 records, 39 studies (46 experiments) contributed to the quantitative synthesis. We conducted separate meta-analyses of four signatures: N1 and N400 pattern-onset effects, emergence of pattern-rate SSRs, and suppression of item-rate SSRs. The results provided some evidence for an N400 effect and strong evidence for pattern-rate SSR enhancement, whereas neither N1 nor item-rate SSR effects reached statistical significance. No moderation effects were observed across the tested characteristics, with the exception of contrast type, which significantly moderated the N400 effect. A comparative model further indicated that pattern-rate SSRs provided the most robust evidence of statistical segmentation. We discuss how our results inform the interpretation of these signatures as neural indices of statistical segmentation and outline directions for future research.

articles_hidden.title: LEWIS: Lund Everyday Waste Image Set of Naturally Sourced, Normalised, and Evaluated Waste Images
articles_hidden.authors: Anton Prip Wrisberg; Annika Wallin; Philip Pärnamets
articles_hidden.abstract: Waste sorting is a cognitively demanding task with high environmental stakes. To support research on the categorisation and decision processes underlying waste sorting behaviour, this paper introduces an evaluated stimulus set of 790 images of naturally occurring waste items. The images were sampled from Danish and Swedish household waste, visually standardised, and evaluated by 526 Swedish participants on real-world frequency, how good an example they are of their waste category, and ease of categorisation. The resulting database offers a valuable resource for experiments in categorisation, judgment and decision-making, and sustainability interventions, enabling researchers to study real-world categorisation with both experimental control and ecological validity.

articles_hidden.title: Factors structuring lexical development intoddlers: The effects of parental education,language exposure, and age
articles_hidden.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Camila Scaff; Laia Fibla; Alejandrina Cristia
articles_hidden.abstract:
A growing body of research suggests that individual variation in young children's word comprehension (indexed by response times and accuracy) is structured and meaningful. In this paper, we assess how children’s word comprehension correlates with three factors: socio-economic status (indexed by maternal education), lingual status (based on language exposure), and age. We present results from 91 2- to 3-year-old children using a paired forced-choice task built on a child-friendly touch screen. Effects associated with maternal education and exposure to the tested language (French) were small, and they were greater for accuracy than response times. This pattern of results is compatible with an interpretation whereby the greatest effects of these two variables are on cumulative knowledge (vocabulary size) rather
than on processing. Effects for age were larger and affected both accuracy and response times. Finally, response time variation did not mediate the effects of socio-economic status on accuracy or vice versa

articles_hidden.title: From Vulnerability to Flourishing: Genetic Sensitivity, Family Environment, and Social Support in Intergenerational Trauma and Resilience
articles_hidden.authors: Vera Bekes; Judit Gervai; Aranyi Tamas; Adel Schein; Zsofia Nemoda
articles_hidden.abstract: Intergenerational trauma research has increasingly emphasized the role of both psychological and biological factors in shaping vulnerability and resilience across generations. The present study examined whether gene × environment interactions involving the DRD4 dopamine receptor exon 3 genetic variant could predict trauma-related and positive mental health outcomes among second- and third-generation offspring of Holocaust survivors. Altogether 256 offspring (175 children and 81 grandchildren) of Holocaust survivors completed self-report measures of childhood adversity, family vulnerability and resilience, current social support, and mental health outcomes, and provided genetic sample. Results showed that Family vulnerability and Social support predicted trauma-related and resilient outcomes, respectively, and that carrying the DRD4 7-repeat allele amplified sensitivity to both adverse and protective environments. Childhood family vulnerability predicted posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms significantly only in DRD4 7-repeat allele carriers but not among those without it, while current social support predicted resilience and flourishing also more strongly in 7-repeat allele carriers. Our findings provide empirical support for the DRD4 7-repeat allele as a differential susceptibility variant in an intergenerational trauma context, indicating that the same genetic variant that increases vulnerability in adverse family environments also enhances capacity for flourishing in supportive contexts. The findings suggest that more vulnerable individuals might also be capable of exceptional thriving, given a supportive environment, and that offering family-based and parenting interventions, and community building initiatives for trauma-affected families have the potential to reduce negative and increase positive mental health outcomes, not only in childhood but throughout the lifespan.

articles_hidden.title: Configurations of Mother-Child and Father-Child Attachment Relationships as Predictors  of Child Social Competence: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Or Dagan; Carlo Schuengel; Sheri Madigan; Glenn I. Roisman; Marian Bakermans-Kranenburg; Marinus H. van IJzendoorn; Marije Verhage; Robbie Duschinsky; Abraham Sagi-Schwartz; Jean-François Bureau
articles_hidden.abstract: Attachment theory posits that early child-caregiver relationships shape socioemotional development. Social competence has received particular attention both because it is theoretically expected to be shaped by early attachment relationships and due to its well-established associations with children’s mental health and adjustment. However, most research has examined a single child-parent relationship, typically the child-mother dyad, overlooking the simultaneous attachment relationships many children form with other significant caregivers. In this study, we used individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis to test whether mother-child and father-child attachment configurations uniquely predict children’s social competence. This pre-registered two-step IPD meta-analysis included studies that assessed child attachment relationships with both mothers and fathers using observational measures, and children’s social competence using parent, teacher, or observer reports. Effects computed for 16 studies, comprising 1,585 children, were synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Children with two insecure attachment relationships showed significantly lower social competence compared to those with one or two secure attachments (g = 0.20, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35]). No difference was observed between children with one versus two secure attachment relationships. We found no evidence that the number of disorganized attachment relationships predicted social competence. Across attachment configurations, mother-child and father-child attachment relationship quality did not differentially predict social competence. The presence of at least one secure attachment relationship, whether with the mother or father, may buffer against the risks of having two insecure attachments for children’s social competence. These findings add to the growing evidence that attachment relationships with mothers and fathers are similarly important in predicting key developmental outcomes. In contrast, organized versus disorganized attachment configurations were not reliably associated with social competence, raising both methodological and conceptual questions.

articles_hidden.title: Steering Generative AI Toward Developmentally Supportive Learning: The SCAFFOLD Framework and a Pilot in a School Setting
articles_hidden.authors: Olga Muss
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents are the fastest-growing users of Large Language Models (LLMs) and many LLM-powered toys are entering homes, transforming their environment. Yet these tools were not designed for their educational, emotional, and developmental needs. Children are particularly vulnerable because their skills are immature, knowledge limited and they are undergoing sensitive periods of development, when the foundations are being laid. Safe, developmentally and pedagogically grounded design for interactions with LLMs are therefore essential for limiting risks and harvesting benefits of this technology. This thesis presents the Steered Contextual AI Framework for Orchestrating Learning Dialogue (SCAFFOLD), which builds upon its technical framework, a layered reliability framework that surrounds LLM-generated text and speech with external verification, targeted repair, and safe fallback, to enable to steer LLM’s behavior towards its conceptual framework that operationalizes the knowledge from developmental psychology and neuroscience, science of learning, science of education and pedagogy and the science of human-computer interactions. Model-agnostic and privacy-preserving, SCAFFOLD helps educators to configure interactions with AI that support safety, learning and development, with transparency and modularity. The thesis includes a piloted minimal SCAFFOLD prototype tested in a classroom with 12–16-year-olds using an LLM-powered social robot in a multi-user co-creation task, where students collaboratively designed a mnemonic on a previously covered topic. Preliminary findings showed that, compared to a prompt-only LLM, the SCAFFOLD prototype elicited more student activity, engagement, and on-topic participation. Co-creation level was associated with post-test knowledge scores after controlling for prior knowledge. These findings provide initial evidence for SCAFFOLD's feasibility and potential to support engagement and learning in educational settings.

articles_hidden.title: COVID-19 Impacts and Child Psychological Distress: A Twin Direction-of-Causation Study
articles_hidden.authors: Mandeep Singh; Hongcui Du; Callie W. Little; Sara Ann Hart
articles_hidden.abstract: COVID-19 disrupted children's social, economic, and psychological circumstances, yet the causal direction of this association with child distress remains unresolved. We applied twin Direction of Causation (DoC) modeling to 579 twin families (183 MZ, 396 DZ pairs; grades 3–12) from the NatPAT COVID 2022 survey. COVID-19 impacts were modeled as a latent construct spanning social, economic, and COVID-specific stress domains; distress was indexed by anxiety and perceived stress. The two constructs showed different genetic and environmental influences: COVID-19 impacts were predominantly environmental, distress substantially heritable, yet were strongly associated (r = .706). Modeling favoured a unidirectional path from COVID-19 impacts to distress per our preregistered tiebreaker (β = .703, p < .001; ΔAIC = 0.29), although this small margin does not rule out a bidirectional relation. These findings suggest that reducing pandemic-related disruptions, rather than targeting stress responses alone, may help protect child mental health during future societal disruptions.

articles_hidden.title: When truthful innocent suspects become less forthcoming: Effects of memory constraints in SUE-based mock interviews
articles_hidden.authors: Helen Wyler; Martina Buchli; Flavia Zaidi-Tinner
articles_hidden.abstract: Past Strategic Use of Evidence studies found innocent suspects to be forthcoming, but usually implicitly assume that they can remember the critical details needed to provide evidence-consistent accounts. Building on Sukumar et al. (2018), we examined how encoding intentionality, retention interval, and type of critical detail affect forthcomingness in a mock investigative interview (S1; N = 193) and observers’ veracity judgements (S2; N = 402). Encoding intentionality had no statistically significant effect. The three-week retention interval substantially reduced forthcomingness among innocent suspects relative to immediate retrieval, although guilty suspects remained less forthcoming. Delayed innocent suspects were descriptively more likely to be judged as deceptive, but this effect was not confirmed by the preregistered interaction. Exploratory analyses suggested that incidental details were both most vulnerable to delay and associated with deception judgements. The findings highlight the importance of conceptualising forthcomingness as a function of both strategic information management and memory constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Towards a genetics of mental disorders as complex dynamical systems: A symptom-specific and symptom-interactive approach
articles_hidden.authors: Omid V. Ebrahimi; Michel Guillaume Nivard; Ludvig Daae Bjørndal
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychiatric genetics has largely mapped genetic liability onto diagnoses and symptom sum scores. Yet these disorder-level phenotypes are heterogeneous composites: individuals sharing a diagnosis may exhibit markedly different symptoms; the same symptoms recur across multiple disorders; and symptoms influence one another over time. Genetic analyses based on such aggregates may therefore obscure symptom-specific biological signals and overlook the dynamic processes through which genetic liability becomes expressed clinically. We propose a complementary symptom-specific and symptom-interactive framework that conceptualises psychiatric disorders as dynamic systems of mutually influencing symptoms. This framework distinguishes three forms of genetic influence: direct effects of genetic risk on individual symptoms; indirect effects propagated through symptom-to-symptom pathways; and examinations of how genetic risk moderates the strength, persistence, and activation potential of symptom interactions. We show how various genetic and psychometric methods can be integrated to investigate these processes. We identify four priorities for psychiatric genetics research that can be advanced by adopting this framework: improving symptom-level phenotyping; distinguishing disorder-specific and transdiagnostic symptoms; modelling mediated genetic effects across symptoms; and testing whether genetic liability shapes symptom co-activation and their temporal dynamics. Reframing psychopathology as systems of interacting symptoms could sharpen genes-to-phenotype mapping, clarify heterogeneity in illness trajectories, and align psychiatric genetics more closely with novel mechanistic theories of mental disorders and the goals of precision psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Attention Bias in Perfectionism:  Prolonged Dwell Time on Critical Faces Partially Mediates a Link Between Perfectionistic Concerns and Psychological Distress
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Prestele; Christine Altstötter-Gleich; Stephan Koenig; Ulrike Basten
articles_hidden.abstract: Perfectionism is a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor implicated in emotional disorders, including depression and anxiety. Yet, the mechanisms through which perfectionism contributes to psychological distress are only partly understood. A candidate mechanism is attention allocation during social interactions, as attention to evaluative cues may influence subsequent perceptions and affective responses. The present study used eye tracking to examine whether perfectionistic concerns (PC) and perfectionistic strivings (PS) are associated with attention biases toward socially evaluative cues, as indicated by prolonged dwell time on facial expressions of criticism as opposed to appreciation in a free viewing task. For 148 participants (82% female, 1% diverse; age: 18 – 57 years, M = 24 years, SD = 6.4), the proportional dwell-time on critical faces was related to self-reported PC as well as state and trait measures of psychological distress (unpleasant mood and depressiveness). In latent-variable analyses, PC showed small to moderate positive unique associations with the proportional dwell time on critical faces. Path analyses further indicated that this dwell time partially mediated the associations of PC with unpleasant mood and depressiveness. These findings provide novel evidence that PC are linked to biases in attention toward social cues of criticism, suggesting a pathway through which PC may contribute to psychological distress. More broadly, the results underscore the importance of considering attentional mechanisms in models of perfectionism and emotional disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Psychometric Validation of the ‘Psychedelic Flourishing Scale’
articles_hidden.authors: Frederick Pattisson; Sunjeev Kamboj; Devon Stoliker; Rosalind McAlpine
articles_hidden.abstract: Positive psychological changes following psychedelic experiences are widely studied, yet no validated instrument has been developed specifically to assess the breadth of enduring change that individuals attribute to those experiences. We therefore conducted a two-part programme of research to evaluate an existing measure and to develop and validate a more comprehensive scale. In Part 1, a preliminary psychometric analysis of the 11-item Mindset Questionnaire (MQ) was conducted using data from two psilocybin studies (N = 97). Its items were strongly intercorrelated (mean inter-item r = .63) and predominantly reflected a single, relatively narrow dimension of change. Part 2 followed established scale-development procedures to define the broader construct of psychedelic flourishing and develop the Psychedelic Flourishing Scale (PFS). A three-round Delphi study involving 17 experts established the construct definition and generated a 41-item pool. The PFS was then evaluated in a pre-registered cross-sectional survey of 1,296 adults who reported previous serotonergic (“classic”) psychedelic use. The sample was randomly divided for exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, with the structure extracted in the exploratory half rather than specified in advance. In the confirmatory subsample, a model comprising five correlated facets showed good fit (RMSEA = .053, CFI = .965) and fitted better than a unidimensional model, although a four-factor model performed similarly. A full-sample bifactor model indicated that 87.8% of the common variance was attributable to a general factor, with high general-factor reliability (ωh = .960), supporting use of a single total score. Scores showed high test-retest reliability over a median interval of approximately three weeks (ICC = .890) and were more strongly associated with theoretically related constructs, including presence of meaning (r = .45) and well-being (r = .42), than with extraversion (r = .22) or socially desirable responding (r = .17). The MQ appears to assess a narrow dimension of perceived change, whereas the PFS provides a psychometrically robust measure of broader positive psychological change attributed to psychedelic experiences.

articles_hidden.title: The Functional Connectivity of Hallucinations in Psychiatric Disorders and Neurodegenerative Disorders: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Yifan Ren; Huyen Ngoc Pham; Xiong Xiong; Shun-Chin Jim Wu; Emilio Fernandez-Egea; John T. O’Brien; Graham Murray; John suckling
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Hallucinations span psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders, yet unified neurobiological or consciousness-based explanations remain uncertain. Functional connectivity (FC) provides a network-level view with highly heterogeneous findings.
Methods: Following PRISMA, we included studies with FC of hallucinations to ask whether it is sensitive to hallucinations, can distinguish different disorders, and if adopted theories are explanatory. 
Results: 198 studies were included, with far fewer studies in neurodegenerative (35) than psychiatric disorders (163). Across conditions, hallucinations consistently involved dysconnectivity among default mode (DMN), salience (SN), central executive (CEN), sensory systems, and subcortical circuits. Shared alterations included disrupted SN modulation of sensory gating, altered DMN-sensory coupling and within DMN coherence, limbic system involvement, and reduced CEN regulation of perceptual networks. Disorder‑specific patterns were evident: psychiatric hallucinations preferentially involved auditory-language networks, cortico‑striatal circuits, and salience hubs, whereas neurodegenerative hallucinations were characterised by visual and attentional network dysfunction, including dorsal and ventral attention systems and visual cortices.
Conclusions: FC is sensitive to hallucinations and shows different disorder-linked patterns while revealing shared mechanisms, supporting the transdiagnostic nature of hallucinations at the level of functional brain networks. Despite the involvement of multiple transdiagnostic networks, the current literature does not converge on a unified cognitive or consciousness-based theory of hallucinations, underscoring a critical theoretical gap and the need for integrative models.

articles_hidden.title: Gambling disorder symptoms as an indirect marker of microtransaction spending in video games
articles_hidden.authors: Charles-Etienne Benoit; Szymon Pałubinski; Akito Miura; Takahide Etani; Floris Tijmen van Vugt; Piotr Kałowski; Andrzej Cudo
articles_hidden.abstract: Video games have gained a lot of popularity over the past decades, generating large global revenue, mostly through in-game monetization referred to as microtransactions. Game developers have studied the psychological mechanisms in video game monetization presumably to increase potential revenues, which could for some gamers exacerbate negative personality traits. This is particularly true for microtransactions which may associate with gaming disorder symptoms and gambling disorder symptoms. There is currently insufficient research as to how the various forms of microtransactions relate to symptoms of gaming disorder and gambling disorder. We collected questionnaire data from 461 gamer participants. In order to explore the structure and interrelations between the variables, network analysis was applied. Our results align with previous findings that showed that the amount of money individuals spend on microtransactions increases with the risk of gaming disorder symptoms. However, we demonstrate that gambling disorder symptoms relate only indirectly to online spending through a direct link to physical game purchases. This finding is interesting considering the immaterial nature of microtransactions. Altogether, our findings highlight the need to disentangle gaming and gambling disorder symptoms and microtransactions, isolate psychological markers of problematic behavior, and aim to develop support or preventive technologies to come to the help of vulnerable gamers.

articles_hidden.title: Can Large Language Models Simulate Child-Like Theory of Mind?
articles_hidden.authors: Anja Brand; Tobias Wingen; Oliver Christ
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified debates about the validity of using silicon samples, of artificial participants simulated by AI. This question is especially relevant for developmental psychology, where valid simulation requires models not only to solve tasks, but also to reproduce age-typical limitations in cognitive ability. We tested whether standard autoregressive models (e.g., OpenAI's GPT-4) and more advanced reasoning models can simulate such developmental trajectories in Theory of Mind (ToM). Six LLMs were prompted with child-age personas ranging from 2.5 to 6.0 years and completed classic false-belief tasks. Most models showed strong baseline ToM performance, and many also successfully downplayed their abilities in line with human developmental trajectories. However, performance varied substantially across model type, provider, and task. These findings suggest that silicon sampling may be promising for developmental research, but relying on silicon samples alone is not yet a valid method.

articles_hidden.title: Relationship Quality Moderates Depressive-Symptom Associations With Negative Self-Perceptions and Partner Metaperceptions
articles_hidden.authors: Nida Civici; Andrew Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression is associated with persistent negative self-beliefs and altered social information processing. Although considerable research has examined self-perception in depression, less is known about how depressive symptoms relate to beliefs about how romantic partners perceive the self and whether relationship quality moderates these associations. The present study investigated associations between depressive symptoms, self-perceptions, metaperceptions of partner evaluations, and memory for self-referential information across multiple social perspectives. A sample of 171 adults in romantic relationships completed measures of depressive symptoms and relationship quality, an adapted Self-Referential Encoding Task assessing evaluations from the self, a romantic partner, and a neutral researcher, and a subsequent memory assessment. Higher depressive symptoms were associated with more negative self-perceptions and more negative beliefs about how romantic partners viewed the self, but not with perceptions attributed to the neutral researcher. Relationship quality moderated the association between depressive symptoms and negative self- and partner-related perceptions, with weaker associations observed among participants reporting higher-quality relationships. Memory analyses focused on self-reference effects across social perspectives. Memory sensitivity was higher for self- and partner-encoded items than for researcher-encoded items and for negative than positive items. However, there was no consistent evidence that depressive symptoms, relationship quality, or their interaction predicted these self-reference effects. These findings suggest that depressive symptoms extend beyond self-evaluation to include assumptions about how emotionally significant others perceive the self, with relationship quality shaping the strength of these associations. The findings underscore the importance of considering partner-related metaperceptions and relationship context when examining interpersonal processes associated with depression.

articles_hidden.title: Social influence and information cascades in experience-based decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Kiri Kuroda; Simon Kai Ciranka; Dirk U. Wulff; Ralf Kurvers
articles_hidden.abstract: Many consequential decisions are made in environments where outcome probabilities are not explicitly described but must be inferred from experience. In most modern environments, this information search takes place in the presence of others. Yet, the role of social influence in experience-based decisions has been largely overlooked, leaving it unclear how personal and social information combine to shape what people sample, when they stop searching, and what they finally choose. Here, we address all three decision stages. In a preregistered study, participants could freely sample two options before making a final choice, either alone (solo condition) or while observing the final choices of their group members (group condition). We developed a modeling framework and show that social influence left sampling unaffected but altered stopping and choice. Participants searched longer when the group was more divided and stopped earlier when the majority choice agreed with their own personal sampling information. Consequently, they drew fewer samples and encountered fewer rare events than solo participants. When choosing, group members copied others' choices only when their personal information was ambiguous. Comparing decision sequences in groups with a solo baseline, complemented with agent-based simulations, showed that this strategy gave rise to mild information cascades, with decisions in groups being more similar to each other than in a solo baseline. Our results reveal how social influence shapes search, stopping, and choice, and how these individual-level decision rules scale up to collective dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: The context-dependent evolution of structure learning and metacognition
articles_hidden.authors: Rochelle Kaper; Megan A. K. Peters
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans learn multiple probabilistic regularities at once, and often without feedback, which may be aided by metacognitive evaluations throughout learning. To understand this learning-metacognition relationship, we must first characterize how both capacities co-evolve as environmental structures are internalized, especially when feedback is unavailable. Here, participants learned a two-level probabilistic environment in which stimulus co-occurrences were embedded within a sequence, using unfamiliar fractals and familiar line drawings in a two-session, within-subjects design (N=63; N=50 completed both sessions). For each stimulus set, we measured learning across six repeating exposure-test cycles, using a cover task during exposure phases and forced-choice questions in test phases; test questions also included confidence judgments. Results revealed stimulus- and structure-dependent learning and metacognitive signatures. First, learning dynamics differed across stimuli: fractal sequence test accuracy outpaced co-occurrence accuracy, but vice versa for line drawings. Further, confidence increased across blocks, and was higher for line drawings as well as co-occurrences and first but not second sequence selections. Finally, both metacognitive sensitivity and test accuracy increased in successive exposure-test cycles for fractals, but metacognitive sensitivity remained stagnant for line drawings even as test accuracy improved. These results demonstrate that structure learning and metacognitive processes are highly context- and complexity-dependent rather than being completely generalizable. This study informs future directions for refining theories of learning without feedback, including how people evaluate their own learning and uncertainty and the interaction of both cognitive abilities with task design, stimuli, and environmental structures.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial biases in Arithmetic: The Effect of Operation Order and Visual Spacing on Calculations
articles_hidden.authors: Martyna Sroka; Michał Obidziński; Krzysztof Cipora; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual layout is known to affect computational performance, yet its relation to response format and numerical proficiency remains unclear. This preregistered study examined whether spatial presentation modulates arithmetic problem-solving. We conceptually replicated Experiment 3 of Landy and Goldstone's (2010) study using the Precedence and Proximity Task in a forced-choice format. Additionally, we assessed arithmetic fluency using a speeded test. A total of 201 adults solved 200 mixed addition–multiplication expressions in which spacing either aligned or conflicted with order-of-operations rules. Operation order was also manipulated. Participants were faster and more accurate in congruent spacing conditions, whereas incongruent spacing increased operation-order errors, especially when problems began with addition. A subgroup of participants showed disproportionately poor performance under incongruent spacing, suggesting a prepotent susceptibility to misleading grouping cues. The spacing effect persisted despite differences in task format and response procedure compared to the original study, supporting its robustness. Higher arithmetic fluency was associated with higher accuracy and shorter reaction times in the Precedence and Proximity Task. These findings corroborate that visuospatial layout biases symbolic computation and that individuals differ in their susceptibility to it.

articles_hidden.title: Preparing the University for Generation Alpha: A Research Agenda for the Digital Transformation of Higher Education
articles_hidden.authors: Sandra Grinschgl; Malte Elson; Tina Hascher; Andre Klostermann; Etna Rosa Krakenberger; Adrian Ritz; Thomas Christian Sauter; Amanda Zurkirchen; Michael Schulte-Mecklenbeck
articles_hidden.abstract: Generation Alpha, a cohort growing up with smartphones and generative AI as ordinary features of everyday life, will soon enter a higher education system that is itself undergoing profound digital transformation. We argue that the central challenge of this transformation is not technological alone but human and that it is shaped by three fundamental tensions: upskilling vs. deskilling, autonomy vs. dependence, and individualization vs. collaboration. Developed by an interdisciplinary Community of Practice at the University of Bern (UniBE), we introduce the BRIDGE model, which conceptualizes the university as an ecosystem of three interdependent groups: students, academic (researchers and lecturers) and organizational support staff whose psycho-social, health, well-being, and performance competencies must be understood across the trajectory from school to working life. Building on this model, we propose a two-phase research agenda: systematic identification of competencies, expectations, and institutional processes through a multi-year, longitudinal research program spanning all three groups, followed by collaborative transformation of higher education through empirically evaluated interventions. This agenda provides what digital transformation in higher education currently lacks: an empirical basis for deciding where digital tools strengthen learning, work, and well-being--and where they undermine them--and tested interventions to shift that balance. It thereby operationalizes UniBE's Digitalization Strategy 2030 and responds to national as well as international calls for evidence-based, human-centered digital transformation.

articles_hidden.title: Apples to apples: Stability and flexibility trade off only when measured at the same processing level.
articles_hidden.authors: Luca Moretti; Iring Koch; Tobias Egner
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive stability and cognitive flexibility are two crucial abilities supporting goal-directed behaviour. While cognitive stability designates our ability to maintain task-relevant information and shield it against distraction, flexibility allows to choose which information constitutes the task focus. Because of their complementary role, it has long been assumed that cognitive stability and flexibility are inversely related, such that promoting stability should impair flexibility, and vice versa. Recently however, a series of task-switching experiments have failed to observe such a mandatory trade-off, prompting a lively debate on the stability-flexibility relationship. In the present study, we aim to reconcile these findings with the trade-off view, by testing whether the stability and flexibility trade-off depends on the operationalization of these constructs. While previous studies gauged stability via the congruency effect and flexibility via task-switch costs, we here additionally measured cognitive stability via the valency effect. While the congruency effect indexes cross-task interference at the level of response selection, the valency effect is thought to reflect such interference at the level of task selection, which may more closely align with task-switching. Across three experiments and a re-analysis, we provide consistent evidence that manipulations reducing task switch cost increase the valency effect (and vice versa), but do not modulate the congruency effect. These findings suggest that stability and flexibility do trade off, but only when measured at the same level of processing (here, the task-selection level). We discuss the possible reasons why trade-offs may be level-specific, and future approaches to further investigate the stability-flexibility relationship.

articles_hidden.title: Normative and Maladaptive Personality Traits in Borderline Personality Disorder: A Comparative and Hierarchical Analysis of HEXACO and PID-5
articles_hidden.authors: Martin Weiß; Johanna Hepp; Katja Isabell Seitz; Yun-Loe Laura Lai; Nikolaus Kleindienst; Sylvia Steinmann; Katja Bertsch; Inga Niedtfeld
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of personality pathology invite the question of how normative and maladaptive trait systems jointly characterize borderline personality disorder (BPD). This study examined how the HEXACO model of personality and the DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders trait system, operationalized with the Personality Inventory for DSM–5, differentiate individuals with BPD from mentally healthy control (HC) individuals, both separately and jointly.
Methods: Data from two assessment waves of a large clinical research program were combined into a final sample of 575 participants (233 with BPD, 342 HC). A joint item-level PCA was conducted to examine seven- and eleven-component solutions, and a Bass-Ackwards principal components analysis was conducted to examine the joint hierarchical structure of HEXACO and PID-5 items. Both instruments were administered as self-reports. 
Results: Compared with HC, individuals with BPD showed lower HEXACO Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness, and higher Emotionality, as well as higher scores on all PID-5 domains, particularly Negative Affectivity and Disinhibition. In the combined domain model, low Extraversion and high  PID-5 Negative Affectivity, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism uniquely predicted BPD status. At the facet level, low Social Self-Esteem (HEXACO) and high Emotional Lability (PID-5) were especially discriminative. Joint item analyses yielded a sevencomponent solution in which six components corresponded closely to the six HEXACO factors and a dominant seventh component represented broad maladaptivity, with PID-5 items loading positively and HEXACO items largely loading inversely. Group differences were almost entirely confined to this broad component. 
Conclusions: These findings suggest that BPD is characterized by both a broad maladaptivity dimension and a more specific trait profile involving affective instability, interpersonal insecurity, irritability, and reduced behavioral control. The findings support integrating normative and maladaptive trait models in  the dimensional description of BPD, while indicating that the dominant joint dimension cannot be interpreted unambiguously as a substantive general factor of personality pathology.

articles_hidden.title: Memory reactivation levels remain unaffected by anticipated interference
articles_hidden.authors: Nursena Ataseven; I. Efsane Algın; Duygu Yucel; Berna Güler; Lara Todorova; Keisuke Fukuda; Eren Gunseli
articles_hidden.abstract: Most daily tasks require frequent information exchange between working memory (WM) and long-term memory (LTM). However, the factors that modulate the reactivation of LTMs in WM remain to be explored. Here, we tested the effects of anticipated perceptual interference (in Experiment 1) and anticipated dual task interference (in Experiment 2) on reactivation of LTMs in WM using contralateral delay activity (CDA) in the EEG. On each trial, participants saw one or three previously studied or novel objects that were tested after a brief retention interval. In half of the blocks, the retention contained perceptual distractors (Experiment 1) or dual task interference (Experiment 2). In both experiments, the CDA prior to the interference period was similar regardless of the anticipated interference. Additionally, we measured contralateral alpha power suppression as an index of spatial attention. We found that spatial attention allocated to the memorized objects’ locations also was not modulated with anticipated interference. These findings indicate that anticipating interference does not influence the extent to which WM is engaged in representing information stored in LTM.

articles_hidden.title: Healthy attachment for the parents? An investigation on the association between attachment parenting and parental mental health.
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Schlier; Hanna Laura Meder; Mira-Pauline Grapentin; Nora Imlau
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. Attachment parenting (AP) became popular for it promotes responsive caregiving, but has been criticized for over-extensively translating attachment research into challenging parenting standards, mirroring detrimental intensive-parenting beliefs that adversely affect parental health. Meanwhile, evidence on AP remains limited and assessments of AP-beliefs and AP-practice are lacking. This study aims to develop and validate an AP-questionnaire and test the associations between AP and parental mental health and explore the mediating role of intensive-parenting beliefs.
Methods. In a preregistered cross-sectional online-survey, 1664 parents (98.5% mothers) of children aged up to six years answered an extensive item-list assessing AP-beliefs and AP implementation into practice, an intensive parenting questionnaire, and mental health measures. Confirmatory factor analyses were used for AP-questionnaire validation and correlation- and mediation-analyses for exploring the association between AP and mental health.
Results. A 26-item AP-questionnaire was extracted that assesses AP-beliefs and AP- practice, both for the global AP-approach and seven individual core-principles. AP-indicators consistently showed small/minimal correlations with better mental health, whereas mediation analyses revealed parallel, opposing pathways: a positive, direct association from AP to mental health (possibly explained via parental fulfilment) and adverse indirect pathways through intensive-parenting beliefs (challenge-/self-sacrifice and essentialist-beliefs).
Conclusion. AP may be neither uniformly beneficial nor harmful. Rather, it can foster parental fulfilment which increases parental well-being, but also instil dysfunctional beliefs about sacrifice and unavoidable strain that increase parental-stress. To improve evidence-based personalized parenting-recommendations, longitudinal research is needed to disentangle when AP fosters positive parental identity and when it reinforces parental vulnerabilities.

articles_hidden.title: Human outcome-irrelevant value learning is insensitive to its monetary cost
articles_hidden.authors: Ido Ben-Artzi; Noham Wolpe; Nitzan Shahar
articles_hidden.abstract: When learning from reinforcement, individuals should assign credit selectively to features of their actions that causally determine outcomes. Yet, even when explicit instructions and extensive experience clarify which action features predict reward, humans assign credit to outcome-irrelevant features, leading to suboptimal choices. Here, we use computational modeling to test if this suboptimal credit assignment can be controlled depending on the monetary cost at stake. Specifically, we tested whether higher payoffs can increase control over outcome-irrelevant credit assignment. Participants (N = 287) completed a multi-armed bandit task under low and high monetary stakes. Higher stakes increased the influence of outcome-relevant values on choice, but, strikingly, had no influence on outcome-irrelevant values, which influenced choices to a similar degree. These findings demonstrate the automatic nature of credit assignment to outcome-irrelevant features, suggesting that associations between features and reward are formed despite clear instructions and their detrimental consequences for monetary gains.

articles_hidden.title: Selective reproduction of spatial–emotional mappings in large language models
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Fumiya Yonemitsu; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: The vertical-valence metaphor refers to the association between emotional valence and vertical space, whereby positive and negative emotions are linked to upward and downward directions, respectively. While this mapping has been robustly observed in human cognition, it remains unclear whether such associations are also reproduced in artificial intelligence systems. The present study investigated the vertical-valence metaphor in ChatGPT. In Experiments 1–3, ChatGPT-4 showed a consistent pattern in which “up” was evaluated more positively than “down,” and emotional words were spatially organized such that “joy” was placed above “sadness,” with “surprise” positioned in between. This pattern persisted even when the coordinate system was reversed. In Experiments 4–6, we compared silicon and human samples and observed a more nuanced pattern. While the vertical-valence mapping was largely preserved across both groups, the intermediate positioning of “surprise” was not consistently reproduced in ChatGPT-5.2. An additional pilot experiment indicates that this reduction in differentiation may be influenced by prompt language, although the relative contributions of model characteristics and language could not be determined. Exploratory analyses revealed that the horizontal-valence metaphor showed less consistent patterns across all the experiments, indicating lower robustness. Taken together, these findings suggest that large language models do not uniformly reproduce human cognitive mappings but instead exhibit a graded pattern of representation. Robust mappings are preserved, whereas intermediate or weaker mappings may be compressed or destabilized.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the effect of briefing modality on participant experiences, data quality, and data quantity in an experience sampling study
articles_hidden.authors: Elisabeth Hutasoit; Milla Pihlajamäki; Ginette Lafit; Olivia J Kirtley; Inez Myin-Germeys; Gudrun Eisele
articles_hidden.abstract: The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) requires participants to repeatedly complete assessments in daily life, typically without direct researcher supervision. Participant briefing is therefore an important opportunity to prepare participants to follow the protocol independently, but the effects of different characteristics of briefings are poorly understood. This quasi-experimental study examined whether online versus in-person briefing influenced data quantity (compliance), data quality (careless responding), and participant experiences (participant burden, perceived briefing sufficiency). First-year psychology students (N=249) were assigned to an online (n=209) or in-person (n=40) briefing condition based on recruitment phase and completed a seven-day ESM protocol with 10 daily prompts. Results showed that briefing modality did not significantly affect mean levels of compliance, careless responding, participant burden, or perceived briefing sufficiency. However, the effect of briefing modality on compliance changed over time: initial compliance was higher and declined more steeply in the online briefing condition than in the in-person briefing condition, although both conditions reached descriptively similar compliance rates by the end of the study. No significant interactions with time were found for careless responding or momentary burden. These findings suggest that online briefing may be a viable alternative to in-person briefing in relatively short and straightforward ESM protocols. However, in-person briefing may support more sustained compliance over time. Future research should replicate these findings in fully experimental designs and examine whether briefing modality matters more in other samples or longer or more demanding ESM studies.

articles_hidden.title: Educator Preparedness in Navigating Inclusive Education and Sensory Differences in Autism: Qualitative Exploration in Ontario, Canada
articles_hidden.authors: Stephanie Larmer; Gabrielle Czichrak; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Although Ontario, Canada follows an inclusive education model, little is known about the current status regarding the education of autistic students. Specifically, limited research has explored relevant facets of educator experiences and needs, a crucial component of successful inclusive education in autism. We aimed to explore existing gaps through open-ended questions in a questionnaire and follow-up interviews. First, educators and pre-service educators completed the open-ended questions as part of a larger questionnaire. Then, those who opted to participate completed follow-up interviews on their responses to the open-ended questions. The results revealed a pervasive lack of support for educators and pre-service educators and the consequences it can have for both them and autistic students. Specifically, participants detailed a wide range of desired professional development in autism and outlined a high prevalence of sensory experiences with autistic students, desiring guidance. Ultimately, participants emphasized the existing barriers to successful inclusive education in autism and explained the changes that would help in overcoming them. It was evident participants care for autistic students and desire change that leads to greater inclusion and success. This research demonstrates the value in listening to those responsible for implementing inclusive education in autism, providing decision makers with updated evidence based on direct experience that can guide professional development design and policies and may serve as an example for inclusive education more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Factor Structure and Convergent Validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) Among Filipino Licensure Examination Reviewees
articles_hidden.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles_hidden.abstract: The Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP) distinguishes between striving for high yet attainable standards (i.e., excellencism) and the pursuit of rigid, inflexible ones (i.e., perfectionism). The current study examines the psychometric validity of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE) among two samples of Filipino adults preparing for a licensure examination. Results from confirmatory factor analyses supported the two factor structure of the SCOPE. Convergent validity was supported through expected cross-sectional associations with the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale as well as time-lagged associations with subjective well-being. Time 1 excellencism was positively associated with Time 2 life satisfaction and positive affect, whereas Time 1 perfectionism was positively linked with Time 2 negative affect. Overall, these findings provide support for the validity of the SCOPE and the assumptions of the MEP, suggesting that pursuing excellencism—rather than perfectionism—is associated with greater well-being during intense career preparation.

articles_hidden.title: The Unified Model Graph: Drawing the Statistical Models of Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Hsiu Ting Ting Yu
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists describe their statistical models with diagrams. The conventions in use, path diagrams, multilevel panels, plate notation, and causal graphs, each grew inside one modeling tradition, and they disagree on basic symbols. As a result, one figure can stand for two different models. An ellipse with three arrows can show a factor model or a latent profile model. A labeled arrow can show a fixed slope or a person-varying slope. A mediation triangle can show a regression decomposition or a causal claim. This article introduces the Unified Model Graph (UMG), a notation built so that the figure identifies the model that was fitted. Three visual cues type every quantity: fill for observed versus latent, shape for continuous versus categorical, and outline for inferential role. Four edge types separate regression, covariance, deterministic, and mixture relations. Plates mark replication, and a badge states whether the figure makes a causal claim. Every well-formed UMG corresponds to exactly one family of distributions, and path diagrams, plate notation, and causal graphs are special cases; the formal results and proofs are in the supplemental material. The accompanying R package \pkg{} builds diagrams from code or from fitted lavaan, lme4, mirt, and brms objects, validates them, translates them to and from lavaan syntax, checks necessary identification conditions, derives testable implications, and generates model-implied data displays. A benchmark of eight R diagramming packages on ten representational features and ten operations locates what the notation adds. All materials, scripts, and outputs are openly archived.

articles_hidden.title: The Liege Mind-Blanking Scale: a comprehensive scale to assess the heterogeneity of mind-blanking cognitive and experiential aspects
articles_hidden.authors: Paradeisios Alexandros Boulakis; Marion Balla; Agustina Aragón-Daud; David Stawarczyk; Giovanni Briganti; Athena Demertzi; Steve Majerus
articles_hidden.abstract: Our minds are not always full of thoughts. Occasionally, people will report absence of any mental content, an experience termed mind-blanking (MB). So far, MB has been primarily quantified through experience-sampling paradigms. While experience-sampling has allowed researchers to study the behavioural and neurophysiological profile of MB, the practice of asking participants for thought categories, such as “an empty mind”, might undermine the richness and diversity of MB instances. In the present study, we adopted a self-reported, trait approach to MB. We developed a novel MB scale, the Liege Mind-Blanking Scale (L-MBS), with the aim to probe distinct types of MB experiences and relate them to different cognitive functions. A sample of 644 participants completed the L-MBS alongside a cohort of self-report questionnaires measuring trait mind-wandering, attention, memory, metacognition and arousal. The L-MBS showed adequate psychometric properties. Factor analysis validated the presence of 3 discrete factors: one related to the perceived experience of MB, one related to memory failures, and one related to blanking under pressure. Network analysis linked these factors to discrete cognitive domains. The experience of blanking correlated with metacognitive monitoring, while memory failures were associated with autobiographical memory difficulties. Overall, the L-MBS provides a quick, accessible and psychometrically validated measure of an individual’s beliefs about their blank experiences. At the same time, the presence of multiple MB factors suggests that MB is not necessarily a unitary phenomenon and most likely represents a clustering of different moments of no content.

articles_hidden.title: Learning from others’ mistakes: differential effects of observing target errors versus adaptation errors
articles_hidden.authors: Beverley Larssen; Anthony Sze; Ryan Jin; Sarah N Kraeutner; Nicola Jane Hodges
articles_hidden.abstract: How we learn from observing others perform reaching tasks is debated in the adaptation literature.
