When observers see a hand intentionally miss a target to correctly counteract rotated visual feedback (adaptation error), after-effects are typically absent. In contrast, observing consistent target errors, has resulted in unintended compensatory after-effects. The type of observed “error” (adaptation versus target error) may therefore have different effects on observation-induced behaviour, although this has not been tested within the same experiment. We compared participants in a four-group orthogonal design, who saw a model hit or miss a target, with or without rotated cursor feedback. Small compensatory after-effects (pre- to post-test) were seen when reaching to perceived midline in groups that observed target errors (misses). However, there were also small imitative after-effects after observing adaptation errors without target errors, but only when reaching to visual targets. Observing adaptation errors with or without target misses aided later performance in the same rotated environment and was accompanied by explicit knowledge of the rotation. Knowing the task goal is relevant information for eliciting small compensatory aiming biases in observers, perhaps because target errors matter more than adaptation errors when observing, leading to an unintended resolution not needed for “correct” actions.

articles_hidden.title: Time pressure modulates resource-rational planning in online chess
articles_hidden.authors: Ionatan Kuperwajs; Evan Russek; Lisa Schut; Yotam Sagiv; Wei Ji Ma; Tom Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Human planning is incredibly efficient. Even in complex situations with many possible courses of action, people are able to make good decisions. Recent proposals suggest that a primary contributor to this efficiency is the intelligent use of cognitive resources, but how people allocate these resources under time constraints is not fully understood. In this work, we conduct a resource-rational analysis of planning in a large data set of online chess games. We first demonstrate that players spent more time thinking when they had more time to do so, and that this effect was especially prevalent when computation was more valuable. Then, we show that additional time spent planning resulted in better selected moves when one existed, and highlight the role of expertise in this setting. Finally, we scale our analysis by showing that changes in move time, move quality, and move entropy as a function of time control setting correlate across board positions. Our results provide evidence that people make resource-rational choices when planning under time pressure.

articles_hidden.title: Hypothesis Spaces: How Structural Beliefs Shape Uncertainty in the Anxious Mind
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Benita Senfft; Ondrej Zika
articles_hidden.abstract: While uncertainty is ubiquitous, not all uncertainty is the same. In this review, we dissociate between uncertainty in aspects of known problem spaces (e.g. how long are hospital waiting times; “parameter uncertainty”) and uncertainty arising from unknown structure or even the nature of a problem (e.g. how do I get medical help in a new country; “structural uncertainty”). We suggest that much everyday uncertainty is structural: uncertainty about which model of the world applies in the first place. We bring research on uncertainty and structure learning together through the concept of hypothesis spaces - sets of candidate generative structures that an individual considers plausible, together with distribution of beliefs over their likelihood. We propose that properties of these spaces, including their size, complexity and entropy, provide a systematic framework for understanding structural uncertainty and may help explain characteristic features of anxious thought such as worry, overthinking, catastrophizing and overgeneralization. This perspective also offers a way to refine broad constructs such as intolerance of uncertainty by linking them to specific representational and inferential processes and their properties. We suggest that revisiting the role of uncertainty in anxiety from the viewpoint of structural inference holds the key for mechanistic understanding of clinical observations and closer alignment with fundamental research in cognitive neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Educator Preparedness in Navigating Inclusive Education and Sensory Differences in Autism: Quantitative Exploration in Ontario, Canada
articles_hidden.authors: Stephanie Larmer; Gabrielle Czichrak; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Ontario, Canada follows an inclusive education model, however, little is known about the current status of the education of autistic students in this model. Specifically, educators are a crucial component of successful inclusive education in autism, yet there is a dearth of research exploring which educator characteristics and experiences are relevant to successful inclusive education in autism, and whether educator needs are being met. We aimed to explore existing gaps through an online questionnaire evaluating educators’ and pre-service educators’ experience, self-efficacy, and knowledge of autism, both in general and sensory processing, which is particularly relevant in educational settings. Additionally, we explored educators’ needs related to autism and educating autistic students. The results revealed experience, specifically number of autistic students, contributed to greater self-efficacy in educating autistic students. Furthermore, there was a significant impact of professional development in autism on self-efficacy in educating autistic students and a near-unanimous desire for more professional development in autism, underlining the need for more professional development in autism to build valuable qualities in educators and pre-service educators. Also, there was a significant difference and relationship between general and sensory processing knowledge of autism, where general knowledge was greater and predictive of sensory processing knowledge, suggesting professional development should explore more specific components of autism, especially one so relevant at school, and be scaffolding. This research provides decision makers with updated evidence that can guide professional development design and policies related to inclusive education in autism to make improvements that benefit both educators and autistic students.

articles_hidden.title: Psychology in 2125: A Developmental Science of Living Sense-Making
articles_hidden.authors: Peter J. Marshall
articles_hidden.abstract: A century from now, the computational framework at the center of psychology will no longer organize the discipline. As used here, "computational" names a broad information-processing ontology: meaning is specified in advance, rather than generated through the activity, history, and situation of living beings. This assumption fits engineered systems, but it misdescribes living ones. This article argues that three converging shifts are destabilizing that framework. The first undermines the computational account of inheritance: organisms develop through activity within configurations of constraints reconstituted across generations, not through the readout of genetic programs. The second displaces its account of psychological structure: psychological phenomena unfold as trajectories of coordination rather than as stable traits, with reliability and variability arising from the same generative process. The third sharpens the first two: artificial intelligence systems produce fluent performance without embodiment, developmental history, or any stake in the world. This contrast reveals what living organization contributes. The psychology implied by these shifts treats development as foundational, not as a subfield. It understands psychological constructs as patterns of activity that persons sustain over time, and is better positioned to address a century of changing human ecologies. This future psychology will be a developmental science of living sense-making.

articles_hidden.title: Blending Sources of Evidence: Meta-Analysis Combining Aggregated Data and Individual Participant Data from Multilab Replications
articles_hidden.authors: Jingru Zhang; James E Pustejovsky
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional meta-analyses synthesize average treatment effects from sample-level aggregated data (AD) and are limited to addressing questions of moderation only at the sample level. Although associations between study-mean covariates and effect sizes need not reflect individual-level relations, individual-level moderating effects can be investigated using individual participant data (IPD). Multilab replication projects have recently made large, preregistered IPD collections publicly available for effects also synthesized in conventional meta-analyses, so the two data sources could, in principle, be combined. Determining whether they should be combined, however, requires judgment about their compatibility. We propose four guiding questions for the preliminary evaluation of such syntheses, concerning outcome measurement, primary study sample sizes, the distribution of study features, and publication bias, and show how graphical and tabular summaries can inform each consideration. We then describe meta-analytic models for combining AD and IPD from studies with continuous outcomes. We review two-stage and one-stage approaches for estimating the overall effect distribution and study-level moderation, as well as for separating within-study from between-study moderation of individual characteristics, including a novel bivariate two-stage formulation that jointly synthesizes treatment and moderation effects. We illustrate the framework with two examples, each pairing an AD meta-analysis with a multilab replication of the same effect. In an example of moral licensing effects, the preliminary evaluation indicates that combining the sources is not warranted; in an example of social heuristics effects, synthesizing across data sources is warranted. Together, the examples show that whether two sources can be combined is an empirical question best settled before modeling begins, and that the specification that follows should be tailored to the features of the data that the preliminary evaluation brings to light.

articles_hidden.title: Student Attention During Learning Activities: Variability across Instructional Contexts and Student Characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Zoe Mao; Fang Yu Chang; Maya Khalil; Andrea Dillon; Mark Rapport; Sandra Loo; Agatha Lenartowicz; Jennie K Grammer
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s ability to pay attention during instruction is foundational for learning. The growing use of online learning has introduced important questions about how attentional engagement varies across instructional contexts, particularly of those with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Measuring children’s attention in real-world contexts, however, remains challenging. In this semi-naturalistic experiment, we examined attentional behaviors of children with and without an ADHD diagnosis (N = 80; ages 6-10; 37.5% female; 32.5% ADHD) as they participated in four one-on-one science learning activities with an instructor. Activities varied along two instructional dimensions: modality (in-person vs. synchronous online vs. asynchronous video-based) and management of learning (teacher-led vs. student-led). Continuous behavioral coding using the newly developed Student Attention Tracking (SAT) protocol revealed variability in children’s attention both between individuals and across instructional contexts. Linear mixed-effects models, controlling for age, sex at birth, and family socioeconomic status indicated that children’s attentional patterns during synchronous online instruction were comparable to in-person learning, when the amount of teacher-student interaction was comparable. Children also demonstrated lower fidgeting and off-task behaviors during asynchronous video-based learning. Compared to teacher-led in-person instruction, student-led individual learning was associated with higher engagement and lower fidgeting. A significant interaction with ADHD diagnosis indicated that the increases in engagement and decreases in fidgeting were greater for children with ADHD. Furthermore, instructional context accounted for substantially more variance in attentional behaviors than diagnostic status. Together, findings suggest that features of instructional design may play a larger role in shaping children’s attentional engagement during learning than diagnostic differences alone.

articles_hidden.title: Health Equity Training Decisional Balance Scale for Health Professionals
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Almond
articles_hidden.abstract: Racial health and healthcare inequities are sustained in part by health professionals’ beliefs about the benefits and costs of equity-focused action, yet no validated decisional balance measure exists for this domain. This study introduces and evaluates the Health Equity Decisional Balance (HEDB) scale. Eighty-eight health professionals completed the scale of ten proposed items assessing perceived pros and cons of engaging with health and healthcare equity work, along with a measure of Anti-Racist Efficacy (ARE) (Eschmann et al., 2023). Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were used to test the latent structure of the scale and its predictive validity. A two-factor model retaining eights items with correlated pros and cons showed excellent fit (χ²(25)=32.98, RMSEA=.061, CFI=.982). Pros and cons were strongly and inversely related (r=−.90, p<.001), consistent with decisional balance theory. When modeled as latent predictors, pros showed a strong positive association with anti-racist self-efficacy (ARE) (β=.82, p=.037), whereas cons was not significant. Together, the factors accounted for 20% of variance in efficacy. The HEDB scale provides a brief, psychometrically sound measure of health professionals’ readiness-related beliefs about health and healthcare equity work.

articles_hidden.title: Cue–Appraisal Learning in Organizations: A Theory of Conditioned Appraisal Meaning
articles_hidden.authors: Robin Umbra
articles_hidden.abstract: Employees often respond to recurring workplace cues as if those cues carry the meaning of prior experience. A performance review, complaint channel, supervisor phrase, meeting routine, or organizational space may be appraised differently across employees even when the formal cue is the same. This article develops a theory of cue–appraisal learning in organizations. The theory proposes that recurring organizational cues become psychologically consequential when employees repeatedly encounter them in episodes appraised in similar, concern-relevant ways. Over time, employees may develop conditioned appraisal meanings: learned relations between recurring organizational cues and specific appraisal meanings that become more likely to be activated when those cues are encountered again. This cue-level perspective explains how prior organizational experience can shape appraisal activation before a current event has fully unfolded. It also clarifies how learned cue meanings may influence workplace emotion and action tendencies through appraisal processes that remain sensitive to situational, regulatory, and behavioral constraints. The article defines conditioned appraisal meaning, distinguishes it from adjacent constructs, develops propositions concerning acquisition, appraisal specificity, generalization, discrimination, revision, and downstream response, and outlines implications for research and practice.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic attribute activation explains gaze biases in choice.
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaozhi Taro Yang; Sudeep Bhatia
articles_hidden.abstract:
People tend to choose the options they look at more. Prior work explains this effect by assuming that visual attention increases preference for the attended option. However, it remains unclear why looking at an option increases its preference and when this relationship is
weakened. Using an experimental paradigm that combines eye-tracking and a think-aloud protocol, we provide evidence that visual attention shapes preference by activating attributes associated with the attended option. Critically, the content of these activated attributes
depends on contextual factors such as stimulus desirability and behavioral goals. In standard choice settings, where the goal is to choose the preferred option, visual attention primarily activates positive attributes. In contrast, when these contextual factors are incongruent, activated attributes become less positive, reducing the influence of visual attention on choice. To account for these patterns, we propose a new computational model of gaze-driven attribute activation. Our model subsumes existing theories as special cases, and uniquely predicts which attributes are brought to mind by gaze and how they shape downstream decisions. Together, our work offers a mechanistic explanation of a fundamental driver of choice as well as its boundary conditions.

articles_hidden.title: A Spanish-Language Version of the Emotion Reactivity Scale: Psychometric Properties, Measurement Invariance, and Criterion Validity in a Large Adolescent Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua B Gilbert; Zachary Himmelsbach; Matthew Nock; Nicole R. DeTore; Randi M. Schuster
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The Emotion Reactivity Scale (ERS) is a widely used self-report measure of the sensitivity, intensity, and persistence of emotional responses. It has been translated and evaluated in Dutch, French, German, Portuguese, and Farsi samples, and has been separately adapted into a brief six-item short form in English. However, no validated Spanish-language version currently exists despite Spanish being the most common non-English language spoken in U.S. schools.

Methods: We provide a Spanish translation of the ERS and evaluate its psychometric properties using data from 522 Spanish-language adolescent respondents and a demographically matched sample of 522 English-language adolescent respondents drawn from a school-based survey. We use multigroup item response theory to test measurement invariance across survey language and regularized differential item functioning (DIF) analysis to identify specific noninvariant items. We evaluate criterion validity through association with the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4).

Results: Multigroup item response theory analyses support metric but not scalar invariance across survey languages, with intercept differences identified for four items, none of which appear on the short form. Despite this evidence of differential item functioning, its practical impact is negligible, as adjusted and unadjusted scores are nearly perfectly correlated ($r > .99$). ERS scores show strong and statistically equivalent criterion validity across language groups in predicting concurrent psychological distress on the PHQ-4.

Conclusions: Both the long and short forms of the Spanish ERS are reliable and criterion-valid measures of emotion reactivity for use with Spanish-speaking adolescents.

articles_hidden.title: Intuitions about trait responsibilities
articles_hidden.authors: Yang Xiang; Stephanie Hsu; Samuel J. Gershman
articles_hidden.abstract: Popular depictions of mental life often feature a bustling society of personality traits—distinctive characters whose actions collectively determine behavior, much like how the actions of individual people collectively determine the behavior of a group. Do these depictions capture something important about folk psychology? One implication is that people should reason about trait responsibility similarly to how they reason about personal responsibility in groups. To test this implication quantitatively, we first collected data on judgments about the predictive relationship between traits and actions (Experiment 1), and then elicited trait responsibility judgments for the same actions (Experiment 2). The data from Experiment 1 were used to construct models of responsibility attribution (adapted from prior work on personal responsibility in groups), which we then compared to data from Experiment 2. We found that participants treated personality traits as entities that can bear responsibility for behavior, and their responsibility judgments were best explained by an actual contribution model that assigns responsibility based on a trait’s predictive contribution to behavior. In contrast to findings from studies of personal responsibility, counterfactual-style models did not fare as well. These findings reveal both similarities and differences between responsibility attribution to traits within a person vs. people within a group.

articles_hidden.title: People make inferences from policy decisions regarding default options:  Replication and extension of McKenzie et al. (2006)
articles_hidden.authors: Xiaoru Teng; Ka Wai LAU; Tsz King Ng; Chan Ka Po; Yeung Wing; Siu Kit Yeung; Gilad Feldman
articles_hidden.abstract: Default effect refers to the phenomenon that people tend to choose the default option in a choice-set. McKenzie et al. (2006) showed that one mechanism for the effect is that defaults are perceived as an implicit endorsement and a recommended option by the policy makers that set the defaults. In a pre-registered experiment with a Prolific online sample from the United States (N = 602), we conducted replications and extensions of Studies 1, 2, and 3 from McKenzie et al. (2006). Across the nine target-article tests, the adjusted Cramer's V effects ranged from .24 to .86 with corresponding replication estimates ranging from .41 to .80. We concluded a successful replication of all three studies, with support for their findings showing that: 1) people who report willingness to be organ donors, and people who think others ought to be donors, are more likely to select organ donation as the policy default, and that in turn: 2) people make inferences from policymaker’s set defaults (Study 2: organ donations; Study 3: retirement plans) regarding the policymakers’ own preferences regarding enrollment, and their views regarding whether others should enroll. In our extension we added a control condition with no defaults, finding that 1) people still make inferences about choice architects’ attitudes, even when defaults were not set, and 2) that setting defaults to not act (not enroll) is perceived as closer to no defaults than setting defaults to act (to enroll). Materials, data, and code are available on: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/E5K4J.

articles_hidden.title: Theoretical Considerations of the Common Factor Model and its Alternatives
articles_hidden.authors: Danielle Siegel; Mijke Rhemtulla
articles_hidden.abstract: Accurate psychological measurement typically relies on the common factor model, which assumes observed items reflect an underlying latent construct plus measurement error. However, growing evidence suggests that the factor model is not appropriate for all psychological constructs, and applying it when its assumptions are violated can bias both the measurement and structural parameters in structural equation models (SEMs). The paper reviews the common factor model along with a range of alternative measurement approaches, including composite models with prespecified and estimated weights, psychometric network models, and models that treat individual scale items as unique predictors. We describe the theoretical assumptions, strengths, and limitations of each approach, with particular attention to recent methodological developments that all factor-based and composite-based models to be statistically compared within the SEM framework. Using a running empirical example from Milas et al., (2021), we illustrate how the choice of measurement model changes parameter estimates, model fit, and the substantive interpretation of results. We conclude that researchers should select a measurement approach based on the theoretical relations they hypothesize among their scale items rather than defaulting to the common factor model. We offer recommendations for evaluating and comparing candidate measurement models.

articles_hidden.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles_hidden.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles_hidden.title: Covariate Selection for Doubly Robust Double/debiased Machine Learning Estimators for Causal Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles_hidden.abstract: High-dimensional data create challenges for causal effect estimation because identifying the covariates needed for correct model specification becomes increasingly difficult. Double/debiased machine learning (DML) facilitates the use of machine learning (ML) for causal inference by mitigating regularization and overfitting bias, but comparatively less attention has been given to covariate selection in relation to the double robustness (DR) property possessed by some DML estimators. In particular, ML-based covariate selection may result in differential covariate selection or in misspecification of both models, thereby limiting the practical utility of the DR property. To address these issues, we propose using the union of the covariates selected by the propensity score (PS) and outcome ML models to re-estimate both models. Simulation results show that using the union consistently reduces more confounding bias than using separate selected covariate sets. The results also show that ML-based estimation does not uniformly outperform conventional DR estimation, even under conditions favorable to the Lasso, and that post-Lasso reduces more confounding bias than standard Lasso. These findings demonstrate that successful use of ML for causal inference depends not only on the ML algorithm but also on how the information obtained through covariate selection is incorporated into causal effect estimation.

articles_hidden.title: Within-Person Symptom Dynamics in Serious Mental Illness: Insights from Daily Self-reports and Audio Journals
articles_hidden.authors: Daiil Jun; Jeffrey M. Girard; Yoonho Chung; Scott L. Rauch; Einat Liebenthal; Justin T. Baker
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding how clinical symptoms fluctuate within individuals is crucial for developing personalized treatment, yet these dynamics remain understudied. We examined whether daily self-reports and speech features from audio journals predicted monthly fluctuations in clinician-rated symptoms among 54 outpatients with affective and psychotic disorders. We identified seven within-person symptom dimensions: disorganized thinking, mania, social withdrawal, inexpressivity, affective depression, cognitive depression, and anxiety. Daily self-reports and speech features were summarized on a monthly level across different temporal windows highlighting 3, 7, 14, and 28 days of daily data prior to the clinical interview to assess the predictive value of emphasizing more or less recent daily histories. Bayesian multilevel models indicated that both the intensity and day-to-day variability of daily experiences and speech features tracked month-to-month symptom fluctuations. Daily Positive Affect and speech sentiment were the most broadly informative indicators of fluctuations across symptom domains. Greater Daily Positive Affect or more positive sentiment predicted increased mania, whereas lower levels tracked increased other symptoms except for disorganized thinking. Model comparisons across temporal windows showed that models using daily self-reports were generally robust to different windows, although social withdrawal showed improved performance highlighting longer daily histories. Models using speech features generally performed better with longer temporal windows, whereas mania and anxiety showed no clear temporal window preference. Overall, these findings demonstrate the utility of daily self-reports and audio journals for dynamic symptom tracking and showcase a data-driven approach to investigating the optimal length of daily history for developing personalized monitoring tools in psychiatry.

articles_hidden.title: Learning a novel visual cue to update internal predictions of object weight
articles_hidden.authors: Olaf Kristiansen; Meike Scheller; Marko Nardini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background Efficient manual interactions with objects rely on accurate predictions of object heaviness, informed by both visual cues and prior lifting experience. While
arbitrary visual cues can be learned to guide motor planning, their predictive utility compared to a familiar cue like visual volume remains poorly understood.
Furthermore, it remains unknown whether presenting novel visual cues intrinsically (on the object) or extrinsically (on a screen), impacts predictive utility. This study
investigates the extent to which familiar and novel (intrinsic and extrinsic) visual cues influence anticipatory grip force adjustments.

Results: In a precision-grip lifting task with three object heaviness levels, peak grip force rate (PGFR), an indicator of heaviness predictions, was measured across four
conditions: ‘no-cue’, ‘familiar’, ‘novel intrinsic’, and ‘novel extrinsic’. Intrinsic cues were visual patterns (line orientations) on the surfaces of the objects, while extrinsic
cues were diagrammatic depictions of the same objects and patterns. Without visual cues, PGFR was strongly biased by the preceding lift’s weight. All visual cues
significantly reduced this bias. Contrary to predictions, the familiar volume cue did not exert a stronger influence than novel cues, nor did the intrinsic cues have a
stronger influence than extrinsic cues.

Conclusions: Novel visual cues can be rapidly incorporated into motor planning without a clear performance penalty relative to a familiar cue. Presenting novel cues extrinsically also does not incur a performance penalty relative to intrinsic presentation. These findings highlight the flexibility of sensorimotor control and may inform manual interactions in environments with limited or unconventional weight
predictors.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Substance Use Disorder Treatment: From Brain Awareness to Brain Recovery Capital
articles_hidden.authors: Tara Rezapour; Alex Baldacchino; Andrew Dalley; Jamie Berry; Shweta Chilka; Marc L. Copersino; Ali Farhoudian; Jing Jin; Steven Powers; Timothy Grigsby
articles_hidden.abstract: Substance use disorders continue to affect millions of people worldwide, yet a striking proportion never receive treatment. Poor awareness, internalized stigma, and neurobiological changes in the circuits responsible for self-monitoring all contribute to this gap in ways that conventional psychoeducation has not adequately addressed. Recent advances in addiction neuroscience offer a more precise and less stigmatizing language for understanding these barriers, one that reframes addiction as a brain disorder rather than a moral failure and opens new possibilities for how we educate patients about their condition. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation, or NIPE, builds on this foundation. It integrates current addiction neuroscience into an educational program designed to improve insight, reduce shame, and strengthen motivation for treatment and recovery. This paper proposes a clinical stage-based NIPE framework organized around the Transtheoretical Model of Health Behavior Change, mapping specific educational content and delivery priorities to seven stages of the recovery trajectory. The goal is an approach that meets people where they actually are in both their motivational readiness and their neurobiological capacity to engage. An example of a NIPE package for recovery and future directions to deliver effective NIPE and promote brain recovery are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Getting the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 Ready for Clinical Practice: Population-Representative Norms That Embrace Uncertainty
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Zimmermann; André Kerber; Christoph J. Kemper; Katharina Weweck
articles_hidden.abstract: The Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5) is the standard measure of the maladaptive traits in the Alternative DSM-5 Model for Personality Disorders, but normative information for score interpretation has remained limited. Existing norms refer to the U.S. population, are not conditioned on age and gender, and report point values without any quantification of uncertainty. We derived norms for the facets, domains, and total scores of the full PID-5 and its abbreviated versions, referenced to the German general population and conditional on age and gender. A modular Bayesian pipeline combined a probability-based reference sample (N = 4,727) with three “donor” samples that completed the full instrument (N = 2,471), linked via 34 common items. The norm tables quantify uncertainty at two levels, with credible bands for every norm value and score-conditional intervals for every raw score, and can be applied through a free online scoring platform.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting More Behavior More of the Time: On the Behavioral Nature of Different Personality Trait Measures
articles_hidden.authors: Niclas Kuper; Simon Mats Breil; Katharina Utesch; Mitja D Back
articles_hidden.abstract: Most research focuses on self-reported global trait ratings to approximate behavioral individual differences. However, several alternatives exist. Average self-reported states from experience sampling are thought to be closer to behavior, but little evidence supports this. Further, other-report should rely more strongly on behavior. Here, we predict interpersonal behavior from different personality trait measures, highlighting type of aggregation (global vs. average state measures) and perspective (self- vs. other-report). We provide initial, exploratory evidence with a small multi-methodological study (N = 88) including six trait measures: global self-report, global informant-report, time-based self-reported states (fortnightly diaries), time-based peer-reported states, event-based self-reported states (after social interactions), and event-based peer-reported states. Measures were compared in the prediction of actual behavior in the laboratory one year later. We focused on four behaviors (warmth, expressiveness, self-confidence, nervousness) and corresponding global/state dimensions. Self-reported states were rarely incrementally predictive above global self-report and thus not as close to behavior as commonly believed. When based on multiple raters, other-report was more consistently linked to behavior than self-report. Other-reported states averaged across peers were predictive beyond global informant-report and self-reported states, representing an underused method potentially closer to behavior. We outline future directions to go beyond self-report in behavioral personality science.

articles_hidden.title: How does Sleep Restriction Therapy work? Testing the Triple-R theory as an explanation through computational modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Jill de Ron; Tessa F. Blanken; Denny Borsboom; Hans Gommers; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Jaap Lancee; Leonie Franziska Maurer; Jason Nak; Donald Robinaugh; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep restriction therapy (SRT) is an effective treatment for insomnia, one of the most prevalent mental disorders today. The Triple-R theory has been proposed to explain the efficacy of SRT based on three processes: restricting time in bed, regulating sleep and wake times, and reconditioning of the bed-sleep association. However, based on the verbal theory alone it is difficult to determine whether the proposed processes explain the efficacy of SRT. In the current paper we test whether Triple-R theory explains the efficacy of SRT through computational modeling. Building on the productive explanation framework we (i) define empirical phenomena in sleep diary data before and after SRT; (ii) formalize the Triple-R theory as a computational model; (iii) test whether the empirical phenomena are reproduced by the model. We show that our computational Triple-R model reproduces most data patterns observed in empirical studies. Therefore, we conclude that the Triple-R theory provides a partial explanation of the efficacy of SRT. Moreover, our proposed Triple-R model makes predictions that can guide new clinical trials and provides a better understanding of the mechanisms of SRT.

articles_hidden.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles_hidden.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles_hidden.title: Mentoring Trainees with Lived Experience of Psychopathology: A Strengths-based, Cultural Humility Framework for Psychological Scientists
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Devendorf; Julie Cristello; Cassandra L. Boness; Irene Tung; Cecilia Hinojosa
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health difficulties are prevalent among psychologists, yet professionals in the field are often discouraged from disclosing their lived experience with psychopathology due to persistent stigma. For much of history, lived experience with psychopathology has been treated as a deficit within the profession. However, emerging research and perspectives are beginning to challenge this status quo by highlighting that lived experience can be an asset in psychological science and practice. Despite this shift, there remains little guidance on how to navigate this topic in mentor-mentee relationships. We outline a framework for strengths-based mentorship that is based on six pillars: 1) tenets of strengths-based mentorship; 2) foundational and functional mentorship competencies; 3) mental health literacy; 4) feminist principles; 5) cultural humility; and 6) ethical considerations. This framework can help improve mentor-mentee relationships, reduce stigma, and ultimately improve the professional development of mentees with lived experience. We apply this principle-driven framework to common professional scenarios: recruiting applicants, evaluating personal statements, and navigating situations when a mentee is distressed, requesting accommodations, or interested in leveraging their lived experiences in their work. By offering this framework, we aim to facilitate dialogue and provide actionable guidance for mentors seeking to support trainees with psychopathology.

articles_hidden.title: Schizotypy and Autistic Traits in Bilinguals: Associations with Language Deficits Across Native and Non-Native Languages
articles_hidden.authors: Arthur Hamilton; Synthia Guimond; Olessia Jouravlev
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Schizotypal and autistic traits are increasingly understood as existing on continuous dimensions extending from subclinical variation to clinical schizophrenia (SZ) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), respectively. Language deficits are well documented in SZ and ASD but research on their relationship to subclinical schizotypal and autistic traits remains limited. Moreover, while evidence suggests SZ symptoms manifest more strongly in bilinguals’ native (L1) than non-native (L2) language, little is known about whether associated language deficits similarly differ between L1 and L2.
Methods: The present study examined associations between schizotypy, autistic traits, and language performance in 503 bilinguals (436 English–French and 67 French–English) from the general population. Participants completed lexical, semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic language tasks in both L1 and L2, together with questionnaires on schizotypy and autistic traits.
Results: Higher schizotypy was associated with poorer syntactic and pragmatic performance in both languages and lexical performance in L1 only, while no association was found with semantic performance. Higher schizotypy was also associated with a reduced L1 advantage in lexical performance, but not in other linguistic domains. Autistic traits showed no independent association with linguistic performance or L1-vs-L2 differences. However, autistic traits moderated the relationship between schizotypy and language performance: higher autistic traits attenuated the negative association between schizotypy and performance in L1 while strengthening it in L2.
Conclusion: Overall, the findings partially support dimensional understandings of SZ by showing that some language deficits associated with clinical SZ extend to subclinical schizotypy, without providing clear evidence that ASD-associated language deficits extend to subclinical autistic traits.

articles_hidden.title: Dietary Modulation of Neurobiological Mechanisms Underlying Executive Function and Decision-Making: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Iveta Harris; Ian Evans; Jessica Bayes; Mansi Das Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Executive function (EF) and decision making (DM) are central to adaptive behaviour, yet evidence explaining how diet influences their underlying neurobiological mechanisms remains fragmented. This systematic review examined how dietary exposures influence the neurobiological mechanisms underlying EF and DM. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251173091). Of 12,952 records identified, 26 studies met the inclusion criteria, involving over 2,000 participants. Across the included studies, dietary exposures were associated with changes in metabolic, neurochemical, inflammatory, neural, and gut–brain pathways relevant to EF and DM. Behavioural effects were reported across all dietary domains but were less consistent than biological changes and varied according to intervention duration, task sensitivity, and participant characteristics. EF outcomes were more consistently modulated than DM outcomes, with effects most evident in working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Although less frequently studied, DM findings showed that dietary exposures could shift complex choices—including risk-taking, temporal discounting, and social decision-making—alongside changes in metabolic state and neurotransmitter precursor availability. Notably, none of the reviewed studies specifically examined ultra-processed food exposure, identifying an important gap in the current evidence. Few studies examined when or how biological changes translated into measurable behavioural outcomes. Together, the findings suggest that dietary effects may emerge across biological systems before consistent changes in EF and DM become detectable, potentially explaining variability in previous behavioural findings. Longitudinal, mechanistically integrated studies that account for potential confounding factors, including hormonal status, background dietary intake, and participant characteristics, are needed to test this temporal sequence and determine when biological modulation produces cognitive and behavioural change.

articles_hidden.title: A Continuous Model of Mother, Father, and Infant Relations
articles_hidden.authors: Rukmini Mukkamalla; Benito Chen-Charpentier
articles_hidden.abstract: Many couples' relationship satisfaction declines after the birth of a child, and this decline is usually strongest in mothers. Other mathematical models of couple dynamics treat the mother and father in isolation, but the infant is also an emotional agent, coupled bidirectionally with both parents. We extend the continuous marital-satisfaction model of Chen-Charpentier et al.\ to a three-agent family consisting of a mother, a father, and an infant, using measured data whenever we can. Using equilibrium and stability analysis, a global Sobol sensitivity analysis, and a time-dependent extension, we find that the family has a single stable equilibrium. The sensitivity analysis shows that all three baseline emotional states largely affect the location of this equilibrium, with the infant's and father's baselines contributing the largest share of the variance. The mother's baseline plays a different role, however. It acts as a tipping point as mild maternal depression gets absorbed by the family while severe maternal depression drives the entire family into a distressed state. A time-dependent simulation of the first year, in which the parent--infant coupling is strong early and eases smoothly, shows that the early periods govern the speed of adjustment but not the destination. For example, a healthy family reaches contentment sooner, whereas a family with severe maternal depression dips further before settling into distress. Maternal mental health is thus the key factor in whether the family's emotional outcome is content or distressed.

articles.title: LLM measurements that agree with human coders overall can still distort specific effects
articles.authors: Alexander K. Moore; Bingqing Li; Shane Wang; Matt Thomson
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in the social sciences as surrogates for human coders. Standard practice validates them by their correspondence with human measurements of the same stimuli using statistics like correlation. However, overall correspondence can conceal biases that distort specific claims. We demonstrate this with open-weight LLM ratings of 568 food and 1,811 scene photographs. Ratings inflate, attenuate, or reverse effects, and improving overall correspondence with prompts can improve one contrast while worsening another. Rankings also elevate some categories and demote others beyond what random errors of the same size typically produce. Across six prompts, some of these errors are shared, so sampling across prompts may continue to mask biases. We propose validating LLM coders against specific claims they will test rather than the general coding task.

articles.title: Identifying a Conflict’s Cause: The Theme-Enablers Framework
articles.authors: Moorthy Muthuswamy
articles.abstract:
Conflict studies lack a replicable method for establishing causation because existing frameworks 
conflate an ideology-driven conflict's cause with dependent variables it produces. This bottom
up shortcoming necessitates a top-down approach beginning with a causal framework. The 
Theme-Enablers Framework identifies a conflict's animating theme, its institutional enablers, and 
the agendas they propagate as separable, measurable variables, enabling simultaneous internal 
and external causal validation from the same dataset. The framework is reproducible, falsifiable, 
and generalizable to ideology-driven conflicts for which comparable societal-level data on 
themes, enablers, and agendas can be assembled. This article introduces a methodological 
package combining the framework with difference-in-differences estimation and regression 
analysis to identify and validate causal structure. The methodology is tested on the Islamist 
movement across five world regions and 20 lands, then applied to out-of-sample data from 
Britain, America, India, Gaza, Afghanistan, and Iran. The results demonstrate how the 
framework identifies a conflict's root cause and distinguishes it from downstream effects. The 
designs converge on a much-overlooked cause with direct policy implications: religious leaders 
leverage the Sharia platform to radicalize communities and obtain political power.

articles.title: Beyond the Dark Figure: A Causal and Probabilistic Analysis of Crimes Against Women in India
articles.authors: Rudrani Ghosh
articles.abstract: Most research on violence against women in India depends on administrative police records. However, this raw data often suffers from severe reporting biases and fails to account for massive population differences between districts. To address these flaws, this study applies causal inference, hierarchical modeling, and machine learning to better understand local crime dynamics. By combining two decades of National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) statistics with 2011 Census demographics, we map both the spatial distribution and the true sociological drivers of this violence. We found no evidence of geographic clustering; a Moran's I analysis shows the violence is distributed randomly across the country. Furthermore, our mixed-effects hierarchical models indicate that broad state-level policies explain less than 1% of the variance in local crime rates. Furthermore, by applying Pearl's do-calculus and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), we isolate the causal effects of the male-female literacy gap and urbanization, proving that urbanization is the dominant driver of reporting rates. A Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) correctly isolates the passage of the 2013 Criminal Law (Amendment) Act as an administrative reporting shock yielding an 88,879 annual case surge rather than a behavioral epidemic. Finally, Bayesian Belief Networks are utilized to model highly nonlinear sociological interactions, providing a mathematical framework for proactive risk assessment.

articles.title: Zero FTE Does Not Mean Zero Work: Administrative Classification and the Political Economy of Academic Labor
articles.authors: Pan Liu
articles.abstract: Universities often assign faculty appointments through percentages, salary lines, workload allocations, and other administrative categories. Yet a zero-FTE or unpaid appointment can still carry substantive expectations. This study examines that apparent contradiction as a problem of academic labor. Drawing on Marxian political economy, with selective guidance from Labour Process Theory, I conducted a critical analysis of eight publicly available university policy documents governing zero-FTE, dry, courtesy, affiliate, unpaid, and conflict-of-commitment arrangements. The documents were purposively selected because they explicitly paired zero or absent local compensation with language about contribution, duties, effort, institutional benefit, or professional obligation. Across the policies, three patterns recur. First, zero often describes a budgetary or appointment status rather than the absence of work. Second, the organizational beneficiary of academic labor need not be the unit that bears its salary cost. Third, unpaid activity can remain institutionally visible when universities need to regulate time, contribution, or commitment, even when the same activity creates no local salary obligation. The analysis does not imply that every unpaid affiliation is exploitative, nor does it treat every uncompensated activity as surplus-value production in a strict Marxian sense. Instead, it shows how administrative classification can separate labor from the obligations attached to labor. The central asymmetry is simple: institutions are often better at preventing double payment than at preventing double work. Zero FTE is an administrative category. It is not a description of human activity.

articles.title: Aid Cuts and the Subnational Foundations of Refugee Cooperation
articles.authors: Mae MacDonald
articles.abstract: What happens to public support for international cooperation when the transfers that sustain it are withdrawn? I argue that cooperation with the refugee regime rests partly on a subnational bargain: host communities bear concentrated costs of asylum, which foreign aid can offset through jobs, services, and other benefits. These benefits sustain the local support for hosting that can underpin refugee cooperation, which aid withdrawal may erode. I test this argument using the 2025 aid cuts in Kenya. Drawing on two nationwide surveys, a high-frequency panel and vignette experiment near Kakuma refugee camp, and 52 interviews with refugee leaders, I show that support for refugee hosting declined in hosting regions relative to the rest of the country during the height of the cuts. Within the host community, declines were concentrated among households most exposed to the loss of aid-related jobs or services, while national support remained stable. The findings show that host-community support for refugees depends partly on foreign aid, raising concerns about the durability of international refugee cooperation as donor support recedes.

articles.title: Beyond Screen Time: Context, Valuation, and Self-Limitation of Mobile Phone Use
articles.authors: Jean-Samuel Beuscart; Thomas Beauvisage
articles.abstract: Do people spend too much time on their phones? "Screen time" has come under scrutiny for its effects on health, cognition and sociability. In this paper, we conceptualize mobile phone use as a practice (Shove, 2003; Warde, 2005) and analyze how users evaluate and regulate their digital consumption. We draw on 45 in-depth semi-structured interviews with a diverse sample of French mobile phone users. We report three main findings. First, users’ accounts of their activity distinguish embedded activities and overflowing activities - that compete with other practices. Second, users' valuation of their digital activities depends not only on their nature (e.g. social media), but on their spatial and temporal context. Third, we identify four self-limitation strategies and show that context-based ones are the most effective.  These results contribute to the debates on digital overconsumption, and the role of platform design in generating the practices they claim to help people reduce.

articles.title: Digital Preservation in Academic Libraries: The University of Ibadan Experience
articles.authors: Agwu Patrick Uzodinma
articles.abstract:
This study examines digital preservation practice at Kenneth Dike Library (KDL), University of Ibadan, to identify infrastructure, practices, challenges, and context sensitive strategies for sustainable stewardship in Nigerian academic libraries. Using a descriptive survey of the 15 library and ICT professionals directly involved in preservation activities, the research measures awareness, available infrastructure, preservation practices, major constraints, and preferred sustainability strategies. Results indicate uniformly high awareness and consensus that core preservation practices (digitisation, backups, metadata application, use of preservation tools, and integrity checks) are performed regularly. The library possesses essential digital repository infrastructure and technical support, but respondents identify poor internet connectivity, inadequate funding, and unreliable power as the most significant obstacles. Staff training, adoption of open source tools, inter institutional collaboration, hybrid storage approaches, and increased funding were unanimously recommended as sustainable strategies. Crucially, respondents strongly endorsed the need for locally adaptable, context sensitive preservation frameworks; however, opinions diverged on the adoption of specific low bandwidth or offline first technical designs. The study concludes that while KDL demonstrates strong knowledge and commitment to digital preservation, long term sustainability requires targeted investment, infrastructure resilience, capacity building, and policy formalisation—preferably through solutions adapted to the Nigerian technological context.

Keywords – Digital Preservation, Academic Libraries, Nigeria, Digitisation, Repositories

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and the New Science of Culture
articles.authors: Douglas Guilbeault; Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan; James Evans
articles.abstract:
Cognition and culture have long been treated as parallel objects of study, joined more by metaphor
than by mechanism. We argue they are co-constituted in a manner now empirically tractable:
subjectivities can be measured as local trajectories through a high-dimensional cultural field, and
the field is itself the aggregate of those trajectories. Recent advances in machine learning, including
embedding methods and large generative models, provide the first general framework for
measuring this co-constitution from micro-cognition to macro-social structure. Vector geometry
recovers individual conceptual structure, organizational communication, and large-scale
ideologies; captures multimodal cultural content beyond text; and generates testable predictions
about cultural emergence, including the simultaneous arrival of independent discoveries across
distant minds. We treat this predictability of simultaneous innovation as evidence for the co-
constitutive view: when the geometry of the cultural field is measurable, trajectories of cognitive
search through it become predictable. We then examine generative AI agents as simulators of
human subjectivity and as a qualitatively new coordinating substrate whose insertion into social
life introduces evolutionary dynamics unprecedented in human cultural history. We formalize this
reflexive condition as a Heisenberg-like Uncertainty Principle for generative AI: as instruments for
fixing a culture’s position grow more precise, our capacity to predict its trajectory degrades,
because the machinery of cultural description and cultural action have merged. We close with
ethical questions raised by AI-mediated cultural drift, recursive synthetic culture, and the limits of
human cultural agency, offering guidelines for safe, equitable, and privacy-preserving research on
AI and culture.

articles.title: From Getting Ahead to Staying Ahead: Reference Points and Repeated Investment in Status Maintenance
articles.authors: Hibiki Kamoshita
articles.abstract: As rapid technological change reshapes the skills employers demand and increases the importance of post-entry human capital accumulation, including reskilling, educational attainment no longer determines a person's position once and for all at labor-market entry. Research on stratification has nonetheless concentrated on who attains advantaged positions, and the repeated investment required to hold a position once attained remains underexplored. This study develops a model that extends the relative risk aversion hypothesis to an infinite-horizon setting, incorporating depreciating status and an endogenously updated reference point, to analyze the decision to invest in maintaining status. The results show that past success does not end the need for further learning: those who have reached higher positions face a larger reference-dependent loss and invest defensively even when resources and costs are identical. Moreover, I identify conditions under which more effective training widens rather than narrows status gaps, and show that individual credential renewals aggregate into a rising credential standard. Wider participation in adult learning is therefore compatible with a stable status order, and the locus of stratification may shift from who gets ahead to who can stay ahead.

articles.title: University-affiliated sustainability badges: Shared identity, tourist perceptions, and hotel manager receptivity
articles.authors: Peter Lewin; Danyelle; Anna Kristina Zinn; Sarah MacInnes; Sara Dolnicar
articles.abstract: Hotel sustainability research shows that pro-environmental behaviour‑change interventions are often effective in field experiments, but widespread adoption by hotels remains limited. One possible explanation is that hotels lack external recognition that would make adopting these measures visible to guests and rewarding to managers. This study investigates whether university-affiliated sustainability badges could serve as a recognition mechanism, testing their effectiveness across two studies drawing on Signalling Theory and Social Identity Theory. In an online experiment (N=975), prospective hotel guests viewed simulated hotel booking pages featuring one of the four badge options, or no badge, across budget, mid-range, and luxury hotel pricing segments. All badge variations increased perceived hotel sustainability and guests’ sense of belonging to a community of environmentally conscious travellers (group identification). Badges did not trigger negative emotions, but the university affiliated logo did not perform better than a generic environmental logo on almost all measures, suggesting these effects are based on the presence of any badge, rather than the university partnership specifically. Semi-structured interviews with ten hotel managers found conditional receptivity to university-affiliated badges, primarily through a sense of shared values and community orientation with the partnering institution (collective values) rather than the badge’s function as a credibility signal. These findings suggest that collective values and shared identities, rather than signalling, may be the more promising mechanism for engaging hotels and guests around sustainability initiatives, and offer an encouraging direction for potential university-hotel partnerships that may translate into the future implementation of pro-environmental behaviour change interventions.

articles.title: Who Wants More War? Conflict Exposure, Perceptions of Public Opinion, and Preferences for Conflict Escalation in Israel
articles.authors: Nicholas Sambanis; Itamar Yakir
articles.abstract: We explore whether conformity to perceptions of public opinion shapes individual foreign policy preferences in the aftermath of a militarized conflict between Israel and Iran in June 2025. Exploiting naturally occurring variation in exposure to an Iranian missile attack, we measure Israelis' proneness to hawkish (vs. dovish) policy responses as a function of information concerning the majority's policy preferences. We find that Israelis shift their preferences to align with perceived majority opinion: when they perceive the public to be dovish, they support more dovish positions; whereas they become more hawkish when they perceive the public as hawkish. People who report having been exposed to Iranian attacks show stronger support for belligerence. Partisanship also matters as respondents are more likely to respond to cues aligned with priors that are consistent with their party's positions. We explore mechanisms of these patterns.

articles.title: Climate Change Coverage in The Guardian, 2010–2025
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Simon Wimmer; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Leading news outlets play a central role in shaping how political leaders and the public understand the causes, impacts, and solutions to climate change. Here, we provide the first comprehensive assessment of how The Guardian, a globally influential newspaper widely recognized for high-quality climate journalism, has reported on climate change between 2010 and 2025. We applied a validated methodology based on large language models to analyze N = 18,785 articles and evaluate to what extent reporting covers scientifically grounded causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and adaptation measures. We find that climate coverage increased markedly after 2018 and has remained structurally elevated relative to the preceding decade. Coverage of causes and mitigation is dominated by fossil fuels and renewable energy, whereas agriculture, overconsumption, carbon inequality, and economic growth are mentioned far less frequently. Aspects related to adaptation receive considerably less attention than aspects related to causes, impacts, and mitigation. Our findings highlight opportunities for more comprehensive coverage that better reflects full range of societal transformations needed to address climate change.

articles.title: Local-Oriented Online Communities in Urban Communication Infrastructures: News Media, Engagement, and Emotion in 128 North American City Communities
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: Local-oriented online communities (LOOCs) have become ubiquitous spaces for discussing national and local news as well as urban civic life, yet existing scholarship lacks a consistent framework to explain what shapes their behavioral and emotional outcomes across diverse contexts. This study applies Communication Infrastructure Theory (CIT) to conceptualize LOOCs as meso-level storytellers whose outcomes are shaped by their connections to broader storytelling networks. Analyzing 1,613,650 posts and 32,706,953 comments from 128 North American city subreddits over the full year of 2024, we examine how connections to mainstream media, local media, urban governance topics, and everyday urban life topics predict thread-level engagement and emotional expression. Results show that both mainstream and local media connections substantially increase engagement but correlate with more negative emotional expression. Urban governance topics increase behavioral engagement but elicit negative sentiment, whereas everyday urban life topics exhibit the inverse pattern, showing an engagement–negativity tradeoff.

articles.title: Political Talk in Nonpolitical Digital Spaces
articles.authors: Yibin Fan
articles.abstract: In recent years, scholars in communication and media studies have increasingly turned their attention to political discourse that emerges incidentally within ostensibly nonpolitical digital contexts. These political discussions not only permeate diverse online platforms and communities, but also carry significant democratic potential. Despite growing interest in the phenomenon, existing research remains fragmented across distinct theoretical traditions and lacks a coherent conceptual understanding. This article addresses that gap by reviewing studies in three epistemological orientations—post-positivist, interpretive, and critical—that can guide the analysis of political talk in nonpolitical digital environments. In doing so, it highlights how this group of phenomena can be understood and interpreted with different theoretical assumptions, thereby enabling scholars to better assess their communicative and political significance. This review offers a foundation for more integrative and theoretically informed research on the various dimensions of political expression in digital networked publics.

articles.title: Climate Change Coverage in The Guardian, 2010–2025
articles.authors: Fabian Dablander; Simon Wimmer; Jonas M B Haslbeck
articles.abstract: Leading news outlets play a central role in shaping how political leaders and the public understand the causes, impacts, and solutions to climate change. Here, we provide the first comprehensive assessment of how The Guardian, a globally influential newspaper widely recognized for high-quality climate journalism, has reported on climate change between 2010 and 2025. We applied a validated methodology based on large language models to analyze N = 18,785 articles and evaluate to what extent reporting covers scientifically grounded causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and adaptation measures. We find that climate coverage increased markedly after 2018 and has remained structurally elevated relative to the preceding decade. Coverage of causes and mitigation is dominated by fossil fuels and renewable energy, whereas agriculture, overconsumption, carbon inequality, and economic growth are mentioned far less frequently. Aspects related to adaptation receive considerably less attention than aspects related to causes, impacts, and mitigation. Our findings highlight opportunities for more comprehensive coverage that better reflects full range of societal transformations needed to address climate change.

articles.title: When is Forgetting an Advantage?: Considering Organizational Amnesia at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency
articles.authors: Josh Entsminger
articles.abstract: Organizational amnesia in the public sector is often understood as a pathology and source of capability loss. In response, literature is emerging framing the potential advantages of organizational amnesia; however, the nature and source of potential advantages remain under-developed. In this paper, I argue DARPA provides a counter-intuitive case of organizational design which structurally reinforces organizational amnesia while it is, seemingly paradoxically, perceived as reinforcing capacity for pursuing high-risk, high-reward research & development (R&D) programs. Taking a qualitative perspective, I argue DARPA has evolved an organizational structure which shapes how routinization proceeds, with downstream implications on dynamic capabilities. I frame this work as being driven by memory conditions, oriented around reduced memory formation, reduced memory availability, shaped willingness for memory recall, and shaped utility of memory recall. I pose DARPA as a unique case study in the organization of memory in public sector funding organizations.

articles.title: Daily Team Behaviors as Predictors of Team Effectiveness Outcomes: Evidence from a Technology Entrepreneurship Incubator Program
articles.authors: Meg Small; Sally Dancer; Jonathan Wright; Blake Anthony Colaianne; Gillian Sommerville
articles.abstract: Team effectiveness in high-stakes, time-limited work contexts remains an underexplored area of organizational and applied psychology research. This study examined whether daily process behaviors—specifically team communication and collaboration—predict end-of-program team effectiveness outcomes in the context of an intensive, eight-week technology entrepreneurship incubator program. Participants were members of five start-up teams enrolled in the start-up program at a large research university. As part of a larger mixed-methods study, participants completed daily diary measures of team communication and collaboration using a digital platform (Metricwire) for 15 days. At program end, participants completed a post-program survey assessing team effectiveness outcomes including creativity, psychological safety, team viability, collective efficacy, authentic relationships, opportunities for growth, and program satisfaction. Simple linear regressions revealed that daily collaboration significantly predicted creativity, psychological safety, team viability, and collective efficacy. Daily communication similarly predicted creativity and psychological safety. Authentic relationships were not significantly predicted by either behavioral measure. These findings contribute to the growing literature on team process and performance by demonstrating that observable daily team behaviors capture meaningful variance in team effectiveness outcomes, Implications for team-based intervention design and digital measurement methodology are discussed.

articles.title: The Symbolic Organisation of Political Antagonism: An Integrative Model of Cultural and Social Polarisation
articles.authors: Werner Binder; Matthias Revers; Marcus Morgan; María Luengo
articles.abstract: This article develops a cultural and relational model of political polarisation that integrates insights from currently disconnected streams of scholarship to conceive polarisation as a discursive and performative struggle over sacred meanings. Rather than treating polarisation as mere attitudinal divergence, we frame it as the symbolic organization of political antagonism. We identify three interrelated cultural dimensions and one social dimension. These are (1) ideological divergence as bifurcating responses to contested issues, conceptualized as morally and emotionally charged signifiers; (2) the ideological consistency of these divergent issues, enabling chains of signification held together by what we call 'linking signifiers' that mark group identity; (3) the mutual constitution of opposing semiotic chains and identities, which describes how antagonistic groups performatively mobilise opposing discourses to co-constitutively define themselves in relation to one another; and (4) social polarisation, which is based in e.g., inequalities, segregations, or violent conflicts.  We then present a pathway model which expresses how cultural and social polarisation drive or diminish one another over time. This model thereby offers a sociological theory of polarisation and depolarisation as interlinked processes rather than as separate phenomena requiring separate theories. This paper also maps out the implications of our model for empirical polarisation and depolarisation research.

articles.title: Who influences climate adaptation? Farmer and advisor social networks and differentiated benefits of participation in a climate adaptation fellowship program
articles.authors: Sara Delaney; Rachel E. Schattman; Janica Anderzén
articles.abstract: Due to ongoing and projected environmental change farmers and agricultural advisors need access to up-to-date and relevant information and advice to continue to be effective in their work. Education and advising services aim to transmit new information and facilitate change in behavior, often using peer-to-peer or cohort style approaches. However, given that learning and behavior is continuously shaped by interactions, we must understand the role of these interventions within broader climate adaptation networks. This study explores the social networks of a cohort of farmers and agricultural advisors who participated in a Climate Adaptation Fellowship program. Drawing on pre- and post-program surveys and interviews and longitudinal social network analysis, we first explore the range of sources that farmers and advisors in this cohort reported using for adaptation-related information, advice, and support. We also examine the impact of the program on the inter-cohort network and participants’ individual social networks. We find high diversity in the composition of interviewees’ adaptation networks. Farmers and advisors engage widely on adaptation, and while they use other farmers and advisors as resources for adaptation, they also draw on media, customers, friends, family, and the broader community. This heterogeneity has benefits for effective decision-making but also implies that messaging through single channels will only reach a limited audience. The analysis also shows that the program had variable effects among participants over time. There was a meaningful change in the social networks of approximately half of the fellows. While a subset of the group grew progressively more densely connected, others lost contact. We argue that this uneven engagement and impact is not a fault, but instead an invitation to capitalize on the energy of these most interconnected members and also find opportunities to engage those on the periphery over time. Programming can also be strategically expanded to a wider circle to help participants carry forward new learning.

articles.title: The Electoral Effects of U.S. Prison Construction
articles.authors: Nicholas Ottone; Amanda Weiss
articles.abstract: From 1980 to 2000, the United States opened over 400 prisons, a rapid expansion of carceral capacity mirroring the punitive turn in public policy and public opinion. Yet few studies have examined the impact of prison construction on nearby residents and their political behavior. We develop a theoretical model tracing how prison openings affect economic, attitudinal, and electoral outcomes in surrounding communities. Using modern difference-in-difference methods and a novel county-level dataset covering forty years of prison openings, we find that prison construction decreases county-level vote share for Republican candidates, especially if Republicans represented the county during prison construction. Drawing on analyses of economic outcomes and prison bond measure support, we argue that voters sanction issue-owning Republican candidates for negative economic externalities and turn against funding for prisons. These findings challenge conventional wisdom about the political economy of prisons and have implications for how we understand contemporary expansions of carceral capacity.

articles.title: Concentration Without Representation
articles.authors: Burak Ozturan; David Lazer
articles.abstract:
A small fraction of users produces most of what circulates online, and the expectation that falling
publication costs would flatten this gradient has not been borne out. Two questions about that
concentration remain open. Published estimates of how concentrated sharing is vary by a factor
of three at comparable thresholds, with no account of why, and the demographic composition of
heavy sharers has received little systematic attention outside the study of misinformation, where
existing work does not separate the users who share the most from those whose shares reach the
most people. Using 38 million news shares by 493,237 registered US voters matched to their Twit-
ter accounts across 57 months, we address both. Observation-window length alone reproduces
the full factor-of-three range within a single dataset, holding population and content fixed. The
top one percent accounts for 22 percent of shares at a one-week window and 52 percent at 57
months. Two tests establish that the rise is compositional and not behavioral, since holding sample
size fixed does not flatten the curve and a cohort of the same users followed across all windows
stays near 21 percent throughout. Matching observation windows to prior studies that overlap our
