own panel narrows the gap for comparable content almost entirely, while a residual gap against
misinformation-specific estimates reflects a difference in content class rather than window choice.
Ranking the same users by sharing volume and by audience reach identifies substantially overlap-
ping but still distinct populations, overlapping by 49.9 percent at the top one percent against one
percent expected by chance. Both elites are older and more Democratic than the panel, with mean
age rising from 40.5 years to 57.0 under activity ranking. Gender behaves differently. Male and
female users share at statistically indistinguishable rates throughout the activity distribution, and
a thirteen-point gap appears only at the extreme of the follower tail, where female share falls to
34.8 percent. Elite position is durable at the head of the distribution and close to memoryless in
the middle. The users who share the most only partly overlap with the users whose shares travel
furthest, and both groups are unrepresentative of the voting public in overlapping but distinct ways.

articles.title: Review bombing the video game industries: Sabotage as political consumer practice
articles.authors: Andrew Wirzburger
articles.abstract: Spaces of consumption have long been sites of tension and contestation between corporations and consumers. Since the late 2010s, review bombing has emerged as a persistent feature of this conflict. Consumers practice review bombing to take action in response to perceived grievances by inundating products with negative online reviews to drive down their aggregate ratings. Online reviews have been touted as part of a shift in power from producers to consumers championed by the logics of social commerce, and yet companies wield tremendous power over consumers. This study frames review bombing as sabotage, a withdrawal of efficiency. Through relational-ethnographic approaches to two cases of review bombing in the video game industries, the study argues that the efficacy of review bombing depends on a combination of spectacle and policy. While specific outcomes vary, review bombing is exceedingly effective at sabotaging the logics of the video games industries more broadly.

articles.title: Modelación Lógico-Proposicional y Reducción Forense Frente a la Infoxicación Procesal: Epistemología Jurídica "Desde Abajo" en la Defensa del Parque La Valvanera  /  Logical-Propositional Modeling and Forensic Reduction Against Procedural Information Overload: "Bottom-Up" Legal Epistemology in the Defense of La Valvanera Park
articles.authors: Luis Felipe Narvaez Galindez
articles.abstract:
RESUMEN:
El presente artículo analiza las asimetrías epistémicas y procesales en el litigio de derechos colectivos en Colombia. Desde la sociología reflexiva de Alvin Gouldner y la Investigación-Acción Participativa (IAP) de Orlando Fals Borda, se examina la resistencia comunitaria frente a la privatización del Parque La Valvanera en Pitalito, Huila. Se documenta la trayectoria del colectivo popular desde la tutela hasta el cauce contencioso-administrativo, abordando el ensayo decolonial con Enrique Dussel y categorías autónomas. Frente al dilema de Audre Lorde sobre las herramientas hegemónicas, se fundamenta cómo el repliegue provisional de los conceptos propios y la adopción de la lógica formal constituyeron una apropiación táctica de la racionalidad procesal dominante para salvaguardar un derecho material inminente, preservando la doctrina comunitaria para el debate sociológico formal. Asimismo, ante la infoxicación procesal desplegada por las demandadas mediante el aporte desarticulado de 800 MB de expedientes, se formaliza la introducción de un modelo algebraico booleano (V = A ∧ B ∧ C). Se expone la operacionalización de tres silogismos deónticos, una matriz de confesión cruzada y la extensión del modelo a defensas herméticas mediante prueba documental de puro derecho, situando la argumentación técnica como compuerta procesal hacia la Sentencia Anticipada (Art. 182A del CPACA).

ABSTRACT:
This article analyzes the epistemic and procedural asymmetries in public interest litigation in Colombia. Drawing upon Alvin Gouldner's reflexive sociology and Orlando Fals Borda's Participatory Action Research (PAR), it examines community resistance against the privatization of La Valvanera Park in Pitalito, Huila. The paper documents the collective's trajectory from an initial injunction (tutela) to administrative proceedings, addressing decolonial theory grounded in Enrique Dussel and bottom-up categories. Engaging with Audre Lorde's dilemma regarding hegemonic tools, it theorizes how setting aside indigenous concepts in favor of formal logic was a tactical appropriation of dominant procedural rationality to safeguard an urgent collective right, preserving autonomous doctrine for scholarly debate. Confronted with procedural information overload deployed by the defendants through the disorganized submission of 800 MB of files, the paper formalizes the introduction of a Boolean algebraic reduction model (V = A ∧ B ∧ C). It details three deontic syllogisms, a cross-party admission matrix, and the model's extension to airtight defenses via documentary evidence of pure law, positioning technical argumentation as the procedural mechanism for an Early Judgment under Article 182A of the CPACA.

articles.title: Representation of Police in Television, 2020 Anti-Police Movements, and Audience Reception
articles.authors: Jenny Lee
articles.abstract: Police television is one of the most popular genres of television in the modern age. With its continued popularity and high viewership, police television, from fictional to reality shows, is often the first introduction to the criminal justice system for many viewers. Prior research has also shown that many people believe that the information they see on police television is factual and reflective of reality, whether this information is fact checked or not. In fact, the police institution relies on its cultural power to sustain its status as maintainers of social order and of regulators of deviance. However, with the 2020 anti-police brutality movements, the public atmosphere around police undeniably shifted toward a more negative outlook than before. With this question, I seek to identify whether or not there has been a change in the way police officers are portrayed in television, and if so, how change has been implemented. In addition, I seek to find how police television continues to curate a specific image of police officers without ignoring the social movements that were present. Through the qualitative observation of two television shows, I explore the changes in portrayals of police officers across the two shows. I find that there are more varied portrayals of police officers in specific categories, yet police officers are still shown to be the sole method of maintaining social order and controlling deviance. The police television shows observed in this paper adhere to the promotion of “ideal cop” principles to show the effectiveness of police officers in regulating society.

articles.title: Learning to Speak Green: The Production of Green Conformity in European Cultural Policy
articles.authors: Vânia Rodrigues; Catarina Santos-Silva; Olga Solovova
articles.abstract:
Ecological vocabulary is nearly absent until 2021, when greening became a cross-cutting programme priority, and rises abruptly thereafter. Green, climate and sustainable increasingly appear together as an interchangeable signal of commitment. Sustainable also retains its earlier organisational meaning, binding ecological claims to claims of institutional survival. Modernisation dominates the coded projects, framing sustainability as innovation, capacity-building and better practice. Transformative elements persist only as traces, and the vocabularies of degrowth, commoning and ecological justice are absent or residual across the whole corpus. The programme's explicit greening guidance appears to supply the very terms in which compliance is demonstrated.
The article argues that this narrowing is anticipatory and sincere, which makes it harder to contest than greenwashing. It contributes to debates on travelling cultural policy and multilateral cultural governance by showing how a transnational green idiom, composed largely in English, carries a sustainability paradigm across Europe while constraining the ecological futures cultural institutions can meaningfully articulate.

articles.title: Uncovering Student Thinking from Only the Answer: A GenAI Perspective
articles.authors: Tommy Stell; Darryl Chamberlain; Kelvin Rozier; Yaroslav Molkov; Russell Jeter
articles.abstract: Identifying the underlying reasoning behind a student’s response to a mathematical question is a time-intensive activity for instructors. This work seeks to answer if a Large Language Model (LLM) can be used to identify potential student thinking based solely on their final response. To evaluate the LLM’s identification of potential student thinking, we developed an ordinal scale which describes how well the LLM’s identification aligns with a content expert’s identification of potential student thinking. We then utilized this scale to evaluate the ability of the Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview LLM to identify potential student thinking in a variety of College Algebra questions. We show that the LLM was able to correctly identify the mechanism encoded in the distractor, in a little over half (55.25%) of cases. This work highlights the limits of current LLMs’ ability to identify potential student thinking and further highlights the necessity of instructors to provide targeted feedback based on student thinking.

articles.title: Quo Vadis, Digital Accessibility? A Prerequisite for Democratic Equality
articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha; Gonçalo Cruz
articles.abstract: Digital participation channels may widen access to public decision-making, but formal availability does not ensure substantively equal opportunities for political voice. This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. A bounded exploratory pilot applies the strategy to the publicly accessible, logged-out segment of ConsultaLEX, the Portuguese government portal for legislative and regulatory consultations. The pilot covers discovery, orientation, and authentication and assesses the availability of an entry point to expression and feedback. It identifies enabling conditions in programmatically named controls, structured consultation information, exact dates, and alternative authentication routes. Potentially constraining conditions involve relative deadlines, scripted navigation, registration and identity requirements, and human verification. Because no live commenting process was available, expression and feedback could not be inspected. The study therefore supports mechanism-level inferences rather than claims about participant exclusion or platform-wide conformance. These findings support treating accessibility as a necessary but insufficient condition for equal participation. The paper contributes a proof of concept connecting accessibility evidence to democratic analysis and identifies disability-led participant testing, live-process observation, and cross-platform comparison as priorities for future research.

articles.title: Why Do Immigrant Girls Participate Less in Organized Leisure Activities? The Role of Parental Influence Across the Transition from Adolescence to Adulthood
articles.authors: Mia Stenbro Lorenzen; Frank van Tubergen; Hans-Peter Y. Qvist
articles.abstract: Research documents immigrant-native gaps in girls’ participation in organized leisure activities across Western Europe, particularly among Muslim immigrant-origin girls. While parental characteristics are often assumed to shape these gaps, less is known about which parental factors matter most and how their influence unfolds from adolescence into adulthood. Using German longitudinal data from CILS4EU and CILS4EU-DE, we address these questions by examining participation gaps among non-Muslim and Muslim immigrant-origin girls relative to native girls across the transition from adolescence to early adulthood.In doing so, we estimate a structural equation model that distinguishes between initial parental effects in adolescence, path-dependent effects linking adolescent and adult participation, and persistent parental effects in early adulthood. Differences in parental participation andsocioeconomic resources explain a substantial share of theimmigrant-native participation gaps, whereas parental gender values explain comparatively little. Although participation gaps narrow over time, they persist, primarily through path-dependent processes, as lower participation during adolescence is carried forward into adulthood. Persistent parental effects remain but are comparatively modest. While participation gaps are larger among Muslim immigrant-origin girls, the underlying mechanisms are broadly similar across immigrant-origin groups. The findings highlight how family-based inequalities shape participation trajectories and contribute to the production and reproduction of participation gaps across the life course.

articles.title: How Do Voters Respond to Gradual Climate Costs?  Evidence from the Insurance Crisis
articles.authors: Eric Scheuch
articles.abstract: Climate change is transforming the U.S. economy in gradual but increasingly impactful ways. Existing literature on climate shocks and economic transformation is poorly positioned to explain how these gradual costs shape opinions and behavior. I study this through the U.S. home insurance market. Using panel data (2016–2024) and 246 million insurance records, I show voters recognize the insurance crisis and shift away from homeownership in response, but that rate increases do not significantly change climate opinions. With original survey data, I explain why: voters fail to attribute insurance costs to climate change and to connect insurance to climate policy. I trace this gap to the information environment: analysis of posts from 3,000 public officials and 2.9 million news articles shows that neither officials nor media frequently link insurance to climate change. These findings advance understanding of how gradual climate costs are—and are not—reshaping American opinion and behavior.

articles.title: Unbundling Support for Political Violence
articles.authors: Sam Fuller; Jack T. Rametta; Alexa Federice
articles.abstract: Measures of support for political violence (SPV) vary drastically across what violence they describe, who performs it, against whom, and the stated justification. We argue that these measures are not interchangeable operationalizations of a single latent attitude but rather represent correlated, distinct subdimensions of SPV. Across three studies, we iteratively develop and validate concise batteries that 1) differentiate between actor-target combinations and reactive versus proactive violence and 2) vary across justification and the response's severity. We find that SPV is a multidimensional concept: levels of reactive support are remarkably higher than proactive; support for state-on-mass and mass-on-state violence are only weakly correlated, with Republicans supporting state-on-mass and Democrats supporting mass-on-state violence at significantly higher rates; common SPV measures correlate with proactive more than reactive; and we find mixed evidence that survey disengagement influences SPV. Our findings contextualize disparate and conflicting literatures, offering measurement strategies tailored to specific research questions.

articles.title: Homeschooling as Racial Retreat: The Impact of School District and Leadership Diversity
articles.authors: Maranda Joyce
articles.abstract: What explains the decision to homeschool? This study examines whether local racial context influences families’ decisions to homeschool their children. I argue that many white parents exit public school systems due to concerns about the distribution of school resources to racial out-groups, particularly in racially diverse and resource-constrained districts. I conduct a state-representative survey of over 30,000 respondents to describe the homeschooling population in the United States. Then, using data from Virginia that link student and district leadership demographics (school board members and superintendents) to district-level homeschooling rates, I examine how racial composition and leadership diversity shape educational exit. I find that higher levels of non-white students and certain kinds of leadership diversity are positively associated with increased homeschooling, especially where resources are limited. By showing that homeschooling is often motivated by perceived racial threat, this study informs debates about the regulation and public subsidization of homeschooling.

articles.title: Long-Term Health Financing in Chile: A Historical Analysis of the Segmented System, 1981–2024
articles.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Camilo Cid Pedraza
articles.abstract: The objective of this article is to present the results of reconstructing the historical series of health expenditure in Chile from the creation of the segmented model in 1981 to 2024, and to briefly analyze its evolution in historical context. To this end, data were collected and digitized from primary sources: the Statistical Bulletins and Public Accounts of FONASA (1989–2016; 2020–2024), the Statistical Series of the Isapre System (SUPER, 1990–2024), and the Public Finance Statistics of DIPRES (2004–2025). The results show accelerated growth in private spending until the 1990s, followed by a sustained increase in public health expenditure associated with higher fiscal contributions and mandatory contributions. However, the long-term analysis reveals periods of slowdown in public spending coinciding with the expansion of private infrastructure, revealing the persistence of a segmented and unequal financing system. The trajectory of Chilean health expenditure shows significant variation in proportions and pace, conditioned by political and economic contexts. Alongside this analysis, we make the complete series used available to researchers in open access.

articles.title: Quo Vadis, Digital Accessibility? A Prerequisite for Democratic Equality
articles.authors: Tânia de Jesus Vilela da Rocha; Gonçalo Cruz
articles.abstract: Digital participation channels may widen access to public decision-making, but formal availability does not ensure substantively equal opportunities for political voice. This paper asks how accessibility conditions across a digital consultation journey may shape participation costs and what their potential implications are for political equality and procedural legitimacy. It conceptualizes digital accessibility as democratic infrastructure and integrates technical accessibility, journey analysis, socio-technical evaluation, and democratic interpretation. The analytical strategy distinguishes observed conditions, plausible participation risks, and demonstrated outcomes and traces a chain from observed condition to required resource, participation cost, recovery route, and potential democratic relevance. articles.title: Specific Support, Diffuse Trust: Central Banks and the Mass Politics of Unconventional Monetary Policy
articles.authors: Björn Bremer; Jeffrey Chwieroth
articles.abstract: Central banks relied for a decade on unconventional monetary policies (negative interest rates, large-scale asset purchases, and forward guidance) that carry significant distributive consequences and became intensely politicized. Yet little is known about the mass politics of central banking, or whether contestation over specific instruments threatens central banks' broader legitimacy. We provide evidence from two pre-registered survey experiments in Germany and the Netherlands. A conjoint experiment shows that citizens strongly oppose negative interest rates, the most penalized levels in the design, and are skeptical of unconditional asset purchases. A framing experiment shows support for negative rates responds to both egotropic and sociotropic arguments, with pocketbook concerns resonating most strongly. Exploiting a within-respondent measure of trust in the European Central Bank (ECB), we show that these same frames shift citizens' specific support for the policy without eroding their diffuse trust in the ECB, a highly insulated, technocratic, non-elected institution.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: Harnessing Human–AI Interpretive Difference: Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism
articles.authors: Emmanuelle Poncin
articles.abstract: Recent debate over GenAI in qualitative inquiry centres on concerns that computational participation reinforces postpositivist dominance. Critical analysts propose excluding it, out-theorising it, or continuously inspecting its entanglements. In parallel, a growing body of work builds architectures to accommodate human-AI collaboration in interpretive inquiry. While most of this work relies on postpositivist assumptions, an emerging strand develops collaborative architectures grounded in interpretivism, an approach this article adopts. I propose that for computational interpretation to be part of interpretivist inquiry without being granted reflexivity or interpretive authority, it must be deliberately structured into an accountable, productive relationship alongside human interpretation. To that end, I outline Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism, an epistemological position resting on five propositions. First, productive epistemic non-equivalence holds that human and computational interpretation need not share an epistemic basis for their difference to be structured as a resource. Second, interpretive co-construction grounds computational interpretation in meanings negotiated between researcher and participant, rather than a decontextualised corpus. Third, productive divergence treats non-alignment between human and computational interpretations as a potential source of analytic insight. Fourth, interpretive traceability refers to the capacity to see the grounds upon which human and computational interpretations are made, rendering them accountable structurally. Fifth, reflexive engagement holds that computational participation can create occasions for the researcher to interrogate her relationship to her subjectivity. This position is operationalised through Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA). LICA deploys computational interpretation to anchor interpretive insights to the empirical material. It integrates explicit interpretive co-construction between participant and researcher in interviews, scrutinises divergence between researcher and computational interpretations, renders analytic reasoning traceable, and embeds the researcher's subjectivity into the computational process. Together, these features create the conditions for new insights to emerge from the interaction between human and computational interpretations.

articles.title: The Qualitative Network Approach: A Methodological Framework and Tutorial for Relational Coding
articles.authors: Ivonne Lipsch-Wijnen; Femke Nijland; Vanessa Torres van Grinsven; Szilvia Zörgő; Gjalt - Jorn Peters
articles.abstract: Relationships between concepts are often interpreted during qualitative analysis but may remain implicit within coding structures, thematic descriptions, or analytical narratives. This article introduces the Qualitative Network Approach (QNA), a methodological framework for representing qualitative codes as interconnected elements. Its associated method, QNA network coding, specifies interpreted connections between pairs of qualitative codes according to relationship type and, where relevant, directionality. A four-step tutorial demonstrates how researchers can identify two concepts in the data for relational interpretation, identify and specify their relationship using the codebook, assign the three codes to the data fragment, and document a QNA network code. A worked interview example illustrates how individual QNA network codes can form a wider QNA network code structure. QNA may be useful when relationships between concepts are analytically important. By making relational interpretations explicit and traceable to the underlying data, QNA aims to increase the transparency and inspectability of qualitative analysis.

articles.title: Sentiment change points, not peaks, mark when public opinion has yet to settle
articles.authors: Chenying Weng; Yilun Chen; Huazhen Huang; Yiting Yang; He Gong; Hongkai Wang
articles.abstract: Timing interventions during public controversies requires more than identifying when sentiment is strongest: a peak does not tell us whether public opinion can still change. We analyzed about 1.34M Weibo posts about a controversial news event (Company T vs. Company L), separating sentiment strength by referent and tracking the resulting trajectories across the event. After sudden change points (SCPs) sentiment-strength trajectories and public expression continued to change; after peak points (PPs) they largely stabilized (mean absolute displacement 3.291 times; p = 0.035), and discourse-strategy composition changed around SCPs but stayed largely stable around PPs. SCPs, not PPs, are the candidate leverage points. This suggests that the strongest moment is where public opinion settles, so mitigation should act at the SCP.

articles.title: Examining the Multidimensional Structure of Subjective Well-Being: Evidence from Mexico
articles.authors: Carlos Alberto Arellano-Esparza
articles.abstract: Most research on subjective well-being (SWB) relies on the classic tripartite model of life satisfaction, positive affect, and negative affect, which may obscure its multidimensional character. Using nationally representative data from Mexico, this study compares alternative structural models of SWB through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, evaluating configurations that integrate eudaimonic, affective, and cognitive components to test whether a multidimensional structure provides a better statistical account of the data than a unidimensional alternative. Several competing models (correlated three-factor, hierarchical, and bifactor) display robust and largely equivalent fit. This multidimensional representation consistently outperforms a unidimensional one and remains largely stable across sex and region, indicating that no single structural model uniquely captures SWB, calling for more flexible approaches to its study.

articles.title: The nirvana fallacy and the case for friction in responding to online child sexual abuse
articles.authors: Joel Scanlan
articles.abstract: On 3 April 2026 the European Union’s temporary exception for voluntary detection of child sexual abuse material lapsed, and for three months the alternative that perfectionist arguments rarely state became policy: to do nothing. During the previous gap, in 2020–21, reports of abuse material from the EU fell by 58%. This article names the reasoning behind such outcomes as the nirvana fallacy, which Demsetz identified in 1969 as measuring the imperfect against an ideal instead of the real alternative. Four forms recur in the child-safety debate: circumvention, false positives, categorical impossibility and the slippery slope. Each states a real issue and leaves its comparator unstated. The article reframes the measures as friction, drawing on situational crime prevention, public health harm reduction and the economics of adversarial systems, then works along the offending pathway to set out what each friction layer achieves and what it cannot. Randomised trials and field deployments on Google Search, Pornhub and the Tor search engine Ahmia.fi show warnings reducing attempted access and increasing help-seeking, while hash matching, classifiers and age assurance carry known limits alongside measured effects. The article does not propose weakening encryption, and argues that most serious objections to other controls should be treated as design constraints rather than as refusals. A comparative test of four questions applies to objections and proposals alike, along with eight recommendations. Layered friction reduces measured offending-related behaviour at nearly every point it has been tested, and children are safer with it in the system than without it.

articles.title: Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis: A Methodological Architecture for Human–AI Collaboration in Qualitative Inquiry
articles.authors: Emmanuelle Poncin
articles.abstract: When generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is adopted without attention to its epistemological implications, postpositivist commitments to truth-seeking over meaning-making risk becoming more entrenched in qualitative inquiry, eroding reflexivity and interpretive depth. This has prompted scholars to call for the GenAI debate to move beyond binary adoption-or-refusal framings, toward how GenAI might be deployed while preserving reflexivity, theoretical depth, and epistemological plurality. I outline Layered Interpretive Computational Analysis (LICA), an interpretivist human–AI collaboration architecture, as a methodological answer to this call. LICA operationalises the position of Reflexive, Accountable Computational Interpretivism. It maintains distinct human and computational interpretive layers across six analytic steps. The architecture is centred on the live interpretation interview, which yields an initial participant narrative and a co-constructed interpretive narration negotiated between the participant and researcher. The initial narrative serves as a basis for thematic analysis, while the co-constructed interpretive narration grounds ideal-type analysis. Findings are brought together into a thematic-typological integrative analysis, which addresses what the complete thematic-typological configuration means in relation to the research question, and clarifies what it reveals about the underlying reflexive processes and human–AI collaboration. Throughout the process, human–AI divergences are retained and warranted as potential sources of analytic insights, while a traceable genealogy links successive analytic constructs to their empirical origins and interpretative context. Rather than accelerating an existing workflow, LICA relocates analytic effort to the research encounter and structures computational participation to interrogate interpretive judgement and reflexivity. For contexts where GenAI use raises strong ethical, environmental, or participant-vulnerability concerns, the method can be adapted into Layered Interpretive Analysis (LIA), a non-computational variant which retains key features of explicit meaning co-construction and thematic-typological integration.

articles.title: Automated Creativity in the Imagined Network: Creative Writer's View on Generative AI
articles.authors: Tianyu Zhao
articles.abstract:
As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies reshape the creative sector, understanding their implications for writers becomes increasingly vital. The study addresses a significant research gap by the impact of GenAI on creative writers in the United Kingdom, focusing on their perceptions and interactions within professional networks. The research explores two primary questions: how UK creative writers perceive and interact with GenAI technologies in their professional network, and what factors shape these perceptions and interactions within the creative industry. Employing a qualitative approach, the study conducts in-depth interviews with members of the Writers' Guild of Great Britain to gather rich, contextual qualitative response.

Key findings reveal the complex relationship between writers' self-identification within their professional networks and the integration of GenAI technologies. The study also uncovers writers' concerns about potential displacement by AI and examines the interplay between GenAI and capitalist forces in the creative industry. By centring the voices of creative writers, this research contributes to the ongoing discourse on technology and creativity, advocating for a more nuanced understanding of the sociotechnical dynamics in the creative industry. The study informs future discussions on the ethical use of AI in creative fields and provides an STS perspective on the evolving relationship between technology and creative professionals.

articles.title: Localizing the Sustainable Development Goals through Digitally Visible Initiatives: An Exploratory Study in Brazil
articles.authors: Cecilia Kotzias; Tamer Uzun; Hans Michael van Bellen; Roberto Pacheco; Cinthya Mônica da Silva Zanuzzi; Paulo Maurício Selig
articles.abstract: Community-based and other sustainability-oriented initiatives across Brazil address problems central to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), yet their contributions may be less visible within formal SDG monitoring because they are distributed across numerous small actors and often expressed in local rather than SDG terminology. This study frames the challenge of making the contributions of such initiatives legible within SDG localization as a knowledge-translation problem and develops an exploratory digital mapping and classification procedure for identifying and interpreting digitally visible sustainability-oriented initiatives in relation to nationalized SDG targets. An iterative snowball mapping procedure on Instagram identified 2,328 publicly visible profiles, from which 256 sustainability-oriented initiatives were classified in relation to nationalized SDG targets (230 assigned a primary SDG). A documented subset of 50 initiatives, including 47 examined using additional public sources, was analyzed in depth. Coding followed a transparent codebook, and an independent second coder recoded the documented subset, yielding moderate intercoder reliability (Cohen's κ = 0.57), followed by negotiated adjudication of disagreements. The findings indicate that many initiatives address SDG-relevant problems without using SDG terminology, that assigning a single primary SDG entails interpretive loss when representing multidimensional local practices, and that fewer than one quarter of the initiatives in the in-depth subset are directly recognized in Brazil's official civil society registry. The study introduces a transparent and auditable mapping-and-classification procedure grounded in this framing and provides empirical insights into both the analytical potential and the interpretive limits of translating situated local narratives into classifications aligned with nationalized SDG targets.

articles.title: No Reform, No Election: CHADEMA's Campaign and the Legacy of Incomplete Political Reform in Tanzania, 1991–2025
articles.authors: Rutashubanyuma Nestory
articles.abstract:
On 23 March 2025, the Chama cha Demokrasia na Maendeleo (CHADEMA) launched its “No Reform, No Election” campaign in Mbeya City, demanding substantive electoral and political reforms as a condition for participation in Tanzania's forthcoming general election. Although the campaign emerged in the immediate aftermath of the 2024 local-government elections, its political rationale was rooted in a much longer history of incomplete institutional reform dating from the Nyalali Commission of 1991. This article examines the campaign within the historical trajectory of Tanzania's major presidential commissions and reform initiatives, including the Nyalali Commission, the Warioba Commission on corruption, the Kisanga Committee, the Warioba Constitutional Review Commission, and the Presidential Taskforce on Multiparty Democracy chaired by Professor Rwekaza Mukandala.
The article argues that Tanzania's reform trajectory is characterized by a recurring gap between the identification of institutional problems, the production of reform recommendations, and their comprehensive implementation. This article conceptualizes this phenomenon as the reform implementation gap and argues that its cumulative effect has generated a reform expectation gap between citizens' and political actors' expectations and the institutional outcomes delivered by successive governments. The 2025 CHADEMA campaign should therefore be understood not simply as an electoral boycott strategy but as a political claim concerning the relationship between electoral participation and institutional legitimacy. The article further examines the 2023–2024 electoral and political-party legislation, CHADEMA's invocation of President Samia Suluhu Hassan's “4Rs” philosophy, and the opposition's increasing reliance on digital mobilization in a constrained political environment. It concludes that democratic consolidation in Tanzania requires not merely additional reform initiatives but credible implementation of existing recommendations, stronger institutional independence, and political conditions capable of sustaining meaningful electoral competition.

articles.title: Lexical Integration: Introducing Aymara Corpus Evidence into Global English
articles.authors: Robert D. Smith
articles.abstract: Indigenous Andean languages have traditionally been preserved through oral traditions, especially following the historical destruction of non-alphabetic record-keeping systems like khipus (Coletta, 2023). In the face of imperial linguistic hegemony, traditional documentation efforts often prove insufficient for long-term epistemic preservation (van den Berg, 2024). As Global English expands, the decline of Indigenous languages threatens profound Andean ways of knowing with systematic erosion (van den Berg, 2024). This paper proposes a conceptual framework to preserve Highland Andean epistemology by integrating targeted, untranslatable Aymara words—such as ch’ixi, taypi, and suma qamaña—into Global English lexicons using international corpus evidence (Bosch & Griesel, 2020). Anchored in translanguaging theory and decolonial macro- and microethics, this approach maps translational deficiencies where English lacks single-word equivalents for complex Andean concepts. The study demonstrates that bridging these lexical gaps transforms Global English into an additive vehicle for cultural preservation, counteracting academic extractivism and projecting Indigenous philosophies onto the global stage.

articles.title: The Growing Transatlantic Sanctions Divide
articles.authors: Anton Peez
articles.abstract: Multilateral cooperation on sanctions is a key determinant of their success, yet transatlantic collaboration on sanctions is steeply declining. This transatlantic sanctions divide is a symptom of increasingly divergent US and EU foreign policies. Sanctions are likewise best terminated multilaterally to effectively wield them as leverage. Here too, trustful US-EU collaboration is increasingly difficult to imagine. Nonetheless, strong public support for sanctioning Russia in both the EU and US offers a basis for continuing forceful Western sanctions as Russia escalates its war of aggression against Ukraine.

articles.title: FASTrack: A co-designed cloud-based planning support system for interactive cycling infrastructure scenario assessment
articles.authors: Ryan Turner; Afshin Jafari; Sapan Tiwari; Alan Both; Dhirendra Singh; Steve Pemberton; Chris De Gruyter
articles.abstract: Testing transport interventions using city-scale transport models is typically resource intensive, requiring specialist expertise, substantial data and computational capacity. As a result, such modelling is often concentrated on major projects and larger metropolitan areas, while smaller interventions and mid-sized regional cities have limited access to comparable modelling capabilities. This is particularly relevant to active travel, where cycling infrastructure decisions frequently need to be made with relatively limited modelling and decision-support capacity. This study presents FASTrack, a cloud-based planning support software system that integrates agent-based modelling, behavioural simulation, and interactive scenario visualisation to enable proposed cycling infrastructure assessment. A case study is applied to the City of Greater Bendigo, a mid-sized regional Australian city representative of the planning contexts that existing platforms often overlook. FASTrack was developed through a co-design process over three years with local government planning partners, to address the need to rapidly assess infrastructure scenarios, quantify changes in cycling demand and behaviour, and inform infrastructure planning and investment appraisal. These requirements underpin its design, including the use of probabilistic modelling and a cloud-based workflow designed to support rapid, on-demand scenario testing with minimal specialist modelling expertise. Scenario outcomes are presented through interactive dashboard-style interfaces that detail estimated changes in network use, level of traffic stress, mode shift, cycling usage, emissions, and cost-benefit analysis aligned with national appraisal guidelines. This study demonstrates how co-design can directly shape the development of planning support systems by translating practitioner requirements into accessible modelling platforms for cycling infrastructure planning

articles.title: "Platform Popular Culture": Concept Initiative, Theoretical Construction and Case Analysis
articles.authors: Shulun LIAO
articles.abstract: Against the backdrop of an increasingly platformized online culture and new forms of youth-led cultural practice, this study proposes platform popular culture as a mid-range theoretical concept, aiming to move beyond both the "mainstream culture–subculture" binary and the "resistance–incorporation" paradigm long dominant in subcultural analysis. Drawing on youth subculture studies, popular culture studies, and platformization research, the study develops three analytical toolkits: (1) the "negotiation–mutual constitution" relationship between platform popular culture and mainstream culture; (2) a logic of production shaped by the user–platform–capital triad; and (3) the cultural function of interpreting social hotspots. Empirically, it examines two typical cases from Rednote—the "Love Your Old Self" self-care meme and citywalk—combining longitudinal data monitoring with BERTopic modeling to analyze the emergence, circulation, and practice of both value-oriented and practice-oriented forms of platform popular culture. The findings validate the concept's theoretical value and cultural function, clarify the strengths and limitations of the proposed framework, and contribute to a more systematic research agenda on youth online culture while offering a fresh vantage point for studying the platformization of cultural production.

articles.title: Explaining the Decline of impal Marriage among the Karo: An Epidemiological Approach
articles.authors: Geoff Kushnick; Sam Passmore; Fikarwin Zuska; Karmila br. Karo; Daniel M.T. Fessler
articles.abstract: The Karo of North Sumatra, Indonesia, have long expressed a preference for matrilateral cross-cousin (impal) marriage, yet the practice has declined sharply over the past century. To identify the demographic and sociocultural factors underlying this change, we applied an epidemiological approach to cultural evolution, using a case-control design coupled with structural equation modeling (SEM). Ethnographic data from 176 married individuals across 62 villages were analyzed to assess the effects of demographic, alliance, religious, cosocialisation, and modernisation variables on the likelihood of impal marriage. The model fit was strong (CFI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.04), revealing significant direct and indirect effects. Marrying an impal was positively associated with the number of marriageable impal and with arranged or strategically motivated unions but negatively associated with reported religious conflict between spouses. Indicators of modernisation such as schooling and infrastructure were non-significant. These results indicate that the decline of impal marriage reflects demographic contraction and the weakening of alliance-based strategies rather than a rejection of the cultural norm itself. Framed within an epidemiological model of cultural transmission, the findings demonstrate how social practices may fade when the ecological and demographic conditions sustaining them erode, even as their normative value persists.

articles.title: Generational Imprinting: How Political Events Shape Cohorts
articles.authors: Turgut Keskintürk
articles.abstract: Contemporary narratives of generational politics propose that formative experiences produce shared political opinions across an age cohort. In this article, I advance a theory of cohortization to challenge that view, arguing that large-scale political events produce differentiation within cohorts as much as differentiation between them. I investigate the implications of this framework through the killing of George Floyd and the subsequent Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, analyzing attitudes toward law enforcement among non-Hispanic White Americans from 2016 to 2024. Using survey data from Cooperative Congressional Election Study, American National Election Study, and the Nationscape, I show that younger and older cohorts diverged after the event, but this differentiation was driven exclusively by young Democrats and Independents. The end result was not a unified generation, but one internally divided along party lines. This finding qualifies theories of generational politics, emphasizing that formative experiences may intensify existing political divisions within cohorts.

articles.title: Mapping the Discourse Network of Cervical Cancer Screening on Reddit: A Topic-Network Approach
articles.authors: Qiyao Peng
articles.abstract: Online health communities are a primary venue where the public interprets cervical cancer screening, yet how peer discourse, which has no editorial authority, bundles screening concerns remains unclear. Drawing on network agenda setting (NAS), this study treats a peer community as a collective agenda-setter and asks how it organizes screening topics. This paper analyzes 9,851 posts and comments from seven women's-health subreddits (August 2025 to January 2026) using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and the Analysis of Topic Model Networks, with Spearman topic-loading similarity filtered to a significant backbone. Thirteen topics form three communities: a diagnostic-information agenda, an embodied exam-experience agenda, and a narrative-and-support agenda. Embodied, temporally anchored concerns hold them together: timing and bleeding, pelvic pain, and access carry the highest betweenness. Sentiment follows network position, with support positive and cancer risk negative. These findings extend NAS to agenda-less, peer-driven settings and map how health agendas emerge from the bottom up.

articles.title: Generative AI and Society
articles.authors: Laura K. Nelson; Daniel Karell; Thomas Davidson
articles.abstract: For sociologists, generative AI inherits the legacy of earlier computational technologies: it is an advancement of machine learning already adopted as a methodology, and it intervenes in a society already shaped by algorithmic systems. Yet it also has a dimension that distinguishes it from previous computational methods, and one that makes it inherently sociological: its interactivity. In this review, we conceptualize the interactivity of generative AI and introduce a framework for understanding how it operates across individual, organizational, and institutional life. Specifically, the framework specifies how generative AI expands users, functions as a proxy for society, and expresses power, both in sociological practice and in society. We conclude by suggesting three dynamics driven by generative AI that sociology will face in the near future: the transformation of scientific practice, the reorganization of social interaction, and the acceleration of algorithmic governance.

articles.title: Able but unwilling? Mapping citizens’ political GenAI use through the lens of Expectancy-Value Theory
articles.authors: Michael van Straelen; Christopher Starke; Patrick van Erkel; Jessica Piotrowski; Nils Köbis
articles.abstract:
Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise and risk for democracy, yet little is known about how
citizens evaluate and adopt it for political purposes. Drawing on Expectancy-Value Theory
and Uses & Gratifications Theory, this study offers an initial account of political GenAI
adoption, mapping how citizens' cost-value perceptions and expectancy beliefs cluster into
distinct profiles. We investigate how these ‘expectancy-value profiles’ shape political GenAI
use. Using cross-sectional survey data from 947 Dutch respondents, we conduct a latent
profile analysis, identifying four profiles: optimists, cautious pragmatists, sceptics, and
indifferents. Profile differences stem largely from differing cost-value perceptions rather than
expectancy beliefs, suggesting the question is less about whether people feel able to use
GenAI, and more about whether they feel it is worth using. Across all profiles, cost
perceptions are high and political use is low, though optimists report significantly more use
than others. Individuals’ political dispositions predict usage but not profile membership and
among technological dispositions, trust in GenAI and belief in the machine heuristic predict
being an optimist. Findings raise concerns about uncalibrated trust among adopters.

articles.title: The Power of “We” in Science Funding and Publication
articles.authors: Lijian Peng; Wenwen Li; Yi Bu; Hao Peng
articles.abstract:
Linguistic communication supports all stages of scientific innovation. However, we have limited understanding of rhetorical strategies for facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science. 
Drawing on prior literature on the importance of personal pronouns in inter-personal communication, we examine the unique role of first-person plural pronouns (``We'' words, including ``we'', ``us'', ``our'') in science funding and publishing. 
Our study leverages the full sample of 13K grant proposals submitted to the Novo Nordisk Foundation and 47K research papers submitted to BMJO and ICLR between 2011 and 2024. 
We find a strong and universal positive association between ``we'' words and success rates even after accounting for important confounding factors related to content, novelty, and author impact.
Specifically, a one percentage point increase in the percentage of ``We'' words used in the full text is associated with a 36-51% increase in the odds of success for grants and papers.
Furthermore, we find that the effect of ``We'' is applicable to both editors and reviewers of BMJO papers that used the single-blind review and is predictive of more positive and engaging review feedback for ICLR papers that employed the double-blind review.
Crucially, a large-scale LLM-assisted computational experiment that replaces ``We'' words with demonstrative pronouns provides robust causal evidence of ``We'' words on paper acceptance.
Lastly, our causal mediation analysis shows that ``We'' words can lead to more acceptance mainly because they can increase the perceived teamwork, credibility, significance, and robustness in research evaluation.
By revealing the unique strength of ``We'' in facilitating the recognition of new ideas in science, our study highlights the importance of small but mighty linguistic choices in promoting knowledge discoveries and breakthroughs.

articles_hidden.title: You cannot decompose injustice: interaction, intersection, random effects and simple means in the evolution of MAIHDA
articles_hidden.authors: Juan Merlo
articles_hidden.abstract: Random effects intersectional analysis has promoted the multidimensional study of health inequalities, and the intersectional application of Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) is increasingly used to describe them. Its usual implementation fits an empty random effects model followed by a model adjusting for the variables that define the strata, and reads the remaining between-stratum variance as the intersectional effect. In this essay I trace how that convention grew, including my own contribution to it, and explain why my opinion has changed. Intersectionality, as originally formulated, is not about statistical interaction. The expression "more than the sum of its parts" refers to the uniqueness of a social position, not to an arithmetic operation. Intersectional strata are indivisible analytical units. I propose the term intact strata for strata kept whole in the analysis. I recall that random effects shrinkage describes a modelled population rather than the observed one, and present Simple-Means MAIHDA (S-MAIHDA) as the canonical design for the framework. Each stratum is estimated from its own individuals, and the three MAIHDA components, specific contextual effects (SCE), general contextual effects (GCE) and discriminatory accuracy (DA), are obtained on the probability scale. Keeping strata intact does not banish interaction. It relocates it, as effect modification between the intact stratum and the structural axes, such as geography, time or institution, along which the position is lived. You cannot decompose injustice. You can describe it whole, and you can measure what the structures around it do to it.

articles_hidden.title: Research on Gender Contradictions in Contemporary China: Structural Pressures, the Negativity of Marital Surplus, and the Gender Projection of Class Contradictions
articles_hidden.authors: Yuan Di; ZY Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Against the backdrop of a sustained decline in marriage and birth rates in China and intensifying gender tensions, traditional explanations centered on individual preferences or gender norms are insufficient to account for the structural mechanisms involved. Drawing on the economics of marriage and the family, this paper examines how rising costs of housing, weddings, bride price, childbearing, and education affect men's decisions to enter marriage, as well as how the expansion of higher education, the shortage of standardized professional employment, and the motherhood penalty shape women's opportunity costs associated with marriage. Building on these factors, together with declining expectations of economic growth, changing lifestyle expectations, and the rising utility of singlehood as an alternative, the paper proposes the “Dual Marriage Costs–Expectation Mismatch Integrated Model” (the Di Formula) and uses “marital surplus” to characterize the comprehensive net benefits of marriage relative to singlehood. The paper argues that contemporary gender relations in China involve more than a conflict of values, but separately rising direct marriage costs for men and opportunity costs for women, together with a widening structural mismatch between modernity-based expectations and real resource constraints. When marital surplus declines and eventually becomes negative, individually rational decisions to postpone or forgo marriage may, in aggregate, contribute to declining marriage and birth rates and intensified gender tensions. Marriage is therefore increasingly shifting from a traditional mechanism of family cooperation toward a high-cost, high-risk, long-term economic decision.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking nature dependencies and nature-related risks: integrated environmental-economic accounting in Australia
articles_hidden.authors: Crystal Bradley; Sarah Taylor; Michael Vardon; Mitchell Lyons; Sarah Clement; Carl Obst
articles_hidden.abstract: Ecosystems and the services they provide underpin economic production and human wellbeing, yet these dependencies are poorly measured and rarely monitored. As a result, conventional economic statistics often fail to show how ecosystem decline may threaten production and wellbeing. The missing information can be supplied by the United Nations System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA), an international statistical standard for tracking environmental stocks and flows, including ecosystems and their services, which is interoperable with the System of National Accounts (SNA). We assess how a linked system of SEEA and SNA accounts can be used to measure and track nature-economy dependencies, including the transmission of physical risk. We argue that accounting for ecosystem services provides the main connection between nature and the economy. The connection depends upon accounts using consistent classifications and typologies, which we call material join keys, so that information about ecosystems, ecosystem services, industries and economic activities can be reliably linked. Applying the approach to Australia, a gap analysis shows that existing ecosystem service accounts already track several of the dependencies most important and at risk from ecosystem decline, but only partially, and that priority new accounts for water and food security, health, climate resilience and supply chain resilience are needed to close the remaining gaps. Realising the potential of integrated accounting supports the mainstreaming of natural capital considerations into decision-making and public policy, and the proactive management of nature-related risks.

articles_hidden.title: Food Environment Policy Index for the German States: A structured policy analysis with expert consultations
articles_hidden.authors: Franziska Wiebke; Peter von Philipsborn; Anette E. Buyken
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Introduction
Subnational governments can play an important role in influencing food environments, particularly in multilevel governance systems such as Germany, where multiple levels can introduce policy and legislation. Yet the extent to which subnational governments, including the German States, use this potential remains largely unexplored. To make the scope of subnational food environment policies explicit, comparable and assessable, we developed a state-specific Food Environment Policy Index (Food-EPI), using Germany as an example. 
Methods
The INFORMAS Food-EPI served as the starting point for our analysis. To adapt it to the subnational level, we followed an iterative process drawing on four data sources: i) legal and policy documents and secondary sources; ii) key informant interviews; iii) written feedback from experts; and iv) an online expert workshop. 
Results
The state-specific Food-EPI covers 25 indicators across 12 domains, outlining the substantial scope of subnational governments to influence food environments. The policy domains are food labelling, advertising and marketing, subsidies, provision, retail and food service and waste, combined with six infrastructure support domains. We drew on 128 documents to identify 57 good practice examples from subnational governments and adapted the INFORMAS protocol into a streamlined four-step approach.
Conclusion
We demonstrate that it is feasible to develop a tool to assess food environment policy at the subnational level, that systematically outlines the substantial influence of subnational governments on food environments. Applying the state-specific Food-EPI in practice to German States is an important next step to further corroborate its practical relevance.

articles_hidden.title: The Economic Costs of Nepal's Open Border with India: A Case Study on Smuggling
articles_hidden.authors: Nirmal Gurung
articles_hidden.abstract:
The border between Nepal and India, which was opened in 1950 by the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, has created unprecedented conditions for developing cultural and social ties between the countries. However, the open border has also led to severe negative consequences for the national economy of Nepal. This research aims to discuss the effects of smuggling through the 1,880 km border and analyse the situation in the context of the foreign trade deficit and the deteriorating economic situation in the country.
Based on the data presented by the study, it is possible to draw the conclusion that smuggling contributes significantly to the trade deficit between Nepal and India. Smuggling of gold, drugs, agricultural products, and people constitutes a substantial part of trade between the countries. It is reported that 42.5% of the officially recorded trade between Nepal and India is smuggling, which results in a loss of 33.5 billion rupees for the Nepalese economy. In addition to the loss from unofficial trade, the state loses 3.58 billion rupees in duty and 3.71 billion rupees in value-added tax. The article also reports that the trade deficit in Nepal this year amounts to NPR 180 billion, of which a considerable part is caused by smuggling.
Thus, the current situation in which Nepal allows free trade between the countries is extremely disadvantageous for the national economy. The study provides multiple examples that prove the severity of the problem, including the cases of Badhaiyatal and Bardibas, where the largest seizures of marijuana, gold, and peas in recent years were registered. According to official data, 30,000 people are trafficked illegally into Nepal every year, resulting in significant losses for the economy. The causes of the problem include the initial policy of open borders, insufficient control mechanisms, corruption, and taxation issues. However, the authors of the article believe that a smart border is necessary to ensure the prosperity of the Nepalese economy through trade with India.

articles_hidden.title: A Reader’s Guide to the Rubin Report
articles_hidden.authors: John Levi Martin
articles_hidden.abstract: This was written for those readers of the Rubin report who are outsiders to the discipline of sociology, and look to this report as a guide to the state of this field.  Given the publicity this report has received, it would be reasonable for them to imagine that there is warrant for its claims.  There have been many responses to this report, but (as far as I know) none that have simply focused on whether she actually marshaled evidence to support her arguments, and whether she correctly represents her sources.

articles_hidden.title: Cities for Seasons - In favor of microclimate diversity as alternative to the parameter of total yearly comfort hours in competitively livable cities in temperate climates
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Ragnhof
articles_hidden.abstract:
Temperate cities compete to rank the world’s most livable, while competing under the same premise: A summer period with relatively abundant life on the streets, and a winter period with relatively sparse life on the streets, owing to cold stress.
Yet these cities – Copenhagen, London, New York, Melbourne, Paris, Vancouver, Vienna – have been implementing strategies that are directly detrimental to the elongation of their streets’ active seasons: Motivated by increasingly frequent and intense heat events, they have set out to mitigate urban heat island effects, aiming to eliminate any time that any surface exceeds the upper limit of the human thermal comfort range. But with no spatial or temporal limit to these strategies and guidelines – the approach is consistently the more heat island mitigation the better – these strategies inadvertently incentivize a
complete, systematic prevention of warm microclimates that, while they may be too hot during the heat waves, can be highly attractive the rest of the year.
Therefore this thesis employs a tri-seasonal rhythmanalysis to explore the dynamic use of places that are subject to urban heat island effects as well as of places which are subject to cooling effects. In the terminology of the author, these places together constitute an area with “high microclimate niche development”, which stands in contrast
to the areas with low niche development that are predictably reproduced when focusing on UHI mitigation, and when optimizing according to the parameter of total yearly comfort hours.
It finds that when the warm niches are accessible – like at south facing ‘soft edges’ of interactive buildings – they significantly extend the local active season: That in early spring, when people first move out of the buildings, they tend to gravitate toward the warm, south facing edges of these buildings, after which a spillover effect happens from these warm niches, into adjacent cooler niches, and back, throughout the days as well as the seasons, whereby the warm niches exhibit a pulsing, gravitational pull.
This descriptive model is synthesized into a prescriptive model and a series of preliminary methods of analysis, which aim to display and thereby enable assessment of microclimate diversity, and of synergy with complementary parameters. As proof of concept, these models are used to formulate re-designs. 
This approach is found to synergize with contemporary approaches for flood mitigation and for biodiversity, but demands one key shift: acknowledging that, in temperate cities, heat islands can play a substantial positive role. It argues that this shift appears as the logical conclusion of the development started by Jan Gehl when he defended the import of the (at the time) uniquely Mediterranean café culture to ‘cold’ northern Europe. It predicts that this shift may transform urban life in temperate cities in a similarly profound way.

articles_hidden.title: kîkway itôtaman ôta Dante? The nine circles of community-engaged Indigenous research hell
articles_hidden.authors: Malcolm Cole Disbrowe
articles_hidden.abstract: Research involving Indigenous Peoples has historically been harmful to Indigenous Peoples and their communities. In recent years, however, growing public awareness of Indigenous Peoples' experiences and histories through national and international initiatives has made research involving Indigenous Peoples much more equitable. However, in this renaissance of change, researchers who work with Indigenous communities and use community-engaged methodologies often rely on terms such as relational, co-designed, collaborative, and community-engaged. This reliance is not a reliable indicator that Indigenous communities themselves have meaningful authority over research that affects them and the knowledges they share. Because of this, I take a satirical, slightly humorous approach, drawing on Dante's Inferno and Neuroskeptic's Nine Circles of Scientific Hell to elucidate recurring issues in research involving Indigenous Peoples, more specifically research that uses, or seems to use, community-engaged methodologies. In the article, I conceptualize the nine circles while identifying problems that recur in community-engaged research involving Indigenous Peoples. These problems encompass tokenistic engagement, late or forced consultation, extractive relationships, pan-Indigenization, having Indigenous advisory bodies without decision-making power, checkbox approaches to Indigenous methodologies/frameworks, possessive relationships to data, poor knowledge return, and helicopter research. This article thus uses satire to make already existing contradictions around authority, accountability, governance, reciprocity, and relationships harder to ignore and to show that “relational” language is not enough, especially if Indigenous communities are not given meaningful authority to shape research projects involving themselves or their knowledges.

articles_hidden.title: ANTHROPOLOGY, COMPLEXITY AND THE LIMITS OF TOP-DOWN CONFLICT ANALYSIS
articles_hidden.authors: Eleonora Zanetti
articles_hidden.abstract:
Conflict analysis often approaches violence through externally defined categories, scales, and institutional frameworks that simplify complex social relations into identifiable problems and corresponding interventions. Similarly, contemporary localization paradigms seek to bring analysis, decision-making, and intervention closer to affected communities. Yet treating “the local” as a given and bounded site of action can obscure the relations of power through which local social worlds, conflicts, and capacities to act are themselves produced. The problem, I argue, is not only the use of externally defined categories to describe conflict, but also the analytical separation of the local from the wider relations through which it is constituted.
Drawing on long-term ethnographic research among Rendille pastoralists in northern Kenya, I propose an approach that does not treat the community or conflict as a bounded system, but instead reconstructs how actors themselves distinguish forms of violence and the different forms of power through which they are produced and governed, including physical force, symbolic power, and control over information. The ethnographic case shows how resource disputes, ethnic conflict, livestock raiding, political competition, and cross-border processes constitute analytically distinct but increasingly interconnected domains as relationships among socially differentiated actors and their access to different forms of power change across scales. Changes in one domain can alter the conditions through which conflict is interpreted and governed in another, while broader political, economic, ecological, and geopolitical processes are incorporated into local relations and transformed through them.
I argue that complexity emerges not from the simple interconnectedness of everything, or from the number of actors and factors involved, but from changing relationships among systems of order, forms of power, temporalities, and scales. The local is therefore not treated as a pre-existing scale, but as an empirical configuration produced through these relations. Methodologically, I propose an emic, participatory, and multiscalar approach in which ethnographic reconstruction precedes formal modeling. Complexity-science methods, including participatory mapping, System Dynamics, network analysis, and other quantitative approaches, can then formalize and investigate dynamics identified ethnographically, such as feedback, interdependence, emergence, and nonlinearity. This provides a methodological pathway from the emic to the systemic: beginning with local relations to reconstruct how power operates, how processes connect across scales and temporalities, and where change can actually occur.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Validation as a Bandwidth Criterion for Geographically Weighted PCA: An Ethics of Ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Kampfschulte
articles_hidden.abstract:
Geographically weighted principal component analysis (GWPCA) summarizes
spatial multivariate structure through local eigen decompositions whose
output depends strongly on a bandwidth, conventionally chosen by
leave-one-out cross-validation (CV). While locating the bandwidth that minimizes CV, several competing minima are frequently observed. We focus on the implications of multiple ambiguous minima as the
object of study. We formalize it through the CV-equivalent set
($H_{\mathrm{CV}}$) of bandwidths that the data do not distinguish from the
CV minimum ($h_{CV}$) and show that bandwidths within this set differ materially in
their bias--variance composition and loading structure. Simulations across eight data-generating processes show that wherever the covariance subspace varied locally, the
equivalent set spanned roughly a quarter of the candidate range
grid, and the oracle bandwidth typically lay inside the set while
differing from $h_{CV}$. In applications to the Dublin voter
turnout and the Kola geochemical survey, the same ambiguity appeared,
and within-set disagreement between local loadings concentrated where
the local eigengap was small. We offer these findings as the first in-depth study of the characteristics of CV as used in GWPCA, and recommend reporting standards to include the equivalent set, and mapping the local eigengap.

articles_hidden.title: Missing Victims, Hidden Crimes: Improving Estimates of Honor Killings Using Missing Data Imputation
articles_hidden.authors: Mariel Leonard; Teresa Koenig
articles_hidden.abstract:
Very little accurate data on the incidence and prevalence of honor killings exists. While some countries have made strides to identify and track cases on an ongoing basis, many countries either have no official statistics or rely on outdated data and imprecise methodologies. More accurate and up-to-date statistics are needed to better direct resources, identify cases and behaviors for study and intervention, and reduce biases. Unfortunately, measuring honor killings is methodologically difficult. However, while single lists of honor killings cannot accurately estimate the number of events, two or more lists in combination can, using multi-systems estimation (MSE).
In this paper, we test the application of MSE to honor killings in four countries: Canada, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States by comparing estimates from MSE to counts of cases produced by aggregating multiple lists from each country. We find that MSE produces plausible estimates that demonstrate that even in seemingly complete lists of individuals or cases underestimate the scope of honor killings in these countries.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Europe’s Digital Acquis. A Granular History of EU Digital Policymaking
articles_hidden.authors: Timo Seidl; Nir Kosti
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the last decade, digital policy has moved to the center of EU policymaking. Yet we have little systematic knowledge of how much of it the EU has produced, where it is made, or what it does. We map the EU's digital acquis from 1979 to today: we decompose every regulation, directive, and decision into nearly two million recitals and (sub-)articles and classify each with a two-stage pipeline that distills a human-validated ensemble of large language models into open encoder models. The share of digital provisions in newly adopted legislation rose from under one percent in the 1980s to roughly one in ten, and most sit outside the flagship digital acts. Testing two prominent claims, we show that digital legislation has become more assertive over time, with its obligations and prohibitions falling increasingly on private actors, and that it is more rights-oriented than the rest of EU law yet still more market- than rights-oriented, with the rights it invokes being mostly civil. We release our provision-level dataset, classification models, and a Python package for building granular legislative corpora: open infrastructure for measuring not just how much legislation there is, but what it says and does.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Employment in Mothers’ Careers After First Birth: A Comparison of South Korea and the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Wonjeong Jeong
articles_hidden.abstract: Motherhood can reorganize women’s paid work across wage employment, self-employment, and nonemployment. Yet research on mothers’ employment trajectories has rarely examined self-employment as a distinct arrangement. This paper asks where self-employment appears in mothers’ careers after first birth and how its position differs between South Korea and the United States. Using the Korean Labor and Income Panel Study and the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, I follow first-time mothers from the year of first birth through ten years afterward. Descriptive and sequence analyses show that roughly one in five mothers experiences self-employment at least once, although neither country has a continuous self-employment trajectory. In Korea, self-employment more often follows nonemployment and is primarily full-time, appearing within trajectories that lead back into paid work. In the United States, mothers more often enter self-employment from wage work, and part-time self-employment also appears briefly within wage-centered trajectories. These differences show that the same employment status can occupy different positions in mothers’ careers. Self-employment is likely to become increasingly important within workers’ careers as gig and platform work expand and artificial intelligence reshapes occupations and industries. Future research should examine how these changes alter pathways into self-employment and how labor protections, social insurance, and family-support policies can account for its distinctive risks and rewards.

articles_hidden.title: Can Ethnic Divisions Explain  Poor Economic Growth in  Resource Rich Countries? The Case of the Middle East
articles_hidden.authors: Sinem Acar-Burkay
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper addresses the question of the effects of ethnic diversity on economic growth. It extends the cross-country growth regressions in Easterly and Levine (1997) by allowing for growth effects of natural resources to depend on the amount of ethnic fractionalization to see if ethnic diversity, natural resource abundance, and the interaction of the two can explain Middle Eastern Countries' poor economic performance. And, the answer is found to be “yes”: The resource curse applies in ethnically heterogeneous countries but not in homogenous ones.

articles_hidden.title: Toward non-textual representation of social anthropology: Modeling cultures as knowledge graphs
articles_hidden.authors: Manolis Peponakis; Sarantos Kapidakis; Martin Doerr; Eirini Tountasaki
